data.value: At this voltage the current is small enough that the wires stay cool, and only a small share of the power turns into heat on the way.

data.name: Grid_Line_High_Description
data.value: The current is large, and the heat in the wires goes with its square. Raise the voltage, or send less, or not so far.

data.name: Grid_Line_Impossible
data.value: Can't be done: more than half would be lost

data.name: Grid_Line_Impossible_Description
data.value: So much current would flow that over half the power would be lost and the voltage at the far end would collapse. That's why long lines need high voltage.

data.name: Grid_Line_Overloaded
data.value: {0} A per wire, but the limit is {1} A

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Fact1
data.value: The heat in a wire grows with the square of the current. Send the same power at ten times the voltage and the loss falls a hundredfold.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Fact2
data.value: China's AC voltage ladder runs 10, 35, 110, 220, 330, 500, 750 and 1000 kV; its DC lines go up to ±1100 kV.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Fact3
data.value: The ±1100 kV DC line from Changji in Xinjiang to Guquan in Anhui is about 3,300 km long and can carry 12 GW.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Fact4
data.value: Very long lines often use DC: no current sloshes back and forth, and two conductors are enough. But the converter stations at each end are costly.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Fact5
data.value: Across a whole grid, roughly 5% of the electricity is lost on its way through lines and transformers.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Note
data.value: The line is squeezed: a few pylons stand for hundreds of kilometres. The same wires are used at every voltage.

data.name: Grid_Transmission_Subtitle
data.value: Why power travels at high voltage

data.name: Heat_Chart_Eff_Caption
data.value: How much of the fuel's heat becomes work

data.name: Heat_Chart_Eff_Note
data.value: The ideal value depends only on the compression ratio: η = 1 − r^(−0.4). A real engine also loses to the time the burning takes, the early exhaust, the cooled walls and friction; about 30% reaches the wheels.

data.name: Heat_Chart_Energy_Caption
data.value: Electricity a day against the room's temperature

data.name: Heat_Chart_Energy_Note
data.value: In a warmer room more heat seeps into the cabinet, so the compressor runs longer; and the condenser has to be hotter to get rid of it, so each unit of electricity moves less heat.

data.name: Heat_Chart_Limit_Caption
data.value: The limits between these two temperatures

data.name: Heat_Chart_Limit_Note
data.value: Carnot showed in 1824 that no machine working between two temperatures can beat these. Real ones: car engines 30–40%, the best gas-and-steam power stations about 60%, fridges a coefficient of 1.5–2, air-source heat pumps 2.5–4 in winter.

data.name: Heat_Chart_Loop_Caption
data.value: The refrigerant's temperature round the loop

data.name: Heat_Chart_Loop_Note
data.value: Heat only flows from hot to cold. So in the condenser the refrigerant has to be hotter than the room (red), and in the evaporator colder than the freezer (blue). The compressor and the capillary tube make it so.

data.name: Heat_Chart_Pv_Note
data.value: From the spark until the exhaust valve opens, the gas pushes the piston and does work: the area inside the loop is the work of one cycle. The thin loop along the bottom is breathing in and out, which costs a little.

data.name: Heat_Compression_Hint
data.value: Squeeze harder and the same fuel does more work; too hard and it knocks. Petrol engines use 9–13.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Area_Work
data.value: area inside = work out each cycle

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Area_WorkIn
data.value: area inside = work put in each cycle

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Fact1
data.value: In 1824 the 28-year-old French engineer Sadi Carnot showed that the best an engine can do depends only on the two temperatures: 1 − T cold / T hot, in kelvin.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Fact2
data.value: That is why power stations push their steam hotter and hotter: steam at 567 °C (840 K) and cooling water at 27 °C give an ideal 64%; the best real coal plants reach about 45%.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Fact3
data.value: A fridge and a heat pump are the same machine; what differs is which side is wanted. An air conditioner cools in summer and heats in winter by switching one valve so that the refrigerant goes round the other way.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Fact4
data.value: A heat pump puts several times more heat into a house than the electricity it uses: the rest is drawn from the cold outdoor air. Energy is still conserved; the electricity only moves the heat.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Fact5
data.value: The closer the two temperatures, the less an engine can do, but the easier a fridge or heat pump has it: with no difference at all an ideal heat pump's coefficient grows without limit. That is why heat pumps pay best in mild winters.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Note
data.value: The Carnot cycle of an ideal gas: two isothermal and two adiabatic steps, with no friction and no heat crossing a temperature gap. No real machine can do better.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step0_Backward
data.value: Isothermal compression: gives heat to the hot side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step0_Backward_Description
data.value: Touching the hot side, the squeezing goes on and the heat flows out into it. Heat out = heat taken in + work put in, which is why a fridge's back gives out more heat than it takes from the inside.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step0_Forward
data.value: Isothermal expansion: takes heat in from the hot side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step0_Forward_Description
data.value: The gas touches the hot side. It expands, pushing the piston out and doing work, and takes in just as much heat from the hot side, so its temperature stays the same.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step1_Backward
data.value: Adiabatic compression: hotter than the hot side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step1_Backward_Description
data.value: Insulated, the gas is squeezed: the motor does work on it and it warms above the hot side, so that its heat can flow out. This is the compressor's job.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step1_Forward_Description
data.value: Insulated now, the gas keeps expanding. It does the work out of its own energy, so it cools all the way down to the cold side's temperature.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step2_Backward
data.value: Isothermal expansion: takes heat out of the cold side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step2_Backward_Description
data.value: Touching the cold side, the gas expands and takes heat out of it. This is how a fridge makes its inside cold, and how a heat pump takes heat from the winter air.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step2_Forward
data.value: Isothermal compression: gives heat to the cold side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step2_Forward_Description
data.value: Touching the cold side, the gas is squeezed. Squeezing would warm it, but the heat flows straight into the cold side. This heat given away is the loss no engine can avoid.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step3_Backward
data.value: Adiabatic expansion: colder than the cold side

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step3_Backward_Description
data.value: Run backwards, the gas first expands with no heat going in or out. It gets colder than the cold side, so that heat will flow in from it by itself. A fridge's capillary tube does this job.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step3_Forward
data.value: Adiabatic compression: warms back to the start

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Step3_Forward_Description
data.value: Insulated again, the squeezing warms the gas back to the hot side's temperature and the cycle is closed. Expanding while hot and squeezing while cold, it gets more work out than it puts in: the difference is the net work.

data.name: Heat_Cycle_Subtitle
data.value: One cycle: forwards it is an engine, backwards a fridge

data.name: Heat_Direction_Fridge
data.value: Fridge: pumps heat out of the cold

data.name: Heat_Direction_HeatPump
data.value: Heat pump: pumps heat into the warm

data.name: Heat_Engine_AltitudeNote
data.value: {0} is about {1} m up: the air pressure is {2} hPa, {3}% of sea level's, so each intake stroke draws in that much less air and the engine gives that much less power.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Burning_Description
data.value: About 20° before the top the plug sparks. The flame front races outwards at tens of metres a second and has burned the charge within about 50° of the crank. The gas heats to over 2000 °C and the pressure leaps past 50 bar.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Burning_Title
data.value: The spark: a flame spreads out from the middle

data.name: Heat_Engine_Compression_Description
data.value: The piston squeezes the mixture into about a tenth of its space. Squeezed gas gets hot: by the spark it is already near 350 °C at about 14 bar. The harder it is squeezed, the more work the burning will give.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Compression_Title
data.value: 2 Compression: both valves shut, the piston goes up

data.name: Heat_Engine_Exhaust_Description
data.value: The exhaust valve opens before the power stroke ends, and most of the gas rushes out under its own pressure; the piston pushes out the rest. It is still at 700–800 °C: about a third of the fuel's energy leaves by the exhaust pipe.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Exhaust_Title
data.value: 4 Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens, the piston pushes the gas out

data.name: Heat_Engine_Fact1
data.value: A car usually has four of these cylinders, firing in turn, so that one of them is on its power stroke every half turn of the crank. That is what makes it run smoothly.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Fact2
data.value: At 3000 rpm each cylinder fires 25 times a second; the piston averages about 9 m/s and stops and turns round 100 times a second.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Fact3
data.value: Nicolaus Otto built the first working four-stroke engine in 1876, so its ideal cycle is the Otto cycle. A diesel has no spark plug: it squeezes air to a sixteenth or twentieth, hot enough to light the diesel sprayed in.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Fact4
data.value: Roughly a third of the fuel's energy moves the car, a third is carried by the coolant to the radiator, and a third leaves with the exhaust.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Fact5
data.value: The higher up, the thinner the air: in Lhasa, 3650 m up, the pressure is about 64% of sea level's and an engine without a turbo gives about two thirds of its power. A turbocharger uses the exhaust to spin a turbine that blows more air into the cylinders.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Intake_Description
data.value: The intake valve is open. As the piston goes down it makes room in the cylinder, and the air outside, carrying a fine mist of petrol, is pushed in by the atmosphere. The pressure inside is a little below the outside's.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Intake_Title
data.value: 1 Intake: the piston goes down, drawing in air and petrol

data.name: Heat_Engine_Note
data.value: One cylinder of a 2.0-litre four-cylinder petrol engine cut down the middle, to scale (86 mm bore and stroke). The gas's colour shows its temperature; pressures and temperatures come from a simplified model of the burning. Much slower than real.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Power_Description
data.value: The only stroke of the four that gives work out. The expanding gas pushes the piston, and the rod turns the crank; expanding, the gas cools and its pressure falls. The flywheel stores the push and carries the engine through the other three strokes.

data.name: Heat_Engine_Power_Title
data.value: 3 Power: the hot gas drives the piston down

data.name: Heat_Engine_Subtitle
data.value: A four-stroke engine: in, squeeze, bang, out

data.name: Heat_Fridge_DoorOpen_Description
data.value: Cold air is heavier: it spills out at the bottom of the doorway while warm room air comes in at the top. The compressor runs all the time and still cannot keep up. Nor does an open fridge cool the room: the back gives out more heat than the inside takes in.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_DoorOpen_Title
data.value: The door is open: cold air pours out

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Fact1
data.value: A fridge cannot make cold. It is a heat pump that carries the heat from inside to outside; cold is only less heat.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Fact2
data.value: With 1 kWh of electricity this fridge carries about 6 MJ of heat out of the inside: enough to turn about 14 kg of water at 25 °C into ice at 0 °C.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Fact3
data.value: At low pressure a refrigerant boils very cold: isobutane boils at −12 °C at normal air pressure, and at about −25 °C on the fridge's low side (0.6 bar). It is the same as water boiling below 100 °C on a high plateau, put to use.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Fact4
data.value: Early fridges used CFCs ("freon"), which destroy the ozone layer; the Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased them out. Most household fridges now use isobutane, which harms no ozone and adds very little to global warming.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Fact5
data.value: Leave a gap round a fridge: the condenser has to give its heat to the air. Pushed against a wall or beside a cooker, it uses noticeably more electricity.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Hot_Description
data.value: The condenser has to be hotter than the room to lose its heat, so the compressor squeezes harder and each unit of electricity moves less heat; meanwhile more heat seeps in through the walls, so it runs longer. Do not box a fridge into an airless corner.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Hot_Title
data.value: A hot room: the fridge works harder

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Label_Capillary
data.value: Capillary tube: pressure falls from {0} to {1} bar

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Label_Hot
data.value: Heat given out to the {0} °C room

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Note
data.value: A fridge-freezer cut open from the side, roughly to scale (1.8 m tall). The refrigerant is isobutane (R600a): hollow bubbles are vapour, solid drops are liquid, the colour is its temperature. The tubes' layout is a sketch.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Running_Description
data.value: In the evaporator in the freezer's wall the refrigerant boils, taking heat from the food and the air. The compressor squeezes the vapour hot and sends it to the condenser on the back, where it gives the heat to the room and turns liquid. Through the thin capillary its pressure falls, it turns cold, and goes back to the evaporator. Feel the sides or back of a fridge: they are warm.

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Running_Title
data.value: The compressor is carrying heat out to the back

data.name: Heat_Fridge_Subtitle
data.value: A fridge does not make cold: it carries heat out round the back

data.name: Heat_Hint_Cycle
data.value: Drag left or right to move round the cycle

data.name: Heat_Hint_Engine
data.value: Drag left or right to turn the crank by hand

data.name: Heat_Hint_Fridge
data.value: Click the door to open or shut it

data.name: Heat_Lesson_Cycle_Choice1
data.value: Make the hot side hotter, or the cold side colder

data.name: Heat_Lesson_Engine_Choice1
data.value: It burns in an instant, and the pressure leaps

data.name: Heat_Lesson_Fridge_Choice1
data.value: It gives its heat to the room and turns liquid

data.name: Heat_Lesson_Fridge_Choice2
data.value: It takes in heat from the room

data.name: Heat_Obj_Loop
data.value: The loop on the p-V chart

data.name: Heat_Stat_Daily_Value
data.value: {0} kWh a day, about {1} kWh a year

data.name: Heat_Stat_Duty_Always
data.value: all the time, and still cannot keep up

data.name: Heat_Stat_Duty_Value
data.value: {0}% of the time, about {1} minutes an hour

data.name: Heat_Stat_HeatOut_Value
data.value: {0} W taken out + {1} W electricity = {2} W given out

data.name: Heat_Stat_PerHundred_Engine
data.value: of 100 units of heat taken in, at most {0} become work and at least {1} are given out

data.name: Heat_Stat_PerHundred_Fridge
data.value: for 100 units of work, up to {0} units of heat out of the cold side, {1} to the warm side

data.name: Heat_Stat_PerHundred_HeatPump
data.value: for 100 units of work, up to {0} units of heat delivered indoors, {1} of them from outside

data.name: Heat_Stat_Slowdown_Value
data.value: really {0} cycles a second; shown about {1} times slower

data.name: Heat_Timeline_Engine
data.value: Crank angle (a cycle is two turns)

data.name: Hole_Chart_Lensing_Caption
data.value: How much brighter the source looks

data.name: Hole_Chart_Lensing_Note
data.value: As the hole drifts along its track, the light from the source's middle is focused and it brightens, then fades again. Click or drag the chart to move the hole.

data.name: Hole_Chart_Orbits_Caption
data.value: The probe's energy and the hill it must climb

data.name: Hole_Chart_Orbits_Note
data.value: The curves are the effective potential for the probe's spin round the hole. The blue line is its energy: where the line is above the curve, it can go. Einstein's curve has a top near the hole that Newton's lacks; above it, the probe falls in.

data.name: Hole_Chart_Shadow_Note
data.value: The closer light passes, the more it is turned. Below 5.2 M it is caught: that is the edge of the shadow. The dashed line is Einstein's rule for light passing far away, 4M/b.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Lensing
data.value: Drag the black hole across the sky, or click anywhere to put it there.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Orbits
data.value: Drag the probe to move its start, or drag its green arrow to launch it your own way.

data.name: Hole_Hint_Shadow
data.value: Drag up or down on the picture to tilt the view.

data.name: Hole_Label_Hat
data.value: Far side of the disk, bent over the top

data.name: Hole_Lens_Far_Text
data.value: Far from the line to the source, the hole bends its light only a little: the picture is nudged outwards round the hole, like looking through the foot of a wine glass.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Inside_Text
data.value: The source is now within one Einstein radius of the line: both images sit close to the ring and the light is strongly focused.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Near_Text
data.value: The source is stretched round the hole into an arc, and a second, smaller image appears on the other side. Together they are brighter than the source alone.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Off_Text
data.value: This is the sky as it really is. Switch the bending back on to see what the black hole does to it.

data.name: Hole_Lens_Ring_Text
data.value: Lined up exactly, the light comes round every side alike, and the source becomes a complete ring round the hole.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact1
data.value: In 1919, during a total eclipse, Arthur Eddington measured stars near the Sun shifted by 1.75 arcseconds, as Einstein predicted, twice what Newton's ideas gave. It made Einstein famous overnight.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact2
data.value: The first lensed quasar, found in 1979, appeared as two identical 'twins' side by side: one quasar seen twice through a galaxy in front of it.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact3
data.value: Galaxy clusters bend the light of galaxies far behind them into long arcs. How much they bend shows how much mass they hold: far more than their stars, most of it dark matter.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact4
data.value: In 2022 astronomers announced the first lone black hole found by lensing: about 7 Suns, 5000 light years away, seen when it made a background star brighten for months.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Fact5
data.value: A supernova seen through a lensing cluster in 2014 appeared four times at once. Astronomers predicted it would appear once more, by a longer path, and it did, in 2015.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Note
data.value: Not to scale: the black hole itself is far too small to see, and the bending is hugely enlarged.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Panel_Note
data.value: The real ring's size depends on the lens: about a thousandth of an arcsecond for a star-sized hole, arcseconds for a galaxy.

data.name: Hole_Lensing_Subtitle
data.value: A black hole far away bends the light behind it

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Orbits_Choice3
data.value: They run at the same pace

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Shadow_Choice1
data.value: The gas there is moving towards us

data.name: Hole_Lesson_Shadow_Choice3
data.value: That side is closer to us

data.name: Hole_Obj_Hat
data.value: The far side, bent over the top

data.name: Hole_Obj_Inner
data.value: The inner edge of the disk

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Circle_Text
data.value: At 10 M the probe circles steadily, as a planet circles a star. Newton's probe, started the same way, swings out on an ellipse: this close in, gravity pulls harder than Newton's law says. Far out, the two agree.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Custom_Text
data.value: Watch the chart: if the blue energy line is below the hill near the hole, the probe is held in orbit; above it, the probe falls in, unless it is fast enough to escape.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Escape_Text
data.value: With more energy than it needs, the probe flies off and never comes back, bent a little as it leaves.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Escaped_Text
data.value: The probe is heading out for good. Far from the hole, gravity is weak and its clock runs almost at the far clock's pace again.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Isco_Text
data.value: At 6 M, three times the horizon's radius, is the last circle a probe can keep to. A tiny nudge inwards and it spirals in. Newton's probe, given the same start, never would.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Lost_Text
data.value: The probe has crossed the event horizon and can never send anything out again. Its own clock kept ticking, but seen from far away it would seem to slow, redden and freeze at the edge.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Plunge_Text
data.value: Newton's probe swings close and comes back out. The real one has too little spin to get over the top of the potential near the hole, so it plunges in.

data.name: Hole_Orbit_Rosette_Text
data.value: Newton's probe goes round the same ellipse every time. The real one swings round further at each close pass, so its ellipse turns and traces a rosette.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact1
data.value: Far from a black hole, it pulls just like a star of the same mass. If the Sun became a black hole, the Earth would keep going round it exactly as before (in the dark).

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact2
data.value: Mercury's orbit turns a little more each century than Newton predicts, 43 arcseconds. Einstein's theory explained this in 1915: the same turning as the rosette here, only much smaller.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact3
data.value: Closer in than three times the horizon's radius, there is no steady circular orbit. Gas reaching that line spirals in, so disks round black holes have a sharp inner edge.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact4
data.value: Gravity slows time even on Earth. GPS satellites higher up gain about 45 microseconds a day from weaker gravity (and lose 7 from their speed); without correcting for it, GPS would drift by kilometres a day.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Fact5
data.value: Falling into a small black hole, the pull on your feet would be so much stronger than on your head that you would be stretched like spaghetti. At a giant one you would cross the horizon without feeling anything.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Note
data.value: Seen from above, in units of the hole's mass M (for 10 Suns, 1 M is 15 km). Gold follows Einstein's gravity, grey follows Newton's.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Panel_Note
data.value: Both probes start the same way. Speeds are fractions of the speed of light.

data.name: Hole_Orbits_Subtitle
data.value: How a black hole bends light and steers orbits

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Above_Text
data.value: Looking down on the disk, it is a glowing ring with the shadow in the middle. Its inner edge is the innermost stable orbit; closer than that, gas falls straight in.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Edge_Text
data.value: The disk crosses in front of the hole as a thin band, yet you also see its far side, bent up over the top, and its underside, bent round below. The side coming towards you is brighter.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact1
data.value: A black hole is mass packed so tightly that not even light can climb out. Its boundary, the event horizon, is not a surface: just the point of no return.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact2
data.value: Squeeze the Earth into a ball about 18 mm across, smaller than a marble, and it becomes a black hole. The Sun would need to be just 6 km across.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact3
data.value: The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the Earth into one Earth-sized telescope. It showed the shadow of M87* in 2019 and of Sagittarius A* in 2022.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact4
data.value: The shadow is about 2.6 times as wide as the horizon. Light bent round the hole makes it look much bigger than it is.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Fact5
data.value: The black hole in the film Interstellar was worked out the same way, by tracing light rays. The film left out the Doppler effect, so both sides of its disk look equally bright.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Flat_Text
data.value: Now both sides glow alike, as in the film Interstellar. Only gravity's own redshift is left: light climbing out from near the hole loses energy and looks redder and dimmer.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_NoDisk_Text
data.value: Without gas, a black hole is a black patch on the sky. Round its edge the stars behind it are bent and stretched into a warped mirror of the whole sky.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_NoDisk_Title
data.value: Just the hole and the stars

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Note
data.value: Ray traced: each pixel's light is followed back along its real, bent path. The disk's colours are shifted into visible light.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Panel_Note
data.value: The picture is the same for any black hole that does not spin; only its size changes. Pick one to see its real size.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Straight_Text
data.value: Without bending, you would see a flat disk and a small black ball, the horizon at its real size. The arch, the rings and the big shadow are all made by gravity bending light.

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Subtitle
data.value: What a black hole looks like up close

data.name: Hole_Shadow_Tilted_Text
data.value: The disk looks like a tilted ring, but the far side is lifted up and bent towards you, so the hole is framed by light all the way round.

data.name: Hole_Side_Title
data.value: Seen from the side (not to scale)

data.name: Hole_Value_RingBright
data.value: spread into a ring, hugely brighter

data.name: HowTo_Contents
data.value: Lost your place? The Contents button takes you back to the table of contents.

data.name: HowTo_Explore
data.value: Each chapter is one spread: read on the left, explore on the right. Click anything in a picture to find out what it is.

data.name: HowTo_Listen
data.value: Every lesson can be read aloud. Switch between English and Chinese at the top at any time.

data.name: HowTo_Turn
data.value: Turn a page: drag the outer edge of a page, click it, or press the left and right arrow keys.

data.name: Ice_Chart_Ice
data.value: Northern ice (last glacial maximum = 1) and sea level

data.name: Ice_Chart_Orbit_Caption
data.value: Midsummer sunshine from the equator to the pole

data.name: Ice_Chart_Orbit_Note
data.value: Gold: the time shown, with only the chosen cycle changing. Dashed: today. Most of the change is near the pole.

data.name: Ice_Chart_OutOfWindow
data.value: the time shown is outside this window

data.name: Ice_Chart_Sheet_Caption
data.value: The last ice age: the ice and the ground under it

data.name: Ice_Chart_Sheet_Note
data.value: White: the ice. Orange: how far the ground has sunk, as the ice it has caught up with. The ground lags thousands of years behind. Click or drag to move through time.

data.name: Ice_Chart_Sunshine_Caption
data.value: Sunshine at 65° N through the year

data.name: Ice_Chart_Sunshine_Note
data.value: Gold: the time shown. Dashed: today. When perihelion falls in northern summer, the summer peak is higher and the winter lower.

data.name: Ice_Cycle_All_Text
data.value: The orbit's stretch, the axis's tilt and its wobble all change at once, each at its own pace. Together they move the summer sunshine in the far north up and down by about 10%, and that is what paces the ice ages.

data.name: Ice_Cycle_Eccentricity_Text
data.value: Jupiter and Saturn tug the orbit from nearly round to slightly oval and back, every 100,000 and 405,000 years. On its own it hardly changes the year's sunshine, but it decides how much the wobble matters.

data.name: Ice_Cycle_Precession_Text
data.value: The axis turns round like a spinning top's, so the date of perihelion moves through the year: now early January, 11,000 years ago in northern summer. Northern summers are strongest when they come at perihelion.

data.name: Ice_Cycle_Tilt_Text
data.value: Every 41,000 years the axis leans from 22.1° to 24.5° and back. A bigger tilt gives the poles more summer sun and less winter sun: stronger seasons, and summers that melt more snow.

data.name: Ice_Gauge_TiltPeriod
data.value: 22.1° to 24.5° and back in about 41,000 years

data.name: Ice_Hint_Orbit
data.value: Drag sideways, or along the strip, to move through time. Click a gauge to watch that cycle alone.

data.name: Ice_Hint_Sheet
data.value: Drag sideways, or along the strip, to move through time. Click the snow line, the ground or the coast.

data.name: Ice_Hint_Sunshine
data.value: Drag along either chart to move through time. Click a red number to jump to the end of that ice age.

data.name: Ice_Lesson_Orbit_Choice1
data.value: Warmer: more sun near the pole

data.name: Ice_Lesson_Orbit_Choice2
data.value: Cooler: the Sun is farther away

data.name: Ice_Lesson_Sheet_Choice1
data.value: It reflects sunlight, and its top is high and cold

data.name: Ice_Lesson_Sheet_Choice3
data.value: It pulls Earth farther from the Sun

data.name: Ice_Lesson_Sunshine_Choice1
data.value: Snow stays all summer and piles up

data.name: Ice_Obj_Coast
data.value: The coast and the sea level

data.name: Ice_Obj_SummerHalf
data.value: The two halves of the year

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Fact1
data.value: Milutin Milanković, a Serbian engineer, worked out these cycles and the sunshine they make by hand in the 1920s and 1930s.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Fact2
data.value: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, at 147 million km, and farthest in early July, at 152 million km: about 7% more sunlight in January.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Fact3
data.value: The tilt is slowly getting smaller: it was 24.2° about 10,000 years ago and is 23.44° now.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Fact4
data.value: Because the axis wobbles, the pole star changes: Thuban for the builders of the pyramids, Polaris now, Vega in about 12,000 years.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Fact5
data.value: In 1976 Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton found the same 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000-year rhythms in mud from the ocean floor: the “pacemaker of the ice ages”.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Note
data.value: Seen at a slant. With “Draw bigger” on, the stretch is drawn 5× and the tilt's swings 3×; dates and distances are the real ones.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Panel_Note
data.value: With one cycle chosen, the other two stay as they are today, so you can see what that one does on its own.

data.name: Ice_Orbit_Subtitle
data.value: Earth's orbit stretches, and its axis tilts and wobbles

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Fact1
data.value: At its biggest the Laurentide ice sheet covered most of Canada and reached south of Chicago; over Hudson Bay it was more than 3 km thick.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Fact2
data.value: The ground around Hudson Bay is still rising, about 1 cm a year, 10,000 years after the ice left.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Fact3
data.value: The ice dug out the Great Lakes, and left the hills of sand and stones (moraines) that mark where its edge stood.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Fact4
data.value: Fresh snow sends back about 80–90% of the sunlight; forests and the sea keep about 90% of it. More ice means a cooler, brighter Earth.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Fact5
data.value: Without the CO₂ people have added, the next ice age would start in about 50,000 years; with it, much later.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Growing_Text
data.value: The snow line is low, so more snow falls on the ice than melts. The dome thickens and spreads south, and slowly presses the ground down under it.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Melting_Text
data.value: The snow line has risen above much of the ice. Its edges melt back, meltwater runs to the sea, and the ground, still pressed down, starts to rise again.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_None_Text
data.value: Summers melt all the winter's snow. Where the ice was, the ground is still slowly rising back up, and the sea reaches today's coast.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Note
data.value: Along about 88° W, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic. Heights are drawn about 600× taller; the ice follows the same model.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Panel_Note
data.value: The ice sheet's size follows the model's ice; its shape is the classic dome of a sheet of ice spreading under its own weight.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Steady_Text
data.value: Snow added on top about balances the melt at the edges, so the sheet keeps its size for now.

data.name: Ice_Sheet_Subtitle
data.value: A slice through the North American ice sheet

data.name: Ice_State_Full_Text
data.value: The ice sheets are huge, the sea is far lower and the air holds less CO₂. Such big sheets are fragile: the next strong summers at 65° N bring them down fast.

data.name: Ice_State_Growing_Text
data.value: Summers are too weak to melt the winter's snow, so snow piles up year after year and turns to ice. Sheets of ice spread from northern Canada and Scandinavia, and the sea falls.

data.name: Ice_State_Holding_Text
data.value: Summers have strengthened a little and the ice shrinks a bit, but not enough to end the ice age. The big sheets wait for the next weak summers to grow again.

data.name: Ice_State_Melting_Text
data.value: Strong summers melt the ice far faster than it grew: in under 10,000 years the sheets are gone and the sea rises by more than 100 metres.

data.name: Ice_State_Warm_Text
data.value: Outside Greenland there is little ice in the north. Summers melt each winter's snow. A warm spell lasts until summers at 65° N turn weak enough for snow to stay all year.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Fact1
data.value: Ice sheets grow on land, and most of the land near 65° N is in North America and Eurasia. That is why northern summers, not southern, pace the ice ages.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Fact2
data.value: At the last glacial maximum, about 21,000 years ago, the sea was about 120 m lower: people could walk from Siberia to Alaska, and from Britain to France.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Fact3
data.value: Antarctic ice holds air bubbles 800,000 years old: CO₂ went up and down between about 180 and 280 ppm with the ice ages. It is over 420 ppm now.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Fact4
data.value: Until about a million years ago ice ages came every 41,000 years, with the tilt. Why they then switched to about 100,000 years is still being worked out.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Fact5
data.value: This chapter's ice is a simple model: it gets the timing of the ice ages right, but the real ice also answers to CO₂, the oceans and the dust.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Note
data.value: Sunshine: the day's mean at the top of the air at 65° N on the northern summer solstice (Berger 1978). Ice: a simple model driven by it (Paillard 1998).

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Panel_Note
data.value: The model leaves a warm spell when summers turn weak, grows ice for tens of thousands of years, and ends a big ice age at the next strong summers.

data.name: Ice_Sunshine_Subtitle
data.value: Weak northern summers let the ice grow

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact1
data.value: Kepler actually found this law first, in 1609, before he knew the orbit was an ellipse.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact2
data.value: Equal areas means the planet's angular momentum stays the same: at half the distance it goes twice as fast sideways. A spinning skater who pulls in their arms speeds up for the same reason.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact3
data.value: Earth is fastest in early January (30.3 km/s) and slowest in early July (29.3 km/s).

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact4
data.value: So the northern summer half of the year, from the March to the September equinox, is about 7 days longer than the winter half.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet races past the Sun at about 55 km/s, and crawls at under 1 km/s far out, where it spends most of its 75 years.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Note
data.value: Each coloured slice takes the same time. Near the Sun they are short and wide, far out long and thin, but all have the same area. Not to scale.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Subtitle
data.value: Second law: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times

data.name: Kepler_DragHint_Orbit
data.value: Drag to move the planet along its orbit

data.name: Kepler_DragHint_You
data.value: Drag to move your planet nearer to or farther from the Sun

data.name: Kepler_Earth_Note
data.value: From Earth's orbit, to within a day or two. Earth is closest to the Sun in the northern winter: the seasons come from the tilt of its axis, not from the distance.

data.name: Kepler_Ecc_Note
data.value: c is how far the Sun is from the centre, a half the long axis. The planets are all near 0: their orbits are almost circles, just with the Sun a little off centre. Moving the slider shapes the example orbit.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact1
data.value: Kepler found the ellipse in 1609 from Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars: a circle missed them by 8 arcminutes, a quarter of the Moon's width, and he would not ignore it.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact2
data.value: Earth's orbit is nearly a circle (e = 0.017): its distance from the Sun only goes from 147.1 to 152.1 million km.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact3
data.value: The Sun sits at one focus; the other is just an empty point in space. The centre of the ellipse is empty too.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact4
data.value: Newton showed in 1687 why: a pull that weakens with the square of the distance gives ellipses, or for anything fast enough to escape, open curves that never come back.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet (e = 0.967) goes from inside Venus's orbit to beyond Neptune's. It was last near the Sun in 1986 and comes back in 2061.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Note
data.value: Like drawing with two pins and a loop of string: the two parts of the string always add up to the same length. Not to scale: the Sun and the planet are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Subtitle
data.value: First law: a planet goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus

data.name: Kepler_Label_EqualAreas
data.value: {0} slices of {1} each: all the same area

data.name: Kepler_OpenSolarSystem
data.value: See the planets in the Solar System

data.name: Kepler_PeriodChart_Caption
data.value: Year against distance, on log scales

data.name: Kepler_PeriodChart_Note
data.value: On logarithmic scales T² = a³ is a straight line, rising 3 for every 2 across. Every planet, the dwarf planets and Halley's comet sit on it: one rule for everything going round the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact1
data.value: Kepler published the third law in 1619, ten years after the first two, in his book Harmonices Mundi (The Harmony of the World).

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact2
data.value: Twice as far means 2.8 times as long a year: the path is twice as long and the planet goes 1.4 times slower.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact3
data.value: Neptune takes 165 years: discovered in 1846, it finished its first round since then only in 2011.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact4
data.value: Newton's version includes the mass in the middle, so a moon's orbit weighs its planet: that is how we know Jupiter's mass.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact5
data.value: It works for satellites too: 42,164 km from Earth's centre one round takes 23 h 56 min, just as long as Earth takes to turn, so a geostationary satellite stays over one spot.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Note
data.value: Distances to scale: the planets at their real places today, seen from above the Sun's north pole. The view zooms out to keep your planet in sight; the planets are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Subtitle
data.value: Third law: the square of a planet's year goes with the cube of its distance

data.name: Kepler_Speed_Caption
data.value: Speed and distance through one round

data.name: Kepler_Speed_Note
data.value: Where the distance is smallest the speed is greatest, and the other way round: distance times sideways speed stays the same all the way.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Aphelion_Description
data.value: Farthest from the Sun and slowest. It does not stop: still moving sideways, it begins to fall back towards the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Approaching_Description
data.value: Falling back towards the Sun, the pull now speeds it up, all the way to perihelion.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle
data.value: A circle: the same speed all the way

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle_Description
data.value: On a circle the distance never changes, so neither does the speed: equal areas then simply means equal arcs.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Perihelion_Description
data.value: The Sun's pull is strongest here and the planet is moving fastest. It swings round the Sun and starts to climb away again.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Receding_Description
data.value: The Sun pulls back on it as it climbs outward, so it slows down, like a ball thrown upward.

data.name: Kepler_Stat_Swept_Value
data.value: {0:0}% of the area in {0:0}% of the time

data.name: Kepler_Table_Caption
data.value: Measured: T² ÷ a³ is 1 for all of them

data.name: Kepler_Timeline_Orbit
data.value: Time since perihelion: one round of the orbit

data.name: Kepler_You_Earth
data.value: At Earth's distance its year is Earth's year: the two go round side by side.

data.name: Kepler_You_Inner
data.value: Closer than Earth: the Sun pulls harder, so it goes faster round a shorter path. Its year is shorter than ours and it laps Earth.

data.name: Kepler_You_Outer
data.value: Farther than Earth: a longer path at a slower speed, so its year is longer than ours and it falls behind Earth.

data.name: Kepler_YourAxis_Caption
data.value: Your planet's distance from the Sun

data.name: Kepler_YourAxis_Like
data.value: Put it where a real one is:

data.name: Lens_Auto_Tooltip
data.value: Pick the shutter time that exposes this scene right

data.name: Lens_Bench_Concave_Text
data.value: A concave lens spreads light out wherever the candle is. The rays seem to come from a smaller, upright candle nearer the lens. Glasses for short sight are concave.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Fact1
data.value: 1/u + 1/v = 1/f: the closer the candle comes to F, the farther away and bigger its image.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Fact2
data.value: A lens's power in dioptres is 1 over its focal length in metres: a lens with a 10 cm focal length is 10 D.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Fact3
data.value: A single lens's real images are always upside down; its virtual images are always upright.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Fact4
data.value: Glass bends violet light more than red, so a simple lens focuses colours in slightly different places. Camera lenses pair two kinds of glass to cancel it.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Fact5
data.value: A burning glass works because it packs the sunlight falling on the whole lens into one small spot.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Larger_Text
data.value: Between F and 2F, the image lands beyond 2F: larger and upside down. A projector holds its picture here, upside down, so it comes out the right way up.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Magnifier_Text
data.value: Inside F, the rays still spread apart after the lens. Looking back through it, your eye follows them to a larger, upright candle on the same side: a virtual image, which no screen can catch. This is a magnifying glass.

data.name: Lens_Bench_None_Text
data.value: With the candle at the focal point, the light leaves the lens parallel and never meets again. A torch or a lighthouse uses this to send out a straight beam.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Note
data.value: Lengths in centimetres; heights are drawn 4 times larger. The three rays bend at the lens's middle plane (a thin lens).

data.name: Lens_Bench_Same_Text
data.value: At exactly two focal lengths, the image is also two focal lengths away on the other side and just as big, only upside down.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Smaller_Text
data.value: The candle is more than two focal lengths away, so its image lands between F and 2F on the other side: smaller and upside down. Cameras and eyes work like this.

data.name: Lens_Bench_Subtitle
data.value: How a lens makes an image

data.name: Lens_Bench_Sunlight_Text
data.value: Sunlight arrives parallel, and a convex lens brings it to a point at F (a concave one spreads it as if from F). With a real glass lens, the rays near the edge meet a little nearer than those near the middle.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Bright_Text
data.value: Too much light: the bright parts turn white. Use a faster shutter, a smaller aperture (a bigger f-number) or a lower ISO, or press Auto exposure.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Dark_Text
data.value: Too little light. Use a slower shutter, a wider aperture (a smaller f-number) or a higher ISO, or press Auto exposure.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Fact1
data.value: The f-number is the focal length divided by the opening's width: a 50 mm lens at f/2 has a 25 mm hole.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Fact2
data.value: Each full stop (f/2.8 to f/4, 1/250 to 1/125, ISO 100 to 200) halves or doubles the light.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Fact3
data.value: Focus at the hyperfocal distance and everything from half that distance to infinity looks sharp.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Fact4
data.value: A phone's lens has a focal length of only a few millimetres, which gives a huge depth of field, so phones add background blur in software.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Fact5
data.value: A dark room with a small hole in one wall, a camera obscura, makes the same upside-down image without any lens.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Good_Text
data.value: The aperture, shutter and ISO let in just the right amount of light for this scene.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Note
data.value: A full-frame camera. Distances on the track are squeezed and those behind the lens stretched, so the focus shows; the photo itself is to scale.

data.name: Lens_Camera_Panel_Note
data.value: Each step of aperture, shutter or ISO doubles or halves the light. A blur under 0.03 mm on the sensor counts as sharp. The ball crosses at 4 m/s.

data.name: Lens_Chart_Bench_Note
data.value: Both in focal lengths. Gold: a real image behind the lens; blue: a virtual one in front of it. Drag the dot to move the candle.

data.name: Lens_Chart_Camera_Note
data.value: For this focal length and focus distance: the green band runs from the nearest to the farthest sharp distance. Drag to change the aperture.

data.name: Lens_Chart_Eye_Caption
data.value: How much closer the eye can focus, by age

data.name: Lens_Chart_Eye_Note
data.value: Accommodation in dioptres (Hofstetter: the average, and the spread between people); the near point is 1 over it, in metres. Below the orange line, reading at 40 cm needs glasses. Drag the dot to change the age.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Behind_Text
data.value: This eye is too short for its power, and even focusing as hard as it can it cannot bend the light enough. This is long sight. A convex lens adds the missing bending.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Fact1
data.value: About two thirds of the eye's focusing is done by the cornea; the lens adds the adjustable rest.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Fact2
data.value: The image on the retina is upside down; the brain learns to see the world the right way up.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Fact3
data.value: A child can focus closer than 10 cm; by 45 the near point is about 25 cm, and by 60 the lens hardly changes at all.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Fact4
data.value: Each dioptre of short sight is roughly a third of a millimetre of extra eye length.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Fact5
data.value: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light-sensitive cells: everyone has a blind spot, filled in by the brain.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Front_Text
data.value: For this distance the eye bends the light too much, so it meets before the retina and spreads out again. This is short sight, or glasses that are wrong for this distance. A concave lens fixes it.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Front_Title
data.value: Blurred: focus in front of the retina

data.name: Lens_Eye_Note
data.value: The eye is drawn to scale; the distances outside it are squeezed. Light from the chart's top comes in more steeply than it really would, so the upside-down image shows.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Panel_Note
data.value: A model eye: cornea 43 D, lens 19 D when relaxed, and how much it can focus closer at each age from Hofstetter's average. Short sight here is an eye that is too long. In China, “300 degrees” means −3 D.

data.name: Lens_Eye_SharpNear_Text
data.value: Light from near things spreads out more, so the eye works for it: the ciliary muscle tightens, the lens bulges and bends harder, and the image lands on the retina.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Sharp_Text
data.value: Light from the chart meets right on the retina without any effort: the ciliary muscle rests and the lens stays flat.

data.name: Lens_Eye_Subtitle
data.value: How the eye focuses near and far

data.name: Lens_Eye_TooClose_Text
data.value: The lens is already as round as it can get, and the light would still meet behind the retina. Move the chart back past the near point, or wear reading glasses.

data.name: Lens_Eye_TooClose_Title
data.value: Blurred: closer than the near point

data.name: Lens_FindImage_Tooltip
data.value: Move the screen to where the image is sharp

data.name: Lens_Hint_Bench
data.value: Drag the candle (by its flame to change its height), the screen or an F.

data.name: Lens_Hint_Camera
data.value: Drag the focus pin, or click something in the photo to focus on it.

data.name: Lens_Hint_Eye
data.value: Drag the chart nearer or farther along its track.

data.name: Lens_Label_FocusBehind
data.value: light would meet behind the retina

data.name: Lens_Label_FocusFront
data.value: light meets in front of the retina

data.name: Lens_Lesson_Bench_Choice1
data.value: Bigger, and farther from the lens

data.name: Lens_Lesson_Bench_Choice2
data.value: Smaller, and closer to the lens

data.name: Lens_Rays_Note
data.value: Many rays and sunlight are traced through a real glass lens, with Snell's law at both faces: the rays near the edge meet a little nearer (spherical aberration). In colour, the glass's spread of colours is shown 6 times larger.

data.name: Lens_Title
data.value: Lenses, the eye and the camera

data.name: Lesson_Done_Text
data.value: That's the end of this walkthrough. Keep dragging and clicking things in the picture to explore, or switch to another view and listen again.

data.name: Lesson_Start_Tooltip
data.value: A spoken walkthrough of this view, with subtitles

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Charge_Note
data.value: Rubbing builds it up toward a limit (beyond it the air at the surface breaks down); a spark takes a bite out of it; damp air drains it away.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Current_Note
data.value: It peaks within about a microsecond and halves in about 200 µs; later strokes are smaller and quicker (IEC 62305 shapes). Half of all first strokes stay under 30 kA.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Field_Caption
data.value: The field at the ground, last minute

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Field_Note
data.value: Fair weather gives about 0.13 kV/m pointing down. Under a storm it turns over and climbs; each flash knocks it back: the saw-tooth meteorologists' field mills record.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Rate_Note
data.value: Flashes a minute grow as the fifth power of the storm's height (Price and Rind 1992): a storm twice as tall flashes about 30 times as often.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Reach_Caption
data.value: Striking distance and the rolling sphere

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Reach_Note
data.value: Weaker strokes come closer before anything reaches up, so they can slip past a rod: protection standards roll spheres of 20 to 60 m (classes I to IV) over a building to find where it needs rods.

data.name: Lightning_Chart_Series_Note
data.value: Rub two materials together and the higher one gives electrons to the lower one: it ends up positive, the lower one negative. The further apart, the more charge. The order is the usual one; the bar lengths are only illustrative.

data.name: Lightning_CloudTop_Note
data.value: Taller storms have stronger updrafts and more ice and graupel colliding in the cold part of the cloud, so they charge much faster.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Charging_Description
data.value: The updraft carries small ice crystals up past falling graupel. Each knock moves a little charge: the light crystals take positive charge up to the top, the heavy graupel keeps negative charge in the middle. The field at the ground grows.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_CloudToGround_Description
data.value: A flash carried the middle's negative charge down into the ground. The field drops at once, then the cloud charges up again: the meter draws a saw-tooth.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Danger_Description
data.value: The ground under the storm is strongly positive and the field is over 5 kV/m: points such as treetops and hair start to leak charge (corona). A flash could come down at any moment.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact1
data.value: Lightning is one enormous static spark: the ice in the cloud pulls tens of coulombs of charge apart, building up some hundred million volts.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact2
data.value: About −15 °C is where the charging turns over: colder, graupel hit by ice crystals goes negative; warmer, it goes positive (Takahashi's 1978 experiments).

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact3
data.value: Satellites count about 44 flashes a second over the whole Earth, most of them over land, where the afternoon sun drives strong updrafts.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact4
data.value: Most flashes never reach the ground: about six stay in the cloud for each one to the ground in the tropics, about three in middle latitudes (Prentice and Mackerras 1977).

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Fact5
data.value: Hair standing on end, a tingling skin or a buzzing from metal means the field at the ground is already strong: a strike may be seconds away. Get off high ground at once.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Intracloud_Description
data.value: The air broke down inside the cloud, between the negative middle and the positive top. Most flashes are like this: from the ground you only see the cloud light up.

data.name: Lightning_Cloud_Note
data.value: A storm in slice, 36 km across and 16.5 km high, to scale. The tripole of charges is a sketch; flash rate from Price and Rind (1992); the clock runs in real time, the grains move faster than real.

data.name: Lightning_Current
data.value: Peak current of the first stroke

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Cloud
data.value: Click the ground to move the field meter (and the person); grow the storm taller and watch how much more often it flashes.

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Static
data.value: Drag the rod (or balloon) yourself: rub it on the cloth, then take it to the paper, the water and the metal ball. Try other materials, or damper air.

data.name: Lightning_Hint_Strike
data.value: Drag the picture sideways to go back and forth in time; take the rod away or change the current and see what gets hit.

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice1
data.value: It turns positive, pulled up by the cloud's negative middle

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice2
data.value: It turns negative, like the bottom of the cloud

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Cloud_Choice3
data.value: Nothing: the ground can't hold charge

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Static_Choice1
data.value: The balloon holds on to electrons more strongly

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Static_Choice3
data.value: The hair is warmer than the balloon

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice1
data.value: When the leader comes within about a hundred metres

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice2
data.value: Only when the leader touches it

data.name: Lightning_Lesson_Strike_Choice3
data.value: As soon as the leader leaves the cloud

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Hit_House
data.value: {0}: the current goes through roof and walls

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Hit_Person
data.value: {0}: in the open you may be the highest point!

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Share
data.value: In the cloud : to the ground

data.name: Lightning_Stat_Thunder_Value
data.value: {0} s after the flash, from {1} km

data.name: Lightning_Static_Bending_Description
data.value: The stream bends toward the rod whichever charge it has: the side of the water nearest the rod takes the opposite charge, and opposites attract.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Charged_Description
data.value: The rod is an insulator, so its charge stays on the part that was rubbed. It only leaks away slowly, through the thin film of water damp air leaves on its surface.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact1
data.value: Rubbing does not make charge, it moves it: electrons pass from one material to the other, so one ends up exactly as negative as the other is positive.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact2
data.value: Shuffling across a carpet can charge you to about 35 000 V in dry winter air (10–20% humidity), but only about 1500 V when the air is damp (65–90%).

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact3
data.value: The volts are high but the charge is tiny: a balloon's spark carries only a few millijoules, which is why it stings but does no harm.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact4
data.value: You only feel a discharge above about 3000 V, yet the chips in a phone can be damaged by a few hundred volts or less, so electronics factories ground their workers with wrist straps.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Fact5
data.value: Petrol vapour can be lit by a spark of about 0.2 millijoules, less than a static shock: that is why pumps have a metal plate to touch first, to discharge yourself.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Lifting_Description
data.value: The paper has no charge, but the rod pulls its charges a little apart (polarises it): the near side takes the opposite charge and is pulled up. Once it touches, it shares the rod's charge and is pushed off again.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Neutral_Description
data.value: The rod holds as many positive charges as negative ones, so it is neutral. Rub it to and fro on the cloth.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Note
data.value: A bench a metre wide, from the front. Charges from the triboelectric series and the air's breakdown limit; spark gaps from Paschen's law; the number of + and − signs only shows how much.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Rubbing_Description
data.value: Where two materials touch and part, the one that holds electrons more tightly pulls some away from the other. Rubbing just makes more of them touch.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Spark_Description
data.value: The voltage was high enough to break down the air in the gap: the air turned into a glowing, conducting path and the charge rushed across. A lightning bolt in miniature. Only the charge near the tip goes: the rod is an insulator.

data.name: Lightning_Static_Subtitle
data.value: Charging by rubbing: electrons hop from one thing to another

data.name: Lightning_Static_Touched_Description
data.value: Too few volts for a spark you could see: the charge simply flowed into the earthed ball where they touched.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Attach_Description
data.value: When the leader's tip comes within striking distance of something, the field there is strong enough to send a streamer up. Whatever's streamer meets the leader first gets the strike: that is the rolling sphere.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Dart_Description
data.value: The next discharge does not feel its way or branch: it darts straight down the still-warm channel in a millisecond or two.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact1
data.value: The channel is only a few centimetres wide, but within microseconds it is heated to about 30 000 °C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact2
data.value: A flash usually has 3 or 4 return strokes, tens of milliseconds apart, down the same channel: that is why lightning flickers.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact3
data.value: Thunder is the shock wave of air heated and expanding all at once. Count the seconds from the flash and divide by 3: that is roughly how many kilometres away it was.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact4
data.value: A lightning rod does not attract lightning from afar: when a leader comes near, it sends up its streamer first, and leads the current down its conductor into the earth. Benjamin Franklin proposed it around 1750.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Fact5
data.value: Never shelter under a lone tree: the current can jump from its trunk to you, or spread through the ground (step voltage). A building with protection, or a car with its doors shut (a metal cage), is safe.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Glow_Description
data.value: After a stroke the channel glows on for a while as it cools, while charge elsewhere in the cloud gathers at its top, ready to go again.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Heard_Description
data.value: Sound from every part of the long channel arrives one after another, so thunder rumbles instead of banging once. The seconds divided by 3 are about the kilometres to the strike.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Later_Description
data.value: The same channel is used again: the current is smaller but rises faster. These repeated strokes are why lightning flickers.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Leader_Description
data.value: Negative charge from the cloud's base feels its way down along an ionised channel, jumping about 50 m at a time, pausing tens of microseconds, branching as it goes. It is faint: you would hardly see it.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Note
data.value: The lowest 100-odd metres are to scale, the rest up to the cloud (2 km) squeezed. Each part of the flash is slowed by a different amount; after the last stroke time runs at its real pace and the thunder travels at 343 m/s.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Strip_Wait
data.value: The light reaches you at once; the sound will take {0} s

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Stroke_Description
data.value: The moment the channel connects, a huge current (typically 30 000 amps) surges up from the ground at about a third of the speed of light, heating the channel to some 30 000 °C: the flash you see.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Subtitle
data.value: One strike in slow motion, and its thunder

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Thunder_Description
data.value: The light reached you almost at once; the sound covers only 343 m a second. Count the seconds since the flash.

data.name: Lightning_Strike_Thunder_Title
data.value: The thunder is on its way

data.name: Location_Chip_Tooltip
data.value: The place the chapters of the book are seen from. Shared by all of them and saved.

data.name: Location_Custom_Hint
data.value: Latitude north positive, longitude east positive, in degrees. Its clock is the ideal time zone of its meridian.

data.name: Location_Description
data.value: Used by every chapter that depends on where you are: day and night, the tides and more to come. Saved for next time.

data.name: Location_Gravity_Note
data.value: "Earth" uses the pull of gravity at {0}: g = {1} m/s². It is 9.780 at the equator and 9.832 at the poles, because Earth spins and bulges.

data.name: MoonPhases_Chart_Caption
data.value: How much is lit through the month

data.name: MoonPhases_Disc_Caption
data.value: The Moon as seen from Earth

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Month
data.value: Drag left or right to move through the month

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Orbit
data.value: Drag to move the Moon along its orbit

data.name: MoonPhases_DragHint_Sky
data.value: Drag left or right to change the time of day

data.name: MoonPhases_Hemisphere_Hint
data.value: Everyone sees the same phase on the same night, but from the southern hemisphere the Moon looks upside down.

data.name: MoonPhases_Label_DailyPath
data.value: Path of the Sun and the Moon across the sky

data.name: MoonPhases_Legend_Note
data.value: We see only the part of the Moon that is both lit and facing us: that is the phase.

data.name: MoonPhases_Lesson_Month_Choice1
data.value: Earth has moved on around the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Lesson_Sky_Choice1
data.value: In the daytime, with the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Moment_Sidereal
data.value: Once round against the stars, but not yet new moon

data.name: MoonPhases_Moment_Synodic
data.value: Between Earth and the Sun: new moon

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact1
data.value: Sidereal month, 27.32 days: once round Earth, back in line with the same distant star.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact2
data.value: Synodic month, 29.53 days: from new moon to new moon. Earth moves about 29° round the Sun in a month, and the Moon needs about 2.2 more days to catch up.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact3
data.value: Days work the same way: Earth turns once against the stars in 23 h 56 min, but the Sun returns to the same place in the sky after 24 hours.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Fact4
data.value: The months of the Chinese calendar follow the phases: 29 or 30 days, starting at new moon. Twelve of them make only 354 days, so a leap month is added about every three years.

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Note
data.value: Not to scale: the Moon's orbit is drawn far too large for Earth's

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Subtitle
data.value: The Moon goes round Earth in 27.3 days, so why do the phases take 29.5?

data.name: MoonPhases_Month_Text
data.value: Day {0:0.0}: the Moon has gone {1:0}° round Earth against the stars, but only {2:0}° against the Sun, because Earth has moved {3:0.0}° round the Sun meanwhile.

data.name: MoonPhases_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: Earth on its way round the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon and its two halves

data.name: MoonPhases_Observer_Caption
data.value: Where you are on the turning Earth (seen from above the North Pole)

data.name: MoonPhases_Observer_Note
data.value: The shaded half is your sky. When the Moon is in it (ringed), the Moon is above your horizon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_FirstQuarter_Description
data.value: A quarter of the way round: we see half of the lit half. It is due south at sunset and sets around midnight.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_Full_Description
data.value: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon: the whole lit half faces us. It rises at sunset and is up all night.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_LastQuarter_Description
data.value: Three quarters of the way round: half lit again, the other half. It rises around midnight and is due south at sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_New_Description
data.value: The Moon is between Earth and the Sun: its lit half faces away from us. It crosses the sky with the Sun, lost in its glare.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningCrescent_Description
data.value: Only a sliver of the lit half still faces us. Look low in the east just before sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningGibbous_Description
data.value: The lit part shrinks, now from the other side. It rises in the evening and is still up after sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingCrescent_Description
data.value: A thin sliver of the lit half turns towards us. Look low in the west just after sunset.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingGibbous_Description
data.value: More than half the disc is lit and growing. It rises in the afternoon and is up most of the evening.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact1
data.value: The Moon makes no light of its own. Like Earth, it is always half lit by the Sun; the phase is how much of that lit half faces us.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact2
data.value: The phases are not Earth's shadow: at a crescent, Earth's shadow points far away from the Moon. Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon in a lunar eclipse.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact3
data.value: Eclipses can only happen at new moon (solar) and full moon (lunar), yet most months there is none: the Moon's orbit is tilted 5°, so it usually passes above or below.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact4
data.value: The Moon turns once on its axis each time it goes round Earth, so it always shows us the same face. The far side is not dark: it is fully lit at new moon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact5
data.value: Waxing (growing) phases are lit on the right, waning ones on the left, as seen from the northern hemisphere; from the southern hemisphere it is the other way round.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Note
data.value: Seen from far above the North Pole; not to scale. Outer ring: the Moon as seen from Earth ({0})

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Subtitle
data.value: Why does the Moon change shape? It is always half lit by the Sun

data.name: MoonPhases_SkyNow_Down
data.value: {0}: the Moon is below the horizon. {1}

data.name: MoonPhases_SkyNow_Up
data.value: {0}: the Moon is {1:0}° up in the {2}. {3}

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact1
data.value: The Moon moves about 12° east against the stars each day, so it rises about 50 minutes later each day.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact2
data.value: The full moon is opposite the Sun: it rises as the Sun sets and sets as the Sun rises.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact3
data.value: A crescent is always close to the Sun in the sky: in the west after sunset while waxing, in the east before sunrise while waning.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Fact4
data.value: For about half of the month the Moon is up in daylight too. Around first quarter it is easy to see in the afternoon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Note
data.value: Simplified: the Sun and the Moon follow the celestial equator, as at an equinox. Local solar time; the Moon is drawn larger

data.name: MoonPhases_Sky_Subtitle
data.value: When can you see the Moon? It rises about 50 minutes later each day

data.name: MoonPhases_Stat_RiseSet_ToolTip
data.value: Local solar time at an equinox. Through the year real times shift by up to a few hours.

data.name: MoonPhases_Today_Text
data.value: Today: {0}, {1:P0} lit, {2:0.0} days after new moon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Upcoming_Note
data.value: In your time zone. Calculated, to within a few minutes.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_01
data.value: In this flask are twenty five millilitres of hydrochloric acid, with a few drops of phenolphthalein. Colourless, because it is acidic.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_02
data.value: Above it, the burette is full of sodium hydroxide, a base of the same strength. We'll let it in a little at a time and read how much has gone.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_03
data.value: The tap is open and the base is dripping in. Watch the curve: the pH is creeping up, but only slowly.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_04
data.value: Why so slow? In the magnifier, each OH⁻ that arrives meets an H₃O⁺, and they become two water molecules. There is still plenty of acid to use up.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_05
data.value: We've added twenty four millilitres, and the acid is nearly gone. What do you think will happen over the next two millilitres?

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_06
data.value: Watch! Around twenty five millilitres the pH shoots up from about three to about eleven, and the flask flashes pink. With almost no acid left, every drop counts.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_07
data.value: Right here, the base added equals the acid we started with. This is the equivalence point, and for a strong acid it is exactly neutral. Chemists use it to measure how strong an acid is.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_08
data.value: Now look at the thermometer. Neutralising gives off heat. Here the flask warms by under a degree, but with stronger solutions it would get noticeably warm.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_09
data.value: Now acetic acid instead. The curve starts higher, because it is a weak acid. Halfway through it flattens out, and right here the pH equals the acid's pKa. The jump is smaller, and ends on the basic side.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_10
data.value: So which indicator should we use? Methyl orange changes colour in this band, long before the end. For a weak acid, it would fool us. Phenolphthalein changes right inside the jump.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Neutralize_11
data.value: Your turn. The flask is full of fresh acid again. Open the tap, and shut it as soon as the flask turns pink, as close to twenty five millilitres as you can.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Acetic
data.value: Acetic acid is the acid in vinegar. It is a weak acid: most of its molecules hold on to their proton, and only a few give it to water.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_AcidIon
data.value: An acetate ion: an acetic acid molecule that has given its proton away. It would happily take one back, which is what makes a buffer work.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_AcidMolecule
data.value: A whole acetic acid molecule, still holding its proton. In vinegar most molecules look like this, which is why vinegar is a weak acid.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Ammonia
data.value: Household ammonia cleaner is a weak base, around pH eleven and a half. Its sharp smell is ammonia gas escaping from the water.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_AmmoniaBottle
data.value: Ammonia is a weak base. A few of its molecules take a proton from water, becoming ammonium and leaving OH⁻ behind. Most stay as they are.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Antacid
data.value: Milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide in water, around pH ten and a half. Swallowed, it neutralises some stomach acid and eases heartburn.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_BakingSoda
data.value: Baking soda, sodium bicarbonate, makes water a little basic, about eight point three. It fizzes with acids like vinegar because it gives off carbon dioxide.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Band
data.value: This shaded band is where the chosen indicator changes colour. For a sharp end point it should sit inside the steep part of the curve.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_BaseIon
data.value: An ammonium ion: ammonia that has caught a proton from water. For every one of these, an OH⁻ was left behind in the water.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_BaseMolecule
data.value: An ammonia molecule: one nitrogen and three hydrogens. The nitrogen has a spare pair of electrons that can catch a proton.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Beaker
data.value: This beaker started with a hundred millilitres of pure water. Every drop you add changes what is floating in it, and the meter and the colour tell you what that did.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Bleach
data.value: Bleach is strongly basic, around twelve and a half. It can burn skin and eyes, and mixed with acids it releases poisonous chlorine gas.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Blood
data.value: Blood is slightly basic, about seven point four. It is a buffer: watering it down or adding a little acid barely moves its pH, which keeps you alive.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Bromothymol
data.value: Bromothymol blue is yellow in acid, green right around neutral, and blue in base. It is handy for telling whether something is close to pH seven.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Burette
data.value: The burette is a long tube with a scale. It is read from the top, so the number at the liquid's surface is how much has already run out.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Cabbage
data.value: Red cabbage juice is an indicator you can make in your kitchen. Its colour comes from anthocyanins: red in acid, purple near neutral, blue, green and then yellow in strong base.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Chloride
data.value: A chloride ion is what is left of hydrochloric acid after it gives its proton away. It just floats around and takes no part in the pH.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Coffee
data.value: Black coffee is mildly acidic, around pH five, from acids roasted out of the beans.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Cola
data.value: Cola contains phosphoric acid, and with dissolved carbon dioxide it sits around pH two and a half. The sugar hides how sour it really is.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Curve
data.value: The titration curve shows the pH after each amount of base. Drag along it to go back or forward.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Dilute
data.value: Click here to water the liquid down ten times. Watch which way the pH moves, and how far.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Drain
data.value: Drain cleaner is concentrated sodium hydroxide, near the top of the scale. It dissolves hair and grease, and skin too, so it must be handled with gloves.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Equivalence
data.value: At the equivalence point the base added exactly matches the acid that was there. Here that is twenty five millilitres, because both have the same strength.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Flask
data.value: The conical flask holds the acid with a few drops of indicator. Its shape lets you swirl it without spilling. Click it to add a single drop.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_FlaskIndicator
data.value: This is the indicator in the flask. Its colour change is your signal that the acid has run out.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Halfway
data.value: Halfway to the end, half the acetic acid has become acetate. With equal amounts of both, the pH equals the acid's pKa, four point seven six.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Hcl
data.value: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid. Every single HCl molecule hands its proton to water, so you get one H₃O⁺ and one chloride ion for each.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Hydronium
data.value: This is a hydronium ion, H₃O⁺: a water molecule carrying an extra proton. The more of these there are, the more acidic the water, and the lower the pH.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Hydroxide
data.value: This is a hydroxide ion, OH⁻: a water molecule that has lost a proton. When it meets an H₃O⁺, the proton jumps across and both become water.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Jug
data.value: The jug waters the beaker down: it keeps one tenth and fills it back up with water. Everything dissolved becomes ten times thinner.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Jump
data.value: Near the end, the pH leaps. With almost no acid left, a single drop of base changes the amount of H₃O⁺ by thousands of times.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Lemon
data.value: Lemon juice gets its sourness from citric acid, a weak acid. At around pH two point three, it has tens of thousands of times more H₃O⁺ than pure water.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Litmus
data.value: Litmus comes from lichens. It is red in acid and blue in base, with purple in between. It tells you which side you are on, but not by how much.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Magnifier
data.value: The magnifier zooms in on the beaker. The pale bent shapes are water molecules. The bright ones are what is dissolved, drawn in proportion to each other.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Meter
data.value: A pH meter has a thin glass bulb at the tip of its probe. H₃O⁺ ions build up a tiny voltage across the glass, and the meter turns that voltage into a pH.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Methyl
data.value: Methyl orange is red in fairly strong acid and yellow from about pH four and a half upwards. It changes colour on the acid side.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Milk
data.value: Milk is just on the acidic side of neutral, around six point six. As it goes sour, bacteria turn its sugar into lactic acid and the pH drops.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Naoh
data.value: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base. It falls apart into sodium ions and hydroxide ions, and the hydroxide grabs any H₃O⁺ it meets.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Neutral
data.value: Seven is neutral: just as many H₃O⁺ as OH⁻, like pure water. Neutral does not mean nothing is dissolved; salt water is neutral too.

data.name: Narr_Acid_Obj_Orange
