data.value: Add up every push and every pull, and you get this big arrow: lift. Notice that most of it comes from the suction on top, not the push from below.

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_07
data.value: Here's a puzzle. Two puffs of air arrive at the front of the wing side by side. One goes over the top, the other goes underneath. Which one reaches the back edge first?

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_08
data.value: Let's test it. These coloured lines are smoke released at the very same moment. See how the part over the top races ahead, and never meets its partner again. The old equal transit story is simply wrong.

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_09
data.value: Now look behind the wing. The air leaves the back edge heading slightly downward. The wing pushes air down, so by Newton's third law, the air pushes the wing up. Pressure and downwash are two ways of telling the same story.

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_10
data.value: Let's tilt the wing up more. This tilt against the wind is called the angle of attack. More angle turns more air downward, so the lift grows. Watch the chart on the left-hand page climb.

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_11
data.value: But there's a limit. Past about fifteen degrees, the air can't follow the curved top any more. It tears away into a churning wake, the suction collapses, and lift drops suddenly. That's a stall.

data.name: Narr_Flight_Wing_12
data.value: Your turn. Drag the wing to change its angle, try a different wing shape, or flip it upside down. Can an upside-down wing still make lift?

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_01
data.value: Here's a small glass greenhouse and a car, parked in the summer sun. Look at the readings: inside both, it's far warmer than the air outside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_02
data.value: Sunlight passes through the glass easily, and warms the floor and the plants inside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_03
data.value: The warm floor glows in the infrared. Glass doesn't let those rays through: it soaks them up, warms, and glows half of that heat back inside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_04
data.value: So what do you think keeps a greenhouse warm, most of all?

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_05
data.value: Mostly, it's the lid. Warm air rises off the floor and gathers under the roof. With nowhere to go, the heat builds up. Trapping the infrared adds only a few degrees more.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_06
data.value: Open the roof vents. The warm air escapes through the top, cooler air sinks in, and the greenhouse cools down a lot.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_07
data.value: In 1909, Robert Wood tried a roof of rock salt, which lets infrared out. It cooled the greenhouse far less than opening the vents. The air has no lid at all: its greenhouse effect comes only from catching the infrared.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_08
data.value: A parked car is a greenhouse too. In the sun it can be twenty degrees warmer inside within an hour, even on a mild day, and opening a window a crack hardly helps. Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car.

data.name: Narr_Green_Glass_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag across the picture to turn the day, or click the roof vents or the car's window, and watch the temperatures change.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_01
data.value: Why do only some gases catch heat rays? Start with nitrogen, most of the air. It's two identical atoms. When they stretch, the charge stays perfectly even, so light has nothing to push on, and every ray passes straight through.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_02
data.value: Carbon dioxide is different. Its oxygen atoms pull the electrons a little, so they're slightly negative, and the carbon slightly positive. But when it stretches evenly, the charges stay balanced. Still no catch.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_03
data.value: Now watch it bend. The charge swings up and down: see the gold arrow. Light with the same rhythm can push on that swinging charge.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_04
data.value: The bend wiggles in step with infrared of about fifteen micrometres. What happens when a ray like that comes by?

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_05
data.value: It's caught, and the molecule wiggles harder. A moment later, it either bumps into its neighbours, warming the air, or sends a ray out again in a random direction.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_06
data.value: Below is the ground's glow by wavelength. Carbon dioxide's band at fifteen micrometres sits close to its peak. That's why so little carbon dioxide, about four hundredths of a percent of the air, matters so much.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_07
data.value: Between eight and thirteen micrometres, little is caught by anything: this is the atmospheric window. Through it, about a tenth of the ground's glow escapes straight to space.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_08
data.value: Water is bent even at rest, so every one of its wiggles catches light, and it can spin as well. Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas of all, but how much the air holds depends on its temperature.

data.name: Narr_Green_Molecules_09
data.value: Your turn. Pick another gas or another wiggle; you can also click a line on the spectrum. Watch which rays get caught.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Air
data.value: The air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen, and both let heat rays through. A tiny share of greenhouse gases does all the catching.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetAirSun
data.value: Sunlight taken in by the air itself, mostly by water vapour, ozone and clouds: seventy-eight watts per square metre.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetBack
data.value: Back radiation: three hundred and thirty-three watts per square metre of infrared, sent down by the greenhouse gases and the clouds. This is the greenhouse effect at work.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetFromAir
data.value: Infrared sent to space from high in the air and from the tops of clouds: about a hundred and ninety-nine watts per square metre. With the window, it balances the sunlight kept.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetGlow
data.value: The ground's glow: about three hundred and ninety-six watts per square metre of infrared, more than twice the sunlight it takes in. It can glow that much only because the air sends heat back.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetIn
data.value: Sunlight coming in: three hundred and forty-one watts per square metre, averaged over the whole globe, day and night.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetReflected
data.value: Sunlight reflected straight back to space by clouds, air, ice and the ground: about thirty percent of it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetRising
data.value: Heat carried up by rising warm air, and by evaporating water, which gives its heat back when it condenses into clouds: about ninety-seven watts per square metre.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetSurface
data.value: Sunlight taken in by the ground: a hundred and sixty-one watts per square metre, less than half of what arrives.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_BudgetWindow
data.value: Infrared that goes straight from the ground out to space, through the atmospheric window: about forty watts per square metre, a tenth of the ground's glow.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Car
data.value: A car shut in the sun heats up like a greenhouse: sunlight gets in through the windows, and the hot air is trapped inside. Never leave a child or a pet in a parked car.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_CarWindow
data.value: A window open a crack lets very little air through, so the car hardly cools. Click it to open or shut it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Clouds
data.value: Clouds work both ways. Their white tops reflect sunlight back to space, cooling the planet, while their undersides send heat back down, warming it. Overall, today's clouds cool Earth a little.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Dipole
data.value: The gold arrow is the dipole: which way the molecule's charge leans. Light can only push on a molecule whose dipole swings back and forth as it wiggles.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Emission
data.value: This is roughly the height the heat finally leaves from on its way to space. The air there is about minus eighteen degrees, the temperature a planet with no greenhouse gases would have. More carbon dioxide lifts this height.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Floor
data.value: The floor and soil soak up the sunlight and get hotter than the air. They warm the air touching them, and glow in the infrared.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasAr
data.value: Argon is almost one percent of the air. It's a single atom, with nothing to bend or stretch, so it can't catch infrared at all.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasCH4
data.value: Methane is a tiny trace, under two parts per million. Kilogram for kilogram, it warms about thirty times as much as carbon dioxide over a century, but it breaks down in about twelve years.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasCO2
data.value: Carbon dioxide is only about four hundredths of a percent of the air, but its bend catches infrared near the peak of the ground's glow. It stays in the air for centuries, so over the long run it sets the temperature.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasH2O
data.value: Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas. But it rains out within about nine days, so how much there is follows the temperature: it amplifies warming, rather than starting it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasN2
data.value: Nitrogen is seventy-eight percent of the air. Its two identical atoms keep their charge even however they move, so it lets infrared straight through.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GasO2
data.value: Oxygen is twenty-one percent of the air. Like nitrogen, it's two identical atoms, so it doesn't catch the ground's infrared.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Greenhouse
data.value: The air inside the greenhouse. Sunlight gets in, but the warm air can't rise away, so it ends up far warmer than outside.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Ground
data.value: The ground's temperature settles where the heat it loses equals the heat it gets: the sunlight it takes in, plus the heat sent back down by the air.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_GroundRays
data.value: Heat rays from the ground, each labelled with its wavelength. They come in a whole spread of wavelengths, most of them between five and thirty micrometres.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Infrared
data.value: Infrared, drawn as wavy red lines: the heat glow of anything warm. The ground, at about fifteen degrees, glows at wavelengths around ten micrometres, about twenty times longer than visible light.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Outside
data.value: The air outside, measured in the shade. Through the day it changes far less than the air in the greenhouse or the car.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Pane
data.value: The roof and walls. Glass lets through eighty-five to ninety percent of sunlight, but almost no infrared. A rock-salt pane, like the one in Robert Wood's 1909 experiment, lets the infrared out.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Profile
data.value: The air's temperature against height. It gets about six and a half degrees colder for every kilometre up, as far as the top of the weather, about eleven kilometres high.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Space
data.value: Space is cold and dark. The only way Earth can lose heat to it is by glowing in the infrared. Balance comes when the heat sent out equals the sunlight kept.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Spectrum
data.value: The ground's glow, by wavelength. The shaded part is what this gas alone catches; the dashed line is what all the greenhouse gases catch together.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun's light is mostly visible light, which clear air and glass let through. Of every hundred units arriving at the top of the air, about thirty are reflected straight back to space.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Sunlight
data.value: Sunlight, drawn as short gold streaks. The Sun is so hot that most of its light is visible, with short wavelengths that pass through the air easily.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Vents
data.value: The roof vents. Open, they let the warm air out at the top and cooler air in: that's how gardeners keep a greenhouse from overheating. Click them to open or shut them.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibAsymmetricBend
data.value: A lopsided bend: methane's hydrogens fold unevenly, shifting the charge. It catches infrared at about seven point seven micrometres, right at the edge of the atmospheric window.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibAsymmetricStretch
data.value: A lopsided stretch: one side stretches while the other squeezes, so the charge swings from side to side. This wiggle catches infrared, at short wavelengths.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibBend
data.value: A bend: the molecule flexes like a hinge. In carbon dioxide this swings the charge up and down, and catches infrared at about fifteen micrometres, close to the peak of the ground's glow.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibSpin
data.value: Spinning: a water molecule, bent and charged, tumbles round. Its turning charge catches long-wave infrared, beyond about eighteen micrometres.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibStretch
data.value: A stretch: the two atoms move apart and back together. In nitrogen or oxygen the charge stays even, so this wiggle can't catch light.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibSymmetricBend
data.value: An even bend: methane's hydrogens fold in pairs and keep the molecule balanced, so this wiggle doesn't catch infrared.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_VibSymmetricStretch
data.value: An even stretch: the outer atoms move out and in together. In carbon dioxide or methane the molecule stays balanced, so this wiggle doesn't catch infrared. Water is bent, so in water it does.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_WarmAir
data.value: Warm air rising off the floor and gathering under the roof. Without the glass lid, it would simply rise away and take the heat with it.

data.name: Narr_Green_Obj_Window
data.value: The atmospheric window, from eight to thirteen micrometres. Hardly anything in the air catches these wavelengths, so they're the ground's main way to lose heat straight to space.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_01
data.value: Here's a slice of our planet: the ground, the air above it, and space. Sunlight streams in. Most of it passes straight through the air, and almost half of it is taken in by the ground.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_02
data.value: The warmed ground glows too, but not with light you can see. It gives off infrared, heat rays: the wavy red lines rising from the ground.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_03
data.value: Most of the air, nitrogen and oxygen, lets those rays pass. But a few kinds of molecule, carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane, catch them. Watch a molecule flash red when it does.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_04
data.value: A molecule has caught a heat ray. What happens to that heat next?

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_05
data.value: It's sent out again in a random direction, so half of it comes back down. Turn on the energy flows: three hundred and thirty-three watts per square metre come back down to the ground, twice what it gets from sunlight.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_06
data.value: Now take the greenhouse gases away. The heat rays fly straight out to space, and the ground cools until it settles at about minus eighteen degrees. A frozen planet.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_07
data.value: Bring them back, at the level of the year seventeen-fifty: two hundred and eighty ppm of carbon dioxide. The ground warms to about fourteen degrees. Those thirty-odd degrees are the natural greenhouse effect, and they make Earth fit for life.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_08
data.value: Now double the carbon dioxide, to five hundred and sixty ppm. The heat now leaves for space from a few hundred metres higher up, where the air is colder and gives off less. So the ground and the air below must warm, here by about three degrees, until the balance returns.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_09
data.value: The small chart at the right of the picture shows the air's temperature with height: about six and a half degrees colder for every kilometre up. The gold dot marks the height the heat escapes from.

data.name: Narr_Green_Planet_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the carbon dioxide slider, or take the greenhouse gases away, and watch the ground's temperature settle.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_01
data.value: Electricity is hard to store in bulk, so at every moment the power stations must make exactly what everyone is using. Watch the city wake up: demand climbs through the morning.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_02
data.value: It's eight in the evening, the peak. Lights, cooking and air conditioning are all on. Coal runs flat out, and hydro, pumped storage and gas are called on too.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_03
data.value: Now it's noon on a sunny day, with plenty of solar farms. There's more than enough. Coal turns down as far as it safely can, and the pumped storage station pumps water uphill, saving the spare energy for the evening.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_04
data.value: So how does the grid know whether supply matches demand? By the frequency. All the big generators spin in step, fifty cycles a second on this grid. If demand gets ahead, they slow down a little. If supply gets ahead, they speed up.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_05
data.value: Now a big generating unit suddenly trips off. A thousand megawatts, gone. Demand hasn't changed, so the difference comes out of the energy in all those spinning machines. They slow down, and the frequency falls.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_06
data.value: Within seconds, governors on the other plants feel the drop and open their steam and water valves wider. See the extra megawatts appear. The fall stops, just a few tenths of a hertz down.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_07
data.value: Over the next minutes, the control centre asks plants to raise their output for good. On this graph you can see the frequency climbing slowly back.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_08
data.value: Here's a question. At midday, with lots of solar power, the same unit trips. How does the frequency fall this time?

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_09
data.value: Faster, and further. Solar panels and many wind turbines connect through electronics, not spinning machines. With less spinning mass the wheel is smaller, and the frequency drops more quickly. That's why grids with lots of renewables add batteries and other fast helpers.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Balance_10
data.value: Your turn. Trip a unit, lose the DC link, or switch on a big load, at any time of day, and watch the frequency.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_01
data.value: Here's a generator at its simplest: a coil of wire turning between the poles of a magnet. Nothing touches the lamp but two wires, and yet it lights up. So where does that electricity come from?

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_02
data.value: The magnet's field runs straight across the gap, from north to south. As the coil turns, the amount of field passing through it keeps changing. Keep an eye on that.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_03
data.value: Let's stop it here. The coil faces the poles square on, so the most field goes through it. But look at the oscilloscope: right now the voltage is zero. For this instant, the amount isn't changing.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_04
data.value: Now a quarter turn on. The coil lies along the field, so no field passes through it at all. And yet the voltage is at its peak. That was Faraday's discovery: the voltage comes from change, not from how much field there is.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_05
data.value: Here's a question. If you turn the coil twice as fast, what happens to the voltage?

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_06
data.value: Now, how does the current get out? Each end of the coil goes to its own ring, and carbon brushes rub on the rings. Every half turn the voltage reverses, so the current goes back and forth. That's alternating current.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_07
data.value: Swap the two rings for one ring split in half: a commutator. Every half turn the halves swap brushes, so the current outside always flows one way. Look at the oscilloscope: the wave is folded up above zero.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_08
data.value: But there's a catch. With current flowing, the magnet pushes on the coil's sides against the way they're moving. So lighting the lamp makes the handle harder to turn. The lamp's energy comes from your arm, or in a power station, from steam, water or wind.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_09
data.value: A real power station turns all this inside out. The magnet spins in the middle, and three coils sit around it, a third of a turn apart. Watch the three lamps light up one after another.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_10
data.value: On the oscilloscope, three waves rise and fall in turn. Add them up at any moment and you get exactly zero. A two-pole machine spinning three thousand times a minute makes fifty of these cycles every second.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Generator_11
data.value: Your turn. Change how fast it turns, the number of turns in the coil, or the magnet, and watch what happens to the voltage.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Brushes
data.value: Brushes are blocks of carbon pressed against the turning rings. They let the current out of a spinning coil without the wires getting twisted up.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Bus
data.value: All the stations feed one connected grid. Power from every source mixes here, and flows to wherever it's being used.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_City
data.value: The city's demand climbs in the morning, dips a little at noon and peaks in the evening. Every switch flicked changes what the plants must make.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Coal
data.value: Coal plants follow the load up and down, but they can't go below a minimum without shutting down. Their big turbines also add spinning mass.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Coil
data.value: The coil is many turns of copper wire. Its golden tint shows how much field passes through it right now. The voltage comes from that amount changing.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Commutator
data.value: This is one ring split into two halves. Every half turn, just as the voltage passes zero, the halves swap brushes, so the current outside always flows the same way.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Core
data.value: The iron core carries the magnetic field from one coil to the other. It's built from thin sheets to keep it from heating up.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Crank
data.value: The handle turns the axle. Drag across the picture to turn it yourself, fast or slow, and watch the voltage follow your hand.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Dial
data.value: The frequency is the grid's pulse. When it holds steady, supply and demand are in balance. If it drops, demand is ahead; if it rises, supply is.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Field
data.value: These lines show the magnetic field. What matters to the coil is how much of it passes through, and how quickly that amount changes.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Flywheel
data.value: This wheel stands for all the turbines and generators spinning in step. Their stored energy cushions any sudden gap. The bigger the wheel, the slower the frequency falls.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Gas
data.value: Gas turbines start up quickly, so they're used mostly at the peaks.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Heat
data.value: This is the power lost on the way, turned into heat in the wires. It grows with the square of the current.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Hydro
data.value: Hydro can change its output in moments, just by opening or closing its gates. That makes it ideal for following the peaks, and for answering a sudden gap.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Import
data.value: A high-voltage DC line brings power from far away, often from big hydro, wind or solar bases. It's steady, but losing it all at once is a big shock.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Lamp
data.value: The lamp shows the power. Click it to open or close the switch. With the switch open no current flows, and the coil turns freely.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Lamps
data.value: There's one lamp on each phase. Turn the machine slowly and you'll see them light up one after another: A, then B, then C.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Line
data.value: Each wire has some resistance, so the current warms it. The dots show the current: the denser and faster they are, the bigger it is.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_North
data.value: This is the magnet's north pole. The field leaves it and crosses the gap to the south pole.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Nuclear
data.value: Nuclear plants run flat out, day and night. They're cheap to run but slow to change, so they carry the steady base of the load.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_PhaseA
data.value: This is the A phase: one coil, its two sides facing each other across the stator. Its voltage peaks each time a magnet pole sweeps past those sides.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_PhaseB
data.value: The B phase is the same kind of coil, turned a third of the way round. So its voltage peaks a third of a cycle after A's.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_PhaseC
data.value: And the C phase sits another third of the way round. Three waves taking turns: that's why three wires can carry the power without a separate return wire.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Pole
data.value: The last step: a small transformer near the street brings the voltage down to what homes use.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Primary
data.value: The input coil has only a few turns. Alternating current in it makes a field in the iron that keeps reversing.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Pumped
data.value: Pumped storage is a giant battery made of two lakes. Spare power pumps water up; at the peak it runs back down through the turbines.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_PushBack
data.value: When current flows, the magnet pushes on the coil's sides against their motion. That's why lighting the lamp makes the handle harder to turn. The energy comes from you.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Pylon
data.value: Pylons hold the wires high and far apart, hanging from long insulators. The higher the voltage, the longer the insulators and the bigger the towers.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Rings
data.value: Each end of the coil goes to its own ring, and the rings turn with it. Each ring always stays joined to the same end, so the current flips every half turn. That's alternating current.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Rotor
data.value: In a real power station the magnet turns, not the coils. This rotor is an electromagnet, spun by a steam or water turbine.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Scope
data.value: The oscilloscope draws the voltage against time. A coil turning steadily draws a smooth sine wave.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Secondary
data.value: The output coil has many more turns. The changing field makes a voltage in every turn, so more turns mean a higher voltage.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Solar
data.value: Solar follows the Sun: nothing at night, a big bulge at midday. Too much at noon has to be stored, or turned back.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_South
data.value: This is the south pole. Between the two poles the field is strong, and runs straight across.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Station
data.value: The power station's generator makes about twenty thousand volts. To travel far, that has to be stepped up.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Stator
data.value: The stator is the part that stays still: a ring of iron with the coils laid in slots. Keeping the coils still means the huge currents need no sliding contacts.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_StepUp
data.value: The step-up substation raises the voltage many times over. The current drops by the same factor, and that's what saves the energy.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Substation
data.value: Near the town, substations step the voltage back down, a stage at a time, to levels that are safer to bring into the streets.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Supply
data.value: Click here to switch the supply between AC and DC. With steady DC, the field in the iron stops changing, and the output falls to nothing.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Town
data.value: The town's lights show how much power arrives. If too much is lost on the way, windows go dark.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Trace
data.value: This graph follows the frequency after the event: the quick fall, the turn, and the slow climb back.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Obj_Wind
data.value: Wind farms make whatever the wind gives them. Often the wind is stronger at night, just when the least power is needed.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_01
data.value: A power station makes electricity at about twenty thousand volts, but the town it feeds may be hundreds of kilometres away. How do we get the power there without losing it on the way?

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_02
data.value: Every wire has some resistance, so current flowing through it warms it up. That heat is lost power, and it grows with the square of the current. Twice the current means four times the loss.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_03
data.value: So we send the same power with less current. Power is voltage times current. The step-up transformer raises the voltage twenty-five times, so the current is twenty-five times smaller.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_04
data.value: Now drop the line to a hundred and ten thousand volts. The current is several times bigger, the wires glow, and look at the heat: nearly half the power never arrives.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_05
data.value: Same power, same wires. If you double the voltage, what happens to the heat that's lost?

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_06
data.value: Back to five hundred thousand volts. The thing that does the stepping up is a transformer: two coils sharing one iron core. Alternating current in the first coil makes a changing field in the iron.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_07
data.value: That changing field makes a voltage in every turn of the second coil. Give it twenty-five times as many turns, and you get twenty-five times the voltage, with a twenty-fifth of the current. The power stays almost the same.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_08
data.value: Now feed it steady direct current instead. The field in the iron stops changing, and the output drops to nothing. That's a big reason why the grid runs on alternating current.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_09
data.value: Near the town, substations step the voltage back down, stage by stage, and a small transformer near each street brings it to the few hundred volts used at home.

data.name: Narr_Grid_Transmission_10
data.value: Your turn. Pick a different voltage, send more power, or send it further, and see how much reaches the town.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_01
data.value: Every heat engine works the same way. Heat flows from a hot place to a cold place, and a machine in between turns some of it into work.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_02
data.value: Here the machine is a gas in a cylinder. While it touches the hot side, it takes in heat and expands, pushing the piston up. That push is the work.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_03
data.value: But to get back to where it started, the gas has to be squeezed again, and on the way it must give some heat to the cold side. Between five hundred and three hundred kelvin, at least sixty of every hundred units of heat are given away.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_04
data.value: So how could you turn more of the heat into work?

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_05
data.value: Widen the gap between the temperatures. A power station's steam, at about five hundred and sixty degrees, could at best turn sixty-four percent of its heat into work. Real power stations manage roughly forty to sixty.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_06
data.value: On the right, the gas's pressure is drawn against its volume. As an engine it goes round clockwise, and the area inside the loop is the work it does in each cycle.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_07
data.value: Run the same cycle backwards, and it becomes a fridge. Now you put work in, and heat is pumped out of the cold inside, up to the warm room. Here, twenty-one units of work move seventy-nine units of heat out of the cold side.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_08
data.value: A heat pump is the same machine, used to warm a house. It delivers the work you put in, plus the heat it draws from the cold outdoor air. Ideally, here a hundred units of heat come indoors for only sixteen units of work.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Cycle_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the hot and cold temperature sliders, and watch how the arrows and the loop change. What happens when the two get close?

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_01
data.value: This is one cylinder of a car engine, cut open down the middle. It works in four strokes. First, intake: the piston moves down, the intake valve opens, and a mixture of air and petrol is drawn in.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_02
data.value: Who opens the valve at just the right moment? The camshaft, up at the top. It turns at half the speed of the crank, and its egg-shaped lobe pushes the valve down, then lets the spring close it again.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_03
data.value: Second, compression. Both valves are shut and the piston rises, squeezing the mixture into about a tenth of the space. Squeezing a gas heats it: by the time the piston nears the top, it's over five hundred degrees.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_04
data.value: Now the mixture is squeezed tight, and the spark plug fires. What do you think happens?

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_05
data.value: It burns in an instant. Just before the top, a spark jumps across the plug's gap, and a flame spreads out from it. In a few thousandths of a second the gas is over two thousand degrees, and its pressure leaps.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_06
data.value: Third, the power stroke. The hot, high-pressure gas pushes the piston down hard. This is the only one of the four strokes that does work.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_07
data.value: The connecting rod passes that push on to the crankshaft and turns it, the way your legs turn a bicycle's pedals. The crank's momentum then carries the engine through the other three strokes.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_08
data.value: Fourth, exhaust. The exhaust valve opens, and the rising piston pushes the spent gas out. It's still about seven hundred degrees hot, and that heat simply leaves with the exhaust.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_09
data.value: More heat soaks into the cylinder walls, and the coolant carries it away to the radiator. Altogether, only about a third of the fuel's energy actually moves the car.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_10
data.value: Let it run. The dial shows the whole cycle: four strokes in two turns of the crank. On the motorway, at three thousand rpm, each cylinder goes round this cycle twenty-five times every second.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Engine_11
data.value: Your turn. Drag sideways across the picture to turn the crank by hand, or click a stroke on the dial to jump to it.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_01
data.value: A fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat from inside to outside. It starts here, in the freezer's back wall: the evaporator. Inside it the refrigerant boils at about minus twenty-five degrees, soaking up heat from the food.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_02
data.value: The vapour flows down to the compressor, the black dome at the bottom. The compressor runs on electricity and squeezes the vapour, which makes it hot: hotter than the kitchen.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_03
data.value: The vapour leaving the compressor is hotter than the room. What do you think happens to it in the pipes at the back?

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_04
data.value: It gives its heat to the room. In the condenser at the back, the hot vapour cools to about forty degrees and turns back into a liquid. That's why the back of a fridge feels warm.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_05
data.value: The liquid then squeezes through the capillary tube, a long tube thinner than a straw. Its pressure drops, so it starts to boil and cools far below zero, ready to soak up heat in the freezer again.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_06
data.value: So out at the back goes all the heat taken from inside, plus the compressor's electricity: here, a hundred and ten watts from inside and sixty-four from the plug. A fridge always warms the kitchen a little.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_07
data.value: What if you leave the door open? Cold air spills out at the bottom, warm air pours in at the top, and the compressor has to run all the time. Its electricity use more than doubles.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_08
data.value: On a hot summer day, at thirty-five degrees, the condenser has to get even hotter to shed its heat. The compressor works harder and runs longer, and the fridge uses about half as much electricity again.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Fridge_09
data.value: Your turn. Click the fridge door to open or shut it, or change the room's temperature, and watch the heat arrows and the numbers.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Camshaft
data.value: The camshaft turns at exactly half the crank's speed, driven by a belt or a chain. Each egg-shaped lobe pushes one valve open once every two turns of the crank, at just the right moment.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Capillary
data.value: The capillary tube is a few metres of tube, thinner than a straw. Squeezing through it, the liquid loses pressure, so it can boil at a very low temperature in the evaporator.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_ColdFlow
data.value: The heat flowing between the machine and the cold side. As an engine, it's the heat that has to be thrown away; as a fridge, it's the heat pumped out of the cold inside.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_ColdSide
data.value: The cold side. For an engine it's the surrounding air or a river; for a fridge, its inside; for a heat pump, the cold air outdoors.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Compressor
data.value: The compressor is the fridge's only moving part. Its electric motor squeezes the refrigerant vapour, raising its pressure and its temperature, so that it can give heat to the room.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Condenser
data.value: The condenser is the grid of pipes at the back. The hot refrigerant gives its heat to the room air here, and condenses into a liquid. Leave a gap behind the fridge so it can breathe.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Coolant
data.value: Coolant flows through passages around the cylinder and carries heat away to the radiator. Without it, the cylinder walls would soon get hot enough to wreck the engine.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Crank
data.value: The crankshaft turns the pistons' pushes into rotation, which goes on to the gearbox and the wheels. The heavy counterweight opposite the pin keeps it spinning smoothly.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Dial
data.value: This dial is the whole four-stroke cycle: once round the dial is two turns of the crank. The ticks mark where the valves open and close, and the dot marks the spark.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Door
data.value: The door's rubber seal keeps warm air out. Each time it opens, cold air spills out at the bottom and warm, moist air takes its place, which the fridge then has to cool again. Click it to open or shut it.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Evaporator
data.value: The evaporator is hidden in the freezer's back wall. The refrigerant boils inside it at about minus twenty-five degrees, and boiling takes in a lot of heat. That's how the inside is cooled.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_ExhaustPort
data.value: The burned gas leaves through this port, on its way to the exhaust pipe. In many cars it first spins a turbocharger, which puts some of the exhaust's energy back to use.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_ExhaustValve
data.value: The exhaust valve opens near the end of the power stroke, and stays open while the piston pushes the burned gas out. It gets very hot, so it's often made of special heat-resistant steel.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Freezer
data.value: The freezer is kept at about minus eighteen degrees: cold enough to stop almost all bacteria growing, and to keep food for months.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_FridgeInside
data.value: The fridge compartment is kept at about four degrees: cold enough to slow bacteria right down, but not so cold that the food freezes.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Gas
data.value: The gas in the cylinder, coloured by its temperature: blue for the cool fresh mixture, glowing orange and yellow once it burns. The reading beside it shows its pressure and temperature right now.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_HeatOut
data.value: Heat given out to the room: everything taken from inside, plus the electricity the compressor uses. A fridge always gives out more heat than it takes in.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_HotFlow
data.value: The heat flowing between the hot side and the machine, counted here as a hundred units. As an engine it flows in; as a fridge or a heat pump, it flows out.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_HotSide
data.value: The hot side. For an engine it's burning fuel or a boiler; for a fridge, the room; for a heat pump, the inside of the house. Temperatures here are in kelvin, counted from absolute zero.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Insulation
data.value: Thick foam fills the walls. It slows down the heat leaking in from the room, so the compressor doesn't have to run all the time.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_IntakePort
data.value: Air and a fine mist of petrol come in through this port. Its smooth curve helps the mixture swirl into the cylinder, so it burns evenly.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_IntakeValve
data.value: The intake valve opens during the intake stroke to let the air and petrol in, and stays shut tight for the other three strokes. The camshaft pushes it open, and its spring closes it.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Isotherm
data.value: An isotherm is a curve of constant temperature: along it, pressure times volume stays the same. The cycle runs partly along the hot side's isotherm, and partly along the cold side's.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Loop
data.value: The loop on the pressure-volume chart. Each trip round is one cycle, and the area it encloses is the work: given out going clockwise, as an engine, and put in going anticlockwise.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Machine
data.value: The machine is just a gas in a cylinder with a piston. Touching the hot side, touching the cold side, or insulated from both, it goes round the same four steps again and again.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Oil
data.value: Oil in the sump is splashed and pumped onto every moving part, so metal slides on a thin film of oil instead of grinding on metal. It also helps to carry heat away.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Piston
data.value: The piston slides up and down inside the cylinder. The rings around it seal the gas in above, and keep the oil out below.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Rod
data.value: The connecting rod links the piston to the crankshaft. It turns the piston's up-and-down motion into the crank's turning, much like a leg on a bicycle pedal.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Room
data.value: The room's temperature. The warmer the room, the more heat leaks into the fridge, and the hotter the condenser must get to shed it, so the fridge uses more electricity.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Spark
data.value: The spark comes about twenty degrees of crank before the top. The flame needs a moment to spread, so firing early means the pressure peaks just as the piston starts down.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_SparkPlug
data.value: The spark plug makes a spark of tens of thousands of volts across a gap smaller than a millimetre. It fires just before the piston reaches the top, so the flame has time to spread.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Step0
data.value: This step keeps the gas at the hot side's temperature. As an engine, the gas expands here and takes in heat; run backwards, it's squeezed here and gives heat out.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Step1
data.value: Here the gas is insulated, so no heat comes in or goes out. As an engine it keeps expanding, and cools itself down to the cold side's temperature; run backwards, it's squeezed, and heats up past the hot side's.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Step2
data.value: This step keeps the gas at the cold side's temperature. As an engine, it's squeezed here and gives heat to the cold side; as a fridge, it expands here and takes heat out of the cold side.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Step3
data.value: Insulated again. As an engine, squeezing the gas warms it back up to the hot side's temperature, ready to start again; run backwards, it expands, and cools below the cold side's.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_StrokeCompression
data.value: The compression stroke: both valves are shut, and the piston rises and squeezes the mixture to about a tenth of its volume, heating it up.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_StrokeExhaust
data.value: The exhaust stroke: the exhaust valve is open, and the rising piston pushes the burned gas out, making room for the next fresh charge.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_StrokeIntake
data.value: The intake stroke: the piston moves down with the intake valve open, drawing in a fresh charge of air and petrol.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_StrokePower
data.value: The power stroke: the burning gas pushes the piston down. It's the only stroke that gives out work; the other three each take a little.

data.name: Narr_Heat_Obj_Work
data.value: Work. As an engine, it's what the machine gives out to turn a wheel; as a fridge or a heat pump, it's the electricity you put in. The energy always adds up: the heat on one side equals the work plus the heat on the other.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_01
data.value: Now we're very far away. A black hole is drifting in front of a distant galaxy. The hole itself is far too small to see. But watch what it does to the light coming from behind it.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_02
data.value: The green outline shows where the galaxy really is. Keep it in mind as the black hole moves in.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_03
data.value: As the hole comes close, the galaxy is stretched round it into a curved arc. Its light has been bent round the black hole on its way to us.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_04
data.value: Now the black hole is exactly in front. Light comes round every side equally, and the galaxy becomes a complete circle. This is called an Einstein ring.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_05
data.value: This little side view shows why. Light passing above the hole and light passing below it are both bent towards us. So we see the same thing coming from two directions at once.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_06
data.value: Let's put a single star behind instead. Now you see two images of it, one on each side of the black hole. Together, they're brighter than the star would be on its own.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_07
data.value: A question: if the black hole had four times as much mass, how big would its Einstein ring be?

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_08
data.value: Twice as wide. The ring grows with the square root of the mass. Astronomers use rings and arcs like these to weigh things they can't see, such as dark matter.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_09
data.value: For a star-sized black hole in our own galaxy, the ring is far too tiny to see. But as it drifts past, the star behind it brightens and then fades again. The chart shows it. That's how astronomers found a lone black hole in 2022.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Lensing_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the black hole across this grid, and see how it warps the picture of the sky around it.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Arc
data.value: The galaxy is stretched round the black hole into an arc. Huge arcs like this are seen round galaxy clusters, from galaxies billions of light years behind them.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Arrow
data.value: The green arrow is the probe's launch speed and direction. Drag its tip: sideways makes it orbit, outwards helps it escape, and inwards sends it towards the hole.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Below
data.value: This thin arc under the shadow is the bottom side of the disk. Its light went under the black hole and was bent back up towards you.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Bent
data.value: This ray passes further out. Gravity bends it a little, and it carries on. The further away light passes, the less it's turned.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Caught
data.value: This ray passes too close. It curves in and falls through the event horizon. Any light aimed within about two and a half horizon radii of the centre is caught like this.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Clocks
data.value: One clock stays far away, the other travels with the probe. Near the black hole, gravity and speed slow the probe's time. Seen from far away, a probe falling in seems to freeze at the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Coming
data.value: On this side the gas is rushing towards you. Its light is squeezed to higher energy, so it looks bluer and much brighter. This is the Doppler effect, also called beaming.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Critical
data.value: This ray passes at just the critical distance. It's swung round the black hole on the photon sphere before it escapes. Rays like this make the photon ring.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Going
data.value: On this side the gas is moving away from you. Its light is stretched, so it looks redder and dimmer. Gravity stretches it a little more as it climbs out.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Hat
data.value: This arch is the back half of the disk, hidden behind the black hole. Light from it was bent up and over the hole to reach you, so you can see what's behind it.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Horizon
data.value: The event horizon is the point of no return. Inside it, even light can't climb out. It isn't a solid surface, just a boundary. For a black hole as heavy as the Sun, it would be only three kilometres from the centre.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Image1
data.value: This is the brighter image of the star, on the same side as the star really is, pushed a little further out. The number shows how much brighter it looks than the star alone.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Image2
data.value: This fainter image is on the opposite side of the black hole. Its light went round the other way. As the hole lines up with the star, the two images close in on the ring.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Inner
data.value: The disk stops at the innermost stable orbit, three times the horizon's radius. Closer than that, gas can't stay in orbit and pours into the black hole.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Isco
data.value: This dashed circle is the innermost stable orbit, three times the horizon's radius. Further out, a probe can circle forever. Closer in, any orbit spirals into the black hole. Newton's gravity has no such limit.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Lens
data.value: This mark is the black hole. At this distance it's far too small to see, but its gravity bends the light passing round it. Drag it anywhere in front of the sky.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Newton
data.value: The grey probe starts exactly like the gold one, but moves with Newton's gravity. Far out they agree. Close in, Newton's probe never falls in and its ellipse never turns.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_PhotonRing
data.value: The photon ring is a thin, bright ring just outside the shadow. Its light went round the black hole once or more before escaping, so it holds a squeezed picture of everything around the hole.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_PhotonSphere
data.value: At one and a half times the horizon's radius, light can travel in a circle round the black hole. But it's balanced on a knife edge. The slightest nudge sends it either falling in or flying away.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Probe
data.value: The gold probe moves the way Einstein's theory of gravity says. Drag it to start it closer or further out, and watch how its path changes.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Ring
data.value: The dashed circle is the Einstein ring. When the black hole is exactly in front of something, that thing's light is spread all the way round this circle. Its size tells you the mass of the lens.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Scale
data.value: Sizes here are measured in M, a length set by the black hole's mass. For a black hole as heavy as the Sun, one M is about one and a half kilometres. The heavier the hole, the bigger everything gets, but the picture looks the same.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Shadow
data.value: The shadow is the dark patch where no light reaches you: every ray from here would have come out of the black hole. It's about two and a half times wider than the event horizon, because light bends round the hole.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_SideView
data.value: Seen from the side: light from the source passes above and below the black hole, and both paths are bent towards us. We see each image straight back along the last part of its path.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Stars
data.value: Around the shadow, the stars behind the black hole are bent and stretched. Some stars even appear twice, once on each side. The black hole acts like a warped lens on the whole sky.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Start
data.value: This ring marks where the probe starts. Drag it closer to the black hole or further away. The launch speed stays the same.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Track
data.value: The black hole drifts along this dashed line. As it passes close to the source, the light is focused and brightens, then fades again, as the chart shows.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_Trail
data.value: This is the path the probe has taken. Near a black hole, an orbit doesn't close up on itself. Each lap it turns a little further round, tracing a rosette.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Obj_True
data.value: This outline shows where the galaxy or star really is. Everything you see moved away from it is light bent on its way to us.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_01
data.value: Here we're looking down on a black hole from above. The black circle is the event horizon. Anything that crosses it, even light, can never come back out.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_02
data.value: Light comes in from the left. Rays that pass far from the hole are bent only a little, and carry on almost straight.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_03
data.value: Rays aimed closer can't get past. They curve in and fall through the horizon. Once inside, they're gone for good.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_04
data.value: In between is a special distance. Light passing just there is swung all the way round the hole before it escapes. It skims the photon sphere, where light could circle the hole forever.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_05
data.value: Now look at the probe. It's in a circular orbit, round and round like a planet going round a star. The grey dot started off exactly the same way, but follows Newton's gravity. It swings out on an ellipse. This close to a black hole, gravity pulls harder than Newton thought.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_06
data.value: This time the probe moves on an ellipse. Newton's probe repeats the same path every lap. But the real one swings further round at each close pass, so its orbit turns, tracing out a rosette.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_07
data.value: Look at the two clocks in the corner. One is far away from the black hole, the other rides with the probe. Which one is running slower?

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_08
data.value: Now the probe is launched with less sideways speed. Newton's probe just swings in close and back out again. But the real one can't get over the hill near the hole, and it plunges in.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_09
data.value: Watch the far-away clock as the probe falls. Seen from far away, the probe slows down and seems to freeze at the edge. It never quite seems to cross. But its own clock keeps ticking, and it falls straight through.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_10
data.value: This orbit sits on the innermost stable circle, three times the horizon's size. Give it the tiniest nudge, and it spirals in. That's why disks of gas round black holes have an inner edge.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Orbits_11
data.value: Your turn. Drag the green arrow to launch the probe your own way. Can you find a launch that escapes? Or one that just barely stays in orbit?

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_01
data.value: This is what a black hole would look like up close, with a disk of hot gas swirling round it. The black patch in the middle is its shadow. No light at all comes from there.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_02
data.value: The dashed circle shows the event horizon at its real size. Notice that the shadow is much bigger, about two and a half times as wide. Light bending round the hole makes it look larger than it really is.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_03
data.value: Right at the edge of the shadow there's a thin, bright ring. That light went almost all the way round the black hole before it finally escaped towards you.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_04
data.value: Now look at this bright arch over the top. It's the far side of the disk, the part hidden behind the black hole. Its light was bent up and over the hole to reach you.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_05
data.value: And this thinner arc underneath is the bottom side of the disk. Its light was bent round the other way, under the hole. So you can see the top, the back and the bottom of the disk all at once.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_06
data.value: Here's a question. The left side of the disk is much brighter than the right. Why do you think that is?

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_07
data.value: The disk spins very fast, at a good fraction of the speed of light. Gas rushing towards you has its light squeezed, bluer and brighter. Gas rushing away looks redder and dimmer. That's the Doppler effect.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_08
data.value: Now let's imagine light didn't bend at all. All you'd see is a flat disk with a small black ball in the middle. Every strange shape you saw before was made by gravity bending light.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_09
data.value: Let's turn the bending back on and look from above. The disk is a glowing ring. Its inner edge is the innermost stable orbit. Any closer, and gas can't keep circling. It falls straight in.

data.name: Narr_Hole_Shadow_10
data.value: Now it's your turn. Drag up or down on the picture to tilt your view, and watch the arch rise over the top as you look from the side.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Aphelion
data.value: Aphelion is the farthest point, five million kilometres farther out. Today it falls in early July, so northern summers are a little gentler.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Axis
data.value: Earth spins around this tilted axis. The axis keeps pointing the same way all year, so first one hemisphere leans toward the Sun, then the other. That gives us seasons.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Co2
data.value: In ice ages, the cold oceans soaked up carbon dioxide from the air. Less carbon dioxide meant a weaker greenhouse effect, so the whole world cooled, by about six degrees.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Coast
data.value: All that ice was once sea water. So when the ice grows, the sea falls, by up to a hundred and twenty metres. The coast moves far out.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Earth
data.value: Here's Earth on its yearly trip. Watch its speed: it hurries when it's close to the Sun and slows down when it's far away.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Eccentricity
data.value: Eccentricity tells you how stretched the orbit is. Zero would be a perfect circle. The pull of Jupiter and Saturn slowly changes it, over cycles of about a hundred thousand and four hundred thousand years.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Fennoscandian
data.value: This ice sheet spread out from Scandinavia. It covered the Baltic Sea and reached across to Britain and northern Germany.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Future
data.value: This is the future, if only the orbit mattered. The next ice age would begin in about fifty thousand years. But the carbon dioxide people have added will hold it off for much longer.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Globe
data.value: This is the top of the world, seen from straight above the North Pole. North America is on the left and Europe is at the bottom. White shows the ice.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Greenland
data.value: Greenland is the one big northern ice sheet that survives even in warm times like today. It's a leftover from the last ice age.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Ground
data.value: Kilometres of ice are so heavy that they press the ground down, by up to almost a kilometre. The ground is slow to respond, so it keeps sinking, or rising, for thousands of years.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Hudson
data.value: Hudson Bay sits right under the middle of the old ice sheet. The ground there is still rising today, about a centimetre a year.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_IceChart
data.value: This shows how much ice there was in the north, with sea level on the right. Look at its shape: a slow climb, then a sudden drop. Slow to grow, fast to melt.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Laurentide
data.value: The Laurentide ice sheet grew over Canada. At its biggest it was about as large as Antarctica's ice is today, and more than three kilometres thick.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Melt
data.value: At the low southern edge, it's warm enough to melt. Meltwater runs off toward the sea. When melting beats snowfall, the sheet shrinks.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Now
data.value: This line is today. We're in a warm spell called the Holocene, which began about eleven thousand years ago.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Orbit
data.value: Earth's orbit is an ellipse, but a very round one. The gold half is northern spring and summer, the blue half is autumn and winter.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Perihelion
data.value: Perihelion is the point where Earth comes closest to the Sun. Today that happens in early January, during northern winter. But the date slowly moves through the year.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_PoleStar
data.value: Like a spinning top, Earth's axis slowly traces a circle in the sky. Today it points near Polaris. In about twelve thousand years, it will point near Vega instead.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Reflect
data.value: White ice sends most of the sunlight straight back to space. So a big ice sheet keeps itself cold. Scientists call this the ice–albedo feedback.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Ring65
data.value: This circle is sixty-five degrees north. It runs through Canada, Scandinavia and Siberia, right where the great ice sheets grew. So scientists measure summer sunshine here.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SeaIce
data.value: Frozen sea water floats on the Arctic Ocean. In ice ages, summer sea ice reached much farther south, and made the north even brighter and colder.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Sheet
data.value: An ice sheet is a dome of ice kilometres thick. It spreads out under its own weight, like thick honey on a plate.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SnowLine
data.value: Above the snow line, winter snow lasts through the whole summer. Below it, the snow melts. Weak summers bring this line down, and then snow can pile up on the ice.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Snowfall
data.value: Snow falls on top of the dome, gets buried and is squeezed into ice. This is how an ice sheet grows.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Strip
data.value: This strip covers nine hundred thousand years, from eight hundred thousand years ago to a hundred thousand years from now. Drag along it to travel through time.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SummerHalf
data.value: Count the days from the spring equinox to the autumn one, then back again. They aren't equal! Earth moves slowest when it's far from the Sun, so that half of the year lasts longer.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun sits at one focus of the orbit, not in the middle. That's why Earth is a little closer to it at one end of the year than at the other.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SunMeter
data.value: This meter shows the midsummer sunshine at sixty-five degrees north, compared with today. A few tens of watts may not sound like much, but kept up for thousands of years, it decides whether snow survives.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SunRays
data.value: This is the midsummer sunlight. The stronger it is, the more snow it can melt. Its strength is set by the orbit.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_SunshineChart
data.value: This line is the summer sunshine at sixty-five degrees north, worked out from the orbit. It wiggles fast with the wobble, and its wiggles grow and shrink with the stretch.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Terminations
data.value: Each red number marks the end of a big ice age. Notice that they're roughly a hundred thousand years apart. Each one comes when strong summers meet a huge, fragile ice sheet.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Obj_Tilt
data.value: This is the tilt of Earth's axis. Every forty-one thousand years, it rocks between about twenty-two and twenty-four and a half degrees. A bigger tilt means stronger seasons, especially near the poles.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_01
data.value: Have you ever wondered why there were ice ages? The answer starts up in space, with Earth's trip around the Sun. Here's Earth, going round once a year.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_02
data.value: This orbit isn't quite a circle. It's a slightly stretched ellipse, and here we've drawn the stretch five times bigger, so you can see it.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_03
data.value: The first cycle is the stretch. Watch the gauge as time runs by. Over about a hundred thousand years, the orbit goes from nearly round to a bit more oval, and back again.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_04
data.value: The second cycle is the tilt. Earth's axis slowly rocks back and forth, about once every forty-one thousand years.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_05
data.value: Here's a question. When the axis leans more, what happens to summers near the North Pole?

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_06
data.value: The third cycle is the wobble. Look at where perihelion is, the point closest to the Sun. Today, we pass it in early January, in the middle of northern winter.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_07
data.value: Now jump back eleven thousand years. Perihelion has moved into northern summer! Being closest to the Sun in summer made northern summers stronger.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_08
data.value: The wobble also turns the axis around in the sky, like a spinning top. Watch the pole drift slowly from star to star.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_09
data.value: And here's a surprise. Count the days in the two halves of the year. Because Earth is far from the Sun in July, northern spring and summer last about a week longer.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_10
data.value: Now put all three cycles together. The strip shows the summer sunshine they make in the far north. A hundred and fifteen thousand years ago, it dropped very low, and the last ice age began.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Orbit_11
data.value: Your turn! Drag along the strip and look for the low points. Can you find the times when summers in the north were weakest?

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_01
data.value: Let's cut a slice through North America, twenty-one thousand years ago. This white dome is the ice sheet, more than three kilometres thick.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_02
data.value: This dashed line is the summer snow line. Above it, snow survives the summer. When summers are weak, the line sinks, and more of the ice sits above it.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_03
data.value: Snow keeps falling on the high middle of the dome. It gets buried and pressed into ice, so the sheet grows.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_04
data.value: Now look at the sunlight. When it hits the white ice, most of it bounces straight back to space.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_05
data.value: So here's a puzzle. Why does a big ice sheet help itself grow even bigger?

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_06
data.value: Here's something else. The ice is so heavy that it pushes the ground down underneath it, by hundreds of metres.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_07
data.value: And all that ice came from the sea. So the sea level fell, and the coast moved far out into the Gulf of Mexico.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_08
data.value: Now jump to thirteen thousand years ago. Summers are strong, and the snow line has climbed. The edges are melting back fast.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_09
data.value: Nine thousand years ago, most of the ice is gone, but the ground is still pressed down. It rises back slowly, and around Hudson Bay, it's still rising today.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_10
data.value: One more helper: carbon dioxide. In ice ages there was less of it in the air, so the whole world was colder, which helped the ice. When it came back, it helped the melting.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sheet_11
data.value: Your turn! Drag along the strip and watch the ice sheet grow, then melt. Keep an eye on the snow line and the coast.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_01
data.value: Now we're looking down on the North Pole. The gold circle is sixty-five degrees north, where the great ice sheets grew. Summer sunshine here is the key.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_02
data.value: This chart shows that summer sunshine over eight hundred thousand years. It goes up and down by about a tenth, all because of the orbit.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_03
data.value: Let's go back a hundred and fifteen thousand years. Look at the sun meter: summers in the north were much weaker than today.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_04
data.value: So what do you think happens to the snow when summers stay weak for thousands of years?

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_05
data.value: Let's watch it happen. Each summer, a little snow is left over. Year after year it piles up, and a sheet of ice spreads across Canada.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_06
data.value: This is the last glacial maximum, about twenty-one thousand years ago. There's so much ice that the sea has dropped about a hundred and twenty metres.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_07
data.value: Then summers grow strong again, and the ice melts much faster than it grew. The red numbers mark the end of each big ice age like this one.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_08
data.value: Look at the whole pattern: a slow climb, then a sudden collapse, about every hundred thousand years. That's the sawtooth rhythm of the ice ages.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_09
data.value: And this is today. We're in a warm spell that began about eleven thousand years ago, when the last ice sheets melted.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_10
data.value: In this simple model, with the orbit alone, the next ice age would begin about fifty thousand years from now. But the carbon dioxide we've added will delay it far longer.

data.name: Narr_Ice_Sunshine_11
data.value: Your turn! Drag along the sunshine chart. Watch the ice sheets grow when summers are weak, and melt away when they're strong.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_01
data.value: Kepler's second law is about speed. Imagine a line from the Sun to the planet. As the planet moves, this line sweeps across the orbit, a bit like a windscreen wiper.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_02
data.value: The orbit is cut into twelve coloured slices. The planet takes exactly the same time to cross each one: one twelfth of its year.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_03
data.value: Compare these two slices. Near the Sun, the slice is short and wide. Far away, it's long and thin. But their areas are exactly the same.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_04
data.value: So in the same amount of time, the planet covers much more of its orbit when it's near the Sun. This orange arrow shows its speed. Watch it grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_05
data.value: Think about it. Where does the planet move fastest?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_06
data.value: Closest to the Sun. That point is called perihelion. The farthest point is aphelion, where the planet is slowest. Earth does this too: in early January it moves about one kilometre per second faster than in early July.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag the planet around its orbit with the mouse, and watch how its speed changes.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_08
data.value: Halley's comet shows this most of all. It rushes past the Sun in a few months, then crawls through the far end of its orbit for decades. That's Kepler's second law: equal areas in equal times.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_01
data.value: This loop is an orbit, the path a planet takes around the Sun. Look closely: it isn't a circle. It's an ellipse, a circle that's been stretched.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_02
data.value: And the Sun isn't in the middle. It sits off to one side, at a special point called a focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_03
data.value: An ellipse has two foci. The other one is over here, and it's completely empty. Nothing at all is there.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_04
data.value: Now picture a loop of string pinned at both foci, with a pencil pulling it tight. The gold part runs from the Sun to the planet, and the blue part from the planet to the empty focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_05
data.value: Here the planet is at its closest to the Sun, so the gold part is short. Think about it: what about the blue part?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_06
data.value: It's longer. Wherever the planet goes, the two parts always add up to the same length: the long axis of the ellipse. That's how gardeners mark out an oval flower bed, with two pegs and a loop of rope.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_07
data.value: Now you try. Move the orbit shape slider on the left page. Make the orbit rounder, or more stretched, and watch the empty focus move.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_08
data.value: This is Earth's real orbit. It's so close to a circle that you can hardly tell the difference. That's Kepler's first law: every planet moves on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Aphelion
data.value: Aphelion, the point farthest from the Sun. Here the planet moves slowest. Earth passes it in early July.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Center
data.value: The centre of the ellipse. Neither focus is here: the Sun sits off to one side.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Circle
data.value: A circle of the same size, to compare. The more the orbit is stretched, the further it strays from this circle.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our home. One trip round the Sun is one year, about three hundred and sixty-five days.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_EqualAreas
data.value: Each coloured slice takes the same time and has the same area. That's Kepler's second law.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_FocalDistance
data.value: This is how far the Sun sits from the centre. Divide it by half the long axis and you get the eccentricity: zero for a circle, and close to one for a very stretched orbit.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, about five times as far from the Sun as Earth. It takes almost twelve years to go round once.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_MajorAxis
data.value: The long axis of the ellipse, from one end to the other. Half of it is the planet's average distance from the Sun, and that sets how long its year is.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, about one and a half times as far from the Sun as Earth. Its year is almost two of ours.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun. It goes round in just eighty-eight days, faster than any other planet.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_OtherFocus
data.value: The other focus. Nothing is here at all, no star and no planet. It's just a point that belongs to the shape of the ellipse.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Perihelion
data.value: Perihelion, the point of the orbit closest to the Sun. Here the planet moves fastest. Earth passes it in early January.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Planet
data.value: The body going round the Sun. You can drag it along its orbit with the mouse.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, nearly ten times as far from the Sun as Earth. It goes round once in about twenty-nine and a half years.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Scale
data.value: The scale bar. One astronomical unit is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about a hundred and fifty million kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_String
data.value: The string. One part runs from the Sun to the planet, the other from the planet to the empty focus. As one grows, the other shrinks, but together they always make the same length.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Its gravity keeps every planet on its orbit. Notice that it isn't at the centre of an orbit, but at one of its two foci.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Velocity
data.value: The planet's speed right now, in kilometres per second. The arrow points the way it's going.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the second planet. Its year is about two hundred and twenty-five days, and its orbit is almost a perfect circle.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_You
data.value: Your planet. Drag it nearer to the Sun or farther away, and its year changes to follow Kepler's third law.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_01
data.value: Now let's compare planets. Here are the planets out to Saturn, seen from above, at their real places today. Earth goes round once in one year.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_02
data.value: Mercury, closest to the Sun, needs only eighty-eight days. The farther out, the longer the year: Mars takes almost two years, and Jupiter almost twelve.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_03
data.value: This green dot is a planet of your own. It started out in line with Earth, but it's farther from the Sun, so it slowly falls behind.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_04
data.value: Think about it. If your planet were four times as far from the Sun as Earth, how long would its year be?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_05
data.value: Eight years. Kepler found that the year, squared, equals the distance, cubed. Four cubed is sixty-four, and eight squared is sixty-four too. Planets farther out have a longer way to go, and they also move more slowly.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_06
data.value: Now you try. Drag your planet nearer to the Sun or farther away, and see how long its year becomes.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_07
data.value: This rule works for every planet. Later, Isaac Newton showed where it comes from: the Sun's gravity gets weaker the farther away you are. The table on the left page checks it for each planet.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_01
data.value: Here's a convex lens, thicker in the middle than at the edges. On the left stands a candle, on the line through the middle of the lens, called the axis. Let's follow the light from the tip of its flame.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_02
data.value: Start with the gold ray. It leaves the flame parallel to the axis. The lens bends it, and on the far side it passes through a special point.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_03
data.value: That point is the focus, F. Every ray that arrives parallel to the axis is bent through it. Its distance from the lens is the focal length, here fifteen centimetres.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_04
data.value: Now the blue ray. It goes through the very centre of the lens, where the two faces are almost parallel, so it carries straight on without bending.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_05
data.value: And the pink ray. It passes through the focus on the near side first, and the lens turns it parallel to the axis. It's the gold ray, run backwards.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_06
data.value: Where the three rays meet again, the flame forms an image. Notice that it's upside down, and smaller than the candle. With the candle beyond twice the focal length, this is just how a camera works.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_07
data.value: Here's a question. If the candle moves closer, between F and 2F, what do you think happens to the image?

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_08
data.value: The image grows and moves farther from the lens. Now it's even bigger than the candle itself. A projector works this way, throwing a large picture onto a wall.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_09
