data.value: Now the candle is inside the focal point. After the lens, the rays still spread apart and never meet. But trace them backwards, and they seem to come from a bigger, upright candle. That's a virtual image, the one you see through a magnifying glass.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_10
data.value: A real image can be caught on a screen, but only in the right place. This screen is a little too far, so the light from each point has already spread out. Look at the picture in the corner: it's blurred.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_11
data.value: Finally, a concave lens. It's thinner in the middle and spreads light out, so wherever the candle stands, you only get a small, upright, virtual image. Glasses for short sight use lenses like this.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Bench_12
data.value: Your turn. The screen is in the wrong place again. Drag the candle or the screen until the picture in the corner becomes sharp.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_01
data.value: A camera works a lot like an eye. Its lens gathers light from the scene and forms an image on the sensor at the back, upside down, just as on the retina.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_02
data.value: But a camera can't change the shape of its lens. To focus, it moves the whole lens instead. Light from near things meets farther back, so focusing close moves the lens forward.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_03
data.value: Here it's focused on the person, five metres away. Their light meets exactly on the sensor, so in the photo they're sharp.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_04
data.value: Light from the branch close by would meet behind the sensor. The sensor cuts its cone short, so each point lands as a little disc, called a blur circle. That's why the branch looks soft.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_05
data.value: This is the aperture, the hole the light comes through. Open it wide, to f one point four, and the cones get fatter. Everything out of focus blurs much more.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_06
data.value: Close it down to f eleven, and the cones get thin. Now much more of the scene looks sharp. This sharp zone is called the depth of field.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_07
data.value: Quick question. For a portrait with a soft, blurry background, what should you do?

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_08
data.value: Now the light is fading, and the shutter stays open for a fifteenth of a second. The ball keeps moving while it's open, so it smears into a streak.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_09
data.value: A thousandth of a second freezes the ball. But so little light gets in that the photo is nearly black. Look at the meter: we're about six stops short.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_10
data.value: Raising the ISO amplifies the signal to make up for it, but the noise is amplified too, so the photo turns grainy. Aperture, shutter and ISO always trade against each other.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_11
data.value: Last, the focal length. A long, two hundred millimetre lens sees only a narrow slice of the scene and makes it big. A short lens sees wide.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Camera_12
data.value: Your turn. Click something in the photo to focus on it, or change the aperture, the shutter or the zoom, and see how the picture changes.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_01
data.value: This is an eye, cut in half and seen from the side. Light from the chart on the left comes in through the cornea, the clear dome at the front.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_02
data.value: Behind the cornea, the coloured iris leaves a round hole, the pupil. It narrows in bright light and opens wide in the dark, like a camera's aperture.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_03
data.value: The cornea does most of the bending. Then the lens behind the pupil fine-tunes it, so the light from each point of the chart meets again on the retina at the back.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_04
data.value: Look at the image on the retina. It's upside down! The gold light from the top of the chart lands at the bottom. Your brain quietly turns it the right way up.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_05
data.value: Now the chart comes close, a quarter of a metre away. Light from near things spreads out more, so the eye has to bend it harder. The ciliary muscle tightens, and the lens bulges. This is called accommodation.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_06
data.value: But there's a limit, called the near point. Any closer, and the lens can't bulge any more, so things blur. At twenty years old, it's less than ten centimetres away.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_07
data.value: As we age, the lens stiffens. At sixty, the near point has moved out to a couple of metres, so a book at reading distance is a blur. That's why older people need reading glasses.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_08
data.value: Now imagine this eye were a little too long, as happens in short sight. Where do you think the light from a far chart would meet?

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_09
data.value: It meets in front of the retina, then spreads out again, so far things blur. That's short sight. This eye only sees clearly out to its far point, about a third of a metre away.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_10
data.value: Glasses fix it. A concave lens in front spreads the light out a little first, so the eye focuses it right on the retina again, and the far chart is sharp.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Eye_11
data.value: Your turn. Drag the chart nearer or farther, or change the age, the eye or the glasses, and watch what the lens does.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Aberration
data.value: Real lenses have spherical faces, and rays through the edge are bent a little too much. They cross the axis nearer the lens than the middle rays, so the focus is a short smear instead of a point.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Aperture
data.value: Blades inside the lens make an adjustable hole. The f-number is the focal length divided by the hole's width, so a small f-number means a big hole: more light, and a shallower zone of sharpness.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Axis
data.value: This line through the middle of the lens is the optical axis. A ray along it goes straight through without bending, and all the distances are measured along it.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Ball
data.value: The ball keeps moving while the shutter is open, so it's recorded as a streak. A faster shutter freezes it; a slower one smears it more.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_BlindSpot
data.value: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye, there's no room for light-sensitive cells. Light landing here isn't seen at all, but the brain fills in the gap, so you never notice.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_BlurCircle
data.value: Light from the nearby branch would meet behind the sensor. Cut short by the sensor, its cone lands as a little disc. Every point of the branch becomes a disc like this, so the branch looks soft.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_CameraLens
data.value: A camera lens is several pieces of glass working together as one convex lens. To focus closer, the whole lens moves a little forward, away from the sensor.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Candle
data.value: Every point of the flame sends light out in all directions. The lens catches a cone of it and bends it. Drag the candle and see how the image moves.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Centre
data.value: At the very middle of the lens its two faces are parallel, like a thin window. A ray through here goes straight on.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Chart
data.value: This is the chart we're looking at. Drag it along the track, from very close to far away, and watch the lens change its shape.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Chromatic
data.value: Glass bends blue light more than red, so blue focuses a little nearer the lens. Here the effect is drawn six times stronger. It gives cheap lenses coloured fringes.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Ciliary
data.value: This ring of muscle holds the lens by fine fibres. When it relaxes, the fibres pull the lens flat for far vision. When it tightens, they slacken, and the lens bulges to focus near. Long reading tires it.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Cornea
data.value: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye. Light bends most here, going from air into the eye, so it does about two thirds of all the focusing. Laser eye surgery reshapes it.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Dof
data.value: Between these limits, the blur circles are too small to notice, so everything here looks sharp. A smaller aperture, a shorter lens or a farther focus all make it deeper.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_EyeLens
data.value: The eye's own lens is soft and elastic, and it can change its shape: flatter for far things, rounder for near ones. That fine-tunes the focus.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_FarPoint
data.value: The farthest place this eye sees clearly when it is fully relaxed. For a normal eye it's at infinity. A short-sighted eye's far point is close: at minus three dioptres, only a third of a metre.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Focus
data.value: Light arriving parallel to the axis is brought together here, at the focal point. Its distance from the lens is the focal length. The shorter it is, the stronger the lens.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_FocusMark
data.value: The camera is focused at this distance: light from here meets exactly on the sensor. Drag the pin, or click something in the photo, to focus there.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Fov
data.value: A short focal length sees a wide angle and makes everything small; a long one sees a narrow slice and makes it big. That's what a zoom changes.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Fovea
data.value: This small pit is packed with cone cells, so it sees the finest detail and the best colour. Whatever you look straight at lands here.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Glasses
data.value: Glasses add a little bending in front of the eye. A concave lens spreads light for short sight; a convex one adds bending for long sight, or for reading.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Iris
data.value: The coloured iris is a ring of muscle, and the hole in its middle is the pupil. In bright light it shrinks to about two millimetres; in the dark it opens to six or more. A small pupil also makes blur smaller.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Lens
data.value: A lens is a piece of glass with curved faces. Light slows down in glass, so it bends where it goes in and where it comes out. A convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings light together; a concave one, thinner in the middle, spreads it apart.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Meter
data.value: The meter compares the light the settings let in with what this scene needs. Each mark is one stop, a doubling or halving of the light. Zero is just right.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_NearPoint
data.value: The closest place this eye can still focus, with its lens as round as it gets. It moves away with age, from under ten centimetres in children to beyond arm's length after sixty.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Photo
data.value: This is the picture the sensor records. Focus, depth of field, motion blur, brightness and grain all come from the settings. Click anything in it to focus there.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Ray1
data.value: This ray sets off parallel to the axis. A convex lens bends it through the focal point on the far side; a concave lens bends it away, as if it came from the near focal point.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Ray2
data.value: This ray passes through the centre of the lens and carries straight on. It makes finding the image easy: the image of the flame's tip lies somewhere on this line.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Ray3
data.value: This ray passes through the near focal point before the lens, and the lens turns it parallel to the axis. It's the parallel ray, run backwards.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_RealImage
data.value: Here the light really does come together again, so you can catch it on a screen. A real image made by one lens is always upside down.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Retina
data.value: The retina lines the back of the eye with light-sensitive cells, more than a hundred million of them. The picture formed here is turned into nerve signals.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_RetinalImage
data.value: The image on the retina is real, small and upside down: light from the top of the chart lands at the bottom. Your brain turns it the right way up.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Screen
data.value: A white card that catches light. Where the light from each point of the flame meets on it, you see a sharp picture. Move it away, and each point spreads into a blurry patch.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_ScreenView
data.value: This is what the screen shows, enlarged. Notice that the candle is upside down, and that it blurs as the screen moves away from the image.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Sensor
data.value: Millions of tiny light sensors, one for each pixel, sit here, where the retina would be in an eye. The image on it is upside down; the camera simply flips the numbers.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Shutter
data.value: The shutter decides how long light falls on the sensor, from a few thousandths of a second to whole seconds. Longer lets in more light, but moving things smear.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Subject
data.value: The camera now focuses on this. Things nearer or farther blur, more so with a wide aperture. It's what happens when you tap the screen of a phone camera.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_TwoF
data.value: This mark is two focal lengths from the lens. A candle here makes an image of the same size, at 2F on the other side. Beyond it the image is smaller; inside it, bigger.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_View
data.value: This is the chart as this eye sees it. When the light doesn't meet on the retina, each point spreads into a small disc, and the smallest rows blur first.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_VirtualImage
data.value: No light actually reaches this place. The rays only seem to come from it when you look back through the lens, so no screen can catch it. A magnifying glass shows you one.

data.name: Narr_Lens_Obj_Vitreous
data.value: Most of the eye is filled with a clear jelly that keeps it round. Light crosses it on the way to the retina.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_01
data.value: This is a thundercloud cut in half, thirty-six kilometres across and drawn to scale. Its top reaches twelve kilometres up, where it's colder than minus forty degrees.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_02
data.value: A strong updraft carries air up through the cloud. Tiny ice crystals ride up with it, while heavier pellets of soft hail, called graupel, fall slowly through them.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_03
data.value: When they collide, charge moves between them. Above this line, at about minus fifteen degrees, the graupel takes negative charge and the crystals positive. Below it, it's the other way round.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_04
data.value: So the cloud sorts itself out: positive charge at the top, carried up by the crystals, a big negative layer in the middle, and a little positive charge near the bottom.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_05
data.value: Now, what do you think happens to the ground under the storm?

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_06
data.value: It turns positive. The negative middle of the cloud draws positive charge in the ground towards it. The field meter shows the field pointing up, many times stronger than on a fair day: strong enough to make your hair stand on end.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_07
data.value: When the charge grows big enough, the air breaks down, and there's a flash! Most flashes stay inside the cloud. Only some reach the ground, like this one.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_08
data.value: Let's make the storm taller, up to sixteen kilometres. A stronger updraft separates charge much faster, so it flashes about four times as often as before.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Cloud_09
data.value: Your turn. Change the height of the storm, or click the ground to move the field meter, and watch the field and the flashes.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Anvil
data.value: The anvil: at the top of the storm the rising air can go no higher, so it spreads out sideways into a flat sheet of ice cloud.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Ball
data.value: A metal ball, joined to the earth by a wire. The rod draws opposite charge up into its near side, and when the gap is small enough, a spark jumps across. Click to bring the rod up to it.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Cloth
data.value: The cloth it's rubbed on. Whatever the rod takes, the cloth loses, so the cloth ends up with the same amount of the opposite charge. Click it to watch the rubbing.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_CloudBase
data.value: The base of the cloud, two kilometres up, where the leader starts its way down.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Corona
data.value: A tree right under the storm. When the field is strong, the tips of its leaves glow faintly with corona: the air around sharp points starts to conduct.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Dart
data.value: A dart leader: it slides smoothly down the still-hot channel in a couple of thousandths of a second, without stepping or branching, and sets off the next stroke.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Earth
data.value: The wire to earth. The ground is so big that it can give or take any amount of charge, so charge flows to or from it freely.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Field
data.value: The electric field at the ground. On a fair day it points gently down. Under a storm it turns over, points up, and grows dozens of times stronger.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Freezing
data.value: The freezing level, zero degrees. Above it, the cloud holds a mix of ice and supercooled water, which is where the charging happens.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Glaciation
data.value: Minus forty degrees: colder than this, every droplet has frozen, and the cloud is all ice.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Graupel
data.value: Graupel: soft hail, little pellets of rime ice. They're heavy enough to fall through the updraft, colliding with the crystals on the way.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Hit
data.value: What the lightning hit: whatever sent up the streamer that connected first. That's usually the tallest thing near the leader's tip, not simply the tallest thing around.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_House
data.value: A house. Without a rod, a strike to the roof can set it on fire or send current through the wiring. With a rod, the current goes safely down a conductor into the ground.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Humidity
data.value: How damp the air is. In damp air a thin film of water on every surface lets charge leak away in seconds. In dry air it can last for many minutes.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Ice
data.value: Ice crystals: tiny and light, carried up by the updraft. They take positive charge in collisions high in the cloud and carry it to the top.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Later
data.value: A later return stroke, down the same channel. Later strokes usually carry less current than the first, and there's no branching.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Leader
data.value: The stepped leader: a faint channel of charged air, jumping down about fifty metres at a time and branching. It takes a few hundredths of a second to come down.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_LightningRod
data.value: A lightning rod: a metal point on the roof, joined by a thick conductor to a rod in the ground. It doesn't attract lightning from far away; it gives a strike a safe path down.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Lower
data.value: A small positive charge low in the cloud, from graupel that charged positive below the reversal level. It can help a flash get started towards the ground.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Main
data.value: The main negative charge, in the middle of the cloud around minus fifteen degrees. Most flashes start here, to the top of the cloud or down to the ground.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Meter
data.value: A field meter, and you beside it. It measures the electric field at the ground. Click the ground to move it nearer or further from the storm.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Paper
data.value: Bits of paper, with no charge of their own. A charged rod nearby pulls them up anyway, because it shifts their electrons. Click to hold the rod over them.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Person
data.value: A person in the open: the tallest thing around. If you hear thunder, get indoors or into a car. Don't stand under a tree.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Rain
data.value: Rain falling from the cloud base. Below the freezing level, the graupel melts into heavy raindrops.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Reversal
data.value: The charge reversal level, about minus fifteen degrees. Colder than this, graupel turns negative when crystals bounce off it; warmer, it turns positive.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Rod
data.value: The rod or balloon, with its charge drawn as signs and its voltage on the label. On an insulator the charge stays where it was rubbed. Drag it yourself to move it.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Slow
data.value: How much the picture is slowed down. The whole flash is over in a fraction of a second, so each part is slowed by a different amount for you to see it.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Spark
data.value: A spark: the air between the rod and the ball breaks down and conducts for a moment, heats up and glows. The crack you hear is a tiny clap of thunder.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Sphere
data.value: The striking distance, drawn as a circle around the leader's tip. Anything inside it can send up a streamer that connects. Stronger flashes reach further.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Squeezed
data.value: Above this line the heights are squeezed, so the whole two kilometres up to the cloud fit on the screen. Below it, everything is to scale.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Streamer
data.value: Upward streamers: sparks rising from tall, pointed things to meet the leader. Several may rise; the first to connect decides where the lightning strikes.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Strip
data.value: The flash and its thunder on their way to you. Light arrives at once; sound takes about three seconds for every kilometre. Click to play the thunder.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Stroke
data.value: The return stroke: the main flash. A huge current races up the connected channel, heating the air to around thirty thousand degrees, hotter than the Sun's surface.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Top
data.value: The top of the storm and how cold it is up there. The taller the storm, the stronger its updraft, and the more often it flashes.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Tree
data.value: A tall, lone tree: a likely target, and a dangerous place to shelter in a storm. A strike can jump from the trunk to someone standing close by.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Updraft
data.value: The updraft: warm, moist air rising fast up the middle of the storm, often at tens of metres a second. It keeps the ice and graupel mixing, which is what charges the cloud.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Upper
data.value: The upper positive charge, carried up by the ice crystals to the top of the storm.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Water
data.value: A thin stream of water from a tap. Its molecules turn to face the charge, so it bends towards a charged rod, positive or negative. Click to bring the rod beside it.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Obj_Zone
data.value: The protected zone. Roll a ball as big as the striking distance over the ground and everything on it: where the ball can't reach, lightning can't either.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_01
data.value: On this bench, a balloon is being rubbed on some hair. Both are made of atoms, and in each atom the positive and negative charges exactly balance. Until we start rubbing.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_02
data.value: Watch the little blue dots. They're electrons, hopping from the hair onto the balloon. The balloon gains extra electrons and turns negative, and the hair, left short of them, turns positive.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_03
data.value: Here's a question. Why do the electrons go onto the balloon, and not the other way round?

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_04
data.value: Right. Every material grips its electrons differently, and when two touch, electrons move to the one that grips harder. Nothing is made, only moved. The label shows about twenty thousand volts, but so little charge that it's harmless.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_05
data.value: Hold the balloon over bits of paper, and they jump up, though they have no charge of their own. The balloon pushes the paper's electrons to its far side, so the near side is pulled harder than the far side is pushed. Some cling, take a little charge, and are flung off again.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_06
data.value: Now bring it beside a thin stream of water. The stream bends towards the balloon. Water molecules turn their opposite end towards the charge, so the water is pulled whichever sign the balloon has.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_07
data.value: Now up to an earthed metal ball. When the gap is small enough, the air breaks down, and there's a spark! It takes several thousand volts to jump each millimetre of air. A lightning flash is the same thing, only vastly bigger.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_08
data.value: Now make the air damp. Even while it's being rubbed, the balloon holds only a little charge: it leaks away through a thin film of water as fast as it's made. That's why static shocks happen in dry winter air.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Static_09
data.value: Your turn. Try other materials or other air, or drag the rod yourself: rub it on the cloth, then take it to the paper, the water and the ball.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_01
data.value: Now let's watch one strike in slow motion. The cloud base is two kilometres up. The lowest hundred metres are drawn to scale, and everything above is squeezed to fit.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_02
data.value: A stepped leader feels its way down from the cloud, about fifty metres at a jump, branching as it goes. It's faint: you'd hardly see it.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_03
data.value: As it nears the ground, something will reach up to meet it. When do you think that happens?

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_04
data.value: Right. For a thirty-kiloampere flash, once the leader is within about ninety metres, the striking distance, sparks called streamers rise from tall, pointed things. The lightning rod's streamer got there first.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_05
data.value: They connect, and the return stroke races up the channel at about a third of the speed of light, carrying thirty thousand amps. That's the blinding flash we see.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_06
data.value: Now take the rod away. The same leader strikes the roof instead, and with no path to earth, the current finds its own way through the house.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_07
data.value: With the rod back, look at the green zone. A ball as big as the striking distance, rolled over everything, can't touch anything in there. Lightning won't reach it: that's how rods are placed.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_08
data.value: Most flashes don't stop at one stroke. A dart leader slides back down the same hot channel, and another stroke follows. That's why lightning flickers.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_09
data.value: The light reaches you at once, but sound travels only three hundred and forty-three metres a second. From three kilometres away, the thunder takes nearly nine seconds. Count the seconds and divide by three, and you have the distance in kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Lightning_Strike_10
data.value: Your turn. Change the current, take the rod away, move further off, or try another strike, and see what gets hit.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_01
data.value: From one new moon to the next takes twenty-nine and a half days. But the Moon only needs about twenty-seven days to go once around Earth. So where do the extra two days come from?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_02
data.value: Let's measure against a very distant star. This dashed white line always points at that same star.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_03
data.value: After twenty-seven point three days, the Moon is back in line with that star. It has gone once around Earth. But look: it isn't between Earth and the Sun yet, so it isn't a new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_04
data.value: Think about it. Why isn't it there yet?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_05
data.value: During the month, Earth has carried the Moon a good way around the Sun, so the direction of the Sun has turned by this angle. The Moon needs about two more days to catch up.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_06
data.value: At twenty-nine and a half days, the Moon is between Earth and the Sun again, and the new moon is back. So a full round of phases takes about two days longer than one trip around Earth.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Earth
data.value: This is Earth, seen from far above the North Pole. Its day side faces the Sun on the left. From here we watch the Moon go round.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: This is Earth, moving along its orbit around the Sun. As it moves, the direction of the Sun seen from Earth slowly turns.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_FirstQuarter
data.value: First quarter. Half of the face we see is lit. The Moon has gone a quarter of the way round, and it's high in the sky at sunset.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Full
data.value: Full moon. The Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, and its whole lit half faces us. It rises at sunset and shines all night.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_LastQuarter
data.value: Last quarter. Half lit again, but the other half this time. It rises around midnight and is still up in the morning sky.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Moon
data.value: This is the Moon. The gold arc marks its lit half, and the dashed blue arc marks the half facing Earth. The phase is simply how much of the lit half we can see.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_MoonOrbit
data.value: This is the Moon going round Earth. It always keeps the same face towards us, so we never see its far side from Earth.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Moonrise
data.value: These are the times the Moon rises and sets today. On average it rises about fifty minutes later each day, because it moves round Earth in the same direction Earth spins.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_New
data.value: New moon. The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, with its dark side towards us, so we can't see it.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sidereal
data.value: After twenty-seven point three days the Moon has gone once around Earth, measured against the stars. This is called a sidereal month.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_SkyMoon
data.value: This is the Moon in your sky. Its bright side always points back towards the Sun, even when the Sun is below the horizon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_SkySun
data.value: This is the Sun. Each day the Moon lags behind it a little more, which is why the Moon rises later every day.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Star
data.value: This is a very distant star. It's so far away that it lies in the same direction from anywhere on Earth's orbit, which makes it a perfect fixed marker.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Start
data.value: This is where the month starts: a new moon, with the Moon between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is the Sun. Earth goes round it once a year, so in one month Earth covers about a twelfth of its orbit.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sunlight
data.value: Sunlight comes from the left. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, lighting half of Earth and half of the Moon at all times.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Synodic
data.value: After twenty-nine point five days the Moon is back between Earth and the Sun: new moon again. This is called a synodic month, the month of the phases.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaningCrescent
data.value: Waning crescent. A thin curve seen in the east before sunrise, getting thinner until the next new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaningGibbous
data.value: Waning gibbous. Just after full, the bright part starts to shrink, and the Moon rises later each evening.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaxingCrescent
data.value: Waxing crescent. A thin bright curve appears in the west just after sunset, and it grows a little every night.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaxingGibbous
data.value: Waxing gibbous. More than half is lit, and it's still growing towards full.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_01
data.value: Why does the Moon change shape through the month? It doesn't make any light of its own. What we see is the part lit up by the Sun.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_02
data.value: Sunlight comes in from the left. Wherever the Moon is, the half facing the Sun is always lit, and the other half is dark.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_03
data.value: Look at the two arcs beside the Moon. The gold one marks the lit half. The dashed blue one marks the half facing Earth. Where they overlap is the bright part we can see.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_04
data.value: When the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces completely away from us. We can hardly see it at all. That's the new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_05
data.value: Think about it. When the Moon moves round to the far side of Earth, away from the Sun, what will we see?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_06
data.value: It's a full moon. Now the lit half faces Earth completely, so the whole round face shines.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon round until exactly half of it looks lit, a first quarter. Or just click its picture in the outer ring.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_08
data.value: The outer ring shows how the Moon looks from Earth. From new to full, the bright part grows day by day. From full back to new, it shrinks again. The whole round takes about twenty-nine and a half days.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_09
data.value: So the phases aren't made by Earth's shadow. We're simply seeing the Moon's lit half from different angles. Click the little pictures in the outer ring to hear about each phase.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_01
data.value: Now we're standing on the ground, looking across the sky towards the equator. Every day the Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky along this dashed line, and sets in the west.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_02
data.value: The Moon travels the same road, just later than the Sun. This is a first quarter moon. It rises around midday, and it's high in the sky when the Sun sets.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_03
data.value: A full moon sits opposite the Sun. As the Sun goes down in the west, the full moon comes up in the east. It stays up all night and sets around dawn.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_04
data.value: Quick question. At new moon, when is the Moon up in the sky?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_05
data.value: A new moon is in almost the same direction as the Sun, so it crosses the sky with the Sun in the daytime. Its dark side faces us, and it's lost in the Sun's glare, so we don't notice it at all.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_06
data.value: Now let's look at the same time every evening. Each day the Moon has moved a little further east and grown a little fatter. It rises about fifty minutes later each day.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_07
data.value: So the Moon's shape tells you roughly when it rises and sets. Drag across the picture to change the time and go looking for the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Angle
data.value: How far the pendulum is pulled aside. For small swings, it hardly changes the period at all.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Bob
data.value: The bob, the heavy weight at the end of the pendulum. Drag it aside and let go to start a new swing.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Circle
data.value: A dot going round a circle once for every bounce. Seen from the side, it moves exactly like the mass. That's why this kind of motion is called simple harmonic motion.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Formula
data.value: A ghost pendulum, swinging exactly as the formula says: the period is two pi times the square root of the length over g. For big swings, the real pendulum falls a little behind it.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Length
data.value: The length of the pendulum, from the pivot to the middle of the bob. Longer pendulums swing more slowly.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Longest
data.value: The longest pendulum. It swings fifty-one times a minute, the slowest of them all.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Mass
data.value: The mass on the spring. Drag it up or down and let it go. A heavier mass bounces more slowly.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Motor
data.value: The motor shakes the top of the spring up and down. If it shakes at the spring's own rhythm, the bounces grow. That's resonance.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Paper
data.value: The paper record. A pen draws the motion while the paper moves, making a smooth wave. The green brackets measure the period.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Place
data.value: Where the experiment is done, and how strong gravity is there. Try the Moon, Mars or Jupiter.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Rest
data.value: Where the mass rests: here the spring's pull up balances the weight down. The mass bounces evenly above and below this line.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Shortest
data.value: The shortest pendulum. It swings sixty-five times a minute, the fastest of them all.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Spring
data.value: The spring. The more it's stretched, the harder it pulls back. A stiffer spring makes the mass bounce faster.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Stretch
data.value: How far the weight of the mass stretches the spring: the mass times g, divided by the stiffness.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_TopView
data.value: The pendulums seen from straight above. This is where the patterns, the snake and the rows, are easiest to see.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Obj_Unstretched
data.value: How long the spring is on its own, with nothing hanging from it.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_01
data.value: Here's a pendulum: a heavy bob on a light rod, swinging to and fro. Underneath, a pen follows the bob and draws on a strip of paper that keeps sliding down.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_02
data.value: The pen draws a wavy line. The time for one complete swing, over and back again, is called the period. The green numbers measure it on the paper.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_03
data.value: This pendulum is a quarter of a metre long. Its period is about one second.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_04
data.value: Think about it. If you made the pendulum four times as long, what would happen to its period?

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_05
data.value: It doubles, to about two seconds. The period goes with the square root of the length. That's why a grandfather clock has a pendulum about a metre long: each swing one way takes one second.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_06
data.value: Here's a surprise. A smaller swing takes almost exactly the same time as a bigger one. Legend has it that Galileo noticed this watching a lamp swing in a cathedral.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_07
data.value: Now let's take the pendulum to the Moon. Gravity there is only about a sixth as strong, so it swings much more slowly: each full swing takes about five seconds.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the bob to one side, and let it go.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Pendulum_09
data.value: Because their swing is so steady, pendulums kept the world's clocks on time for nearly three hundred years.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_01
data.value: Here's a mass hanging on a spring. Pull it down and let go, and it bounces up and down.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_02
data.value: This dashed line is where the mass would rest. There, the spring is stretched just enough for its pull to balance the mass's weight.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_03
data.value: Watch the dot going round this circle. Its height always matches the mass. Bouncing on a spring is just like going round a circle, seen from the side.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_04
data.value: Think about it. What happens to the bouncing if we hang a heavier mass on the same spring?

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_05
data.value: It bounces more slowly. With four times the mass, each bounce takes twice as long: look at the wider waves on the paper. A stiffer spring does the opposite, and makes it bounce faster.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_06
data.value: Here's something surprising. On the Moon, the spring bounces exactly as fast as on Earth. The mass just rests a little higher, because it weighs less. Gravity changes where it rests, but not how fast it bounces.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_07
data.value: Now a motor shakes the top of the spring, ever so slightly, at exactly the spring's own rhythm. Watch the bounces grow bigger and bigger. This is called resonance. It's how a child on a swing goes higher with small, well-timed pushes.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Spring_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the mass up or down, and let it go.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_01
data.value: Here are fifteen pendulums on one bar, each a little shorter than the one before. They were all let go together, so at first they swing in step.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_02
data.value: The shorter ones swing a little faster. In one minute, the longest swings fifty-one times, and the shortest sixty-five times.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_03
data.value: So they slowly drift out of step. Seen from above, the bobs make a snake that twists and turns.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_04
data.value: Think about it. What happens when the whole minute is up?

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_05
data.value: They all line up again. In that minute, every pendulum makes a whole number of swings, so they all arrive back where they started, together.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_06
data.value: Halfway through the minute, the pendulums split into two rows, swinging against each other.

data.name: Narr_Osc_Wave_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag the timeline to find other patterns, like three or four rows.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_01
data.value: Seven balls fired at the same moment and the same speed, from fifteen degrees up to seventy-five, ten degrees apart.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_02
data.value: Which angle do you think will go the farthest?

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_03
data.value: Forty-five degrees wins. Steeper shots spend their speed climbing; flatter ones hit the ground too soon. Forty-five is the best balance between the two.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_04
data.value: Now look at the landing marks. Thirty-five and fifty-five land together, so do twenty-five and sixty-five, and fifteen and seventy-five. Each pair adds up to ninety degrees.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_05
data.value: The dashed purple line is an edge that no shot at this speed can ever get past. Every path just touches it at one point, and then turns away.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_06
data.value: Now fire from the top of a cliff twenty metres high. The winner is no longer forty-five degrees, but a flatter angle. Up here, the ball already has extra time to fly while it falls, so it pays to throw it more forwards.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_07
data.value: Back on level ground, now with air, and a football. The best angle drops below forty-five degrees again, because air steals the most from long, high flights. That's one reason throws and kicks in sport usually go off lower than forty-five.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Best_08
data.value: Your turn. Change the speed on the left-hand page. Without air and on level ground, does forty-five degrees still win?

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_01
data.value: Here's a cannon firing a ball at twenty metres a second, aimed forty-five degrees up. Everything is drawn to scale: a metre across is as long as a metre up.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_02
data.value: The faint balls are snapshots, taken at equal moments apart. Look at their spacing. Across, the gaps are all the same. Up and down, they shrink on the way up and grow on the way down.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_03
data.value: The green arrow is the ball's speed across. It stays exactly the same for the whole flight, because nothing pushes the ball sideways.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_04
data.value: The blue arrow is its speed upwards. Gravity takes away the same amount every second, so it shrinks to nothing at the top, then grows again pointing down.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_05
data.value: Now look at the shadows. The one on the ground slides along at a steady pace. The one on the post goes up and comes down, like a ball thrown straight up. The curved flight is just these two simple motions happening at once.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_06
data.value: A question. If we fire at thirty degrees, and then at sixty degrees, at the same speed, which one lands farther away?

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_07
data.value: Let's see. Here's thirty degrees: a flatter, quicker flight. Watch where it lands. The forty-five degree shot stays behind as a faint path to compare with.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_08
data.value: And now sixty degrees: higher and slower, but it comes down on the very same spot. Without air, any two angles that add up to ninety land together. And forty-five, right in the middle, still goes the farthest.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_09
data.value: Now let's add air, and fire a ping-pong ball. The dashed line is the same shot with no air. The air keeps slowing the ball down, so it falls well short and comes down more steeply than it went up.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Launch_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag from the cannon to aim your own shot. The direction you drag sets the angle, and how far you drag sets the speed.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Aim
data.value: The aiming line, straight from the blowpipe to the monkey. It's where the dart would fly if there were no gravity.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Airless
data.value: The dashed path is the same shot with no air at all. The gap between it and the real path shows how much the air took away.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Ball
data.value: The ball in flight. Once it leaves the cannon, the only things acting on it are gravity, and the air if there is any.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Cannon
data.value: The cannon. Drag from it to aim: the direction sets the launch angle, and the length of the arrow sets the speed.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Dart
data.value: The dart. It falls below its straight aiming line by exactly as much as the monkey falls below the branch, so the two meet.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Drag
data.value: Air resistance, always pointing against the motion. It grows quickly with speed, and it hits light balls like ping-pong balls and shuttlecocks the hardest.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Dropped
data.value: The dropped ball. It's simply let go, and falls straight down, faster and faster.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Envelope
data.value: The edge of reach, sometimes called the safety parabola. At this speed, no shot at any angle can get past it. Every path touches it once.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Fall
data.value: How far below its no-gravity position each one has fallen: one half g t squared. It's the same for the dart and for the monkey, because both have been falling for the same time.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Farthest
data.value: The angle that throws the farthest at this speed, and how far it goes. Without air and on level ground it's forty-five degrees; from up high, or with air, it's lower.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_GroundShadow
data.value: The ball's shadow on the ground, straight below it. It shows just the motion across: steady without air, slowing down with air.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Hunter
data.value: The hunter's blowpipe, aimed straight at the monkey. Change the dart's speed on the left-hand page: any speed hits, as long as the dart arrives before the monkey reaches the ground.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Landing
data.value: Where each angle landed. Without air, two angles that add up to ninety degrees land in the same place, so they share one label.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Launcher
data.value: The launcher fires seven balls at once, all at the same speed, at angles ten degrees apart. Change the speed, the height or the air on the left-hand page and see which angle wins.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Monkey
data.value: The monkey. It lets go of the branch the moment the dart is fired, and falls just like any dropped ball. Turn off 'Monkey lets go' to see what happens if it holds on.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_OddNumbers
data.value: How far the balls fall in each equal step of time: one, three, five, seven parts, and so on. Add them up and you get one, four, nine, sixteen: the distance grows as the square of the time.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Peak
data.value: The highest point. Here the ball has stopped going up for an instant, but it's still moving across. It never stops completely.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_PostShadow
data.value: The ball's shadow on the post, straight across from it. It shows just the motion up and down: it rises, slows, stops, and falls back, exactly like a ball thrown straight up.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Range
data.value: The range: how far away the ball lands. Without air it depends on the speed, the angle and the strength of gravity. Double the speed and it goes four times as far.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Strobe
data.value: Strobe snapshots: where the ball was at equal moments apart. Even spacing across means a steady speed across; the spacing up and down changes, because gravity speeds it up and slows it down.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Thrown
data.value: The thrown ball. It leaves sideways at the same moment, but falls exactly like the dropped one, so the two are always at the same height.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Velocity
data.value: The white arrow is the ball's velocity: how fast it's going and in which direction. It always points along the path, and it's made of the green part across and the blue part up.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Vx
data.value: The speed across. Without air nothing pushes the ball sideways, so it stays the same from launch to landing.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Vy
data.value: The speed up and down. Gravity changes it by the same amount every second: it shrinks on the way up, is zero at the very top, and grows on the way down.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Obj_Weight
data.value: The ball's weight, the pull of gravity. It's the same size and always points straight down, whether the ball is rising, at the top, or falling.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_01
data.value: Two balls leave this table at exactly the same moment. The pink one is simply let go. The blue one is thrown sideways.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_02
data.value: Which one do you think hits the ground first?

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_03
data.value: They land together. Look at the snapshots: at every moment the two balls are at exactly the same height. Moving sideways doesn't change how fast you fall.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_04
data.value: In each equal step of time they fall farther than before: one, then three, then five, then seven times as far as in the first step. That's what speeding up steadily looks like.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_05
data.value: Now throw the blue ball twice as fast. It lands twice as far away, but still at exactly the same moment as the pink one.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_06
data.value: Here's a famous puzzle. A hunter aims a dart straight at a monkey hanging from a branch. The moment the dart is fired, the monkey lets go and drops.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_07
data.value: So where should the hunter aim, to hit the falling monkey?

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_08
data.value: Straight at it. Gravity pulls the dart and the monkey down by exactly the same amount, one half g t squared, below where each would be without it. So the dart drops just as far as the monkey does, and hits.

data.name: Narr_Proj_Together_09
data.value: Your turn. Change the dart's speed on the left-hand page. Fast or slow, it still hits, as long as it gets there before the monkey reaches the ground.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_01
data.value: Let's dive under the sea, to a mid-ocean ridge. Two plates are moving apart here, a centimetre or two a year on each side. Hot mantle rock rises beneath, partly melts, and the magma fills the crack, cooling into new ocean floor.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_02
data.value: Keep an eye on the compass in the corner. Every few hundred thousand years, Earth's magnetic field flips over, and north becomes south. Nobody can say exactly when the next flip will come.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_03
data.value: As the new rock cools, tiny magnetic grains inside it lock in the field's direction at that moment. So the sea floor carries a barcode of dark and light stripes, and the pattern on one side is a mirror image of the other. Finding these stripes in the nineteen-sixties convinced scientists that the sea floor really does spread.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_04
data.value: This is the sea floor today. Where in this picture is the oldest ocean floor?

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_05
data.value: Now to a place where plates meet. Old ocean floor is cold and heavy, so when it meets a continent it sinks underneath, bending down at a deep-sea trench. This is a subduction zone, a boundary where a plate is used up and returns to the mantle.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_06
data.value: Watch the dots along the sinking plate. They're earthquakes, and they follow the slab down: the farther from the trench, the deeper they are, some as deep as six hundred kilometres. That's why the deep quakes on the map always sit behind the trenches.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_07
data.value: When the sinking plate reaches about a hundred kilometres down, it squeezes out water. The water lowers the melting point of the hot mantle above, so it melts. The magma rises and breaks through, building a line of volcanoes, like the Andes, or the islands of Japan.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_08
data.value: Near the top, the two plates are stuck together. The lower plate keeps moving, dragging the edge of the upper plate down, year after year, storing energy like a bent spring. Watch the stuck zone fill up, until suddenly it snaps. The sea floor jumps, and a tsunami races away.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_09
data.value: What happens when all the ocean between two continents is used up? Watch India. Seventy million years ago it was an island continent, racing north across an ocean called the Tethys at more than fifteen centimetres a year.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_10
data.value: About fifty million years ago, it hit Asia. Continental crust is too light to sink, so India slid under Tibet and everything piled up. The Himalaya rose, and the crust under Tibet is now about twice its usual thickness. India is still pushing north, about five centimetres a year.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_11
data.value: The last kind: plates sliding past each other, seen from above. Far from the fault, each side moves steadily. But the fault itself is stuck, so the ground near it bends, and the fences and the road across it slowly curve.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Boundaries_12
data.value: When the strain gets too great, the fault slips all at once. The bent ground springs back, and the fences are suddenly cut and shifted. That's an earthquake. Scientists call it elastic rebound. Your turn: press Quake now, or just wait for it to snap.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_01
data.value: This is a slice right through the Earth: the thin crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core, all drawn to scale. The red star on the surface is an earthquake. Its shaking spreads through the whole planet as waves.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_02
data.value: The gold front is the P wave. It pushes and pulls the rock along the direction it travels, just like sound does. It's the fastest wave, so it always arrives first. P stands for primary.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_03
data.value: The blue front is the S wave. It shakes the rock from side to side, and it's slower, only a little over half as fast. Notice how both fronts curve as they go deeper, because deep rock carries waves faster.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_04
data.value: This chart is the one in your textbook: how fast each wave travels at each depth. Both speed up sharply at the Moho, the bottom of the crust, and keep getting faster down through the mantle.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_05
data.value: Now look two thousand nine hundred kilometres down, at the Gutenberg discontinuity. The S wave stops dead here, and the P wave suddenly slows right down.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_06
data.value: So, why do S waves stop at the outer core?

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_07
data.value: By now the waves have crossed the whole planet. Look at the far side: a huge area gets no S waves at all. That's the S-wave shadow zone, cast by the liquid outer core.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_08
data.value: There's also a ring, between about a hundred and a hundred and forty-three degrees from the quake, where hardly any P waves arrive, because the core bends them away. In nineteen thirty-six, Inge Lehmann noticed faint P waves in this zone, and realised there had to be a solid inner core.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_09
data.value: The inner core is mostly iron and nickel, and about as hot as the surface of the Sun. Yet it's solid, because the pressure at the centre of the Earth is so enormous.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_10
data.value: The box below magnifies the top seven hundred kilometres. The crust and the hard top of the mantle together make the lithosphere: these are the plates. Beneath them lies the asthenosphere, hot and slightly soft. Magma comes from here, and the plates slide over it.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Inside_11
data.value: Finally, here's the great Japan earthquake of twenty eleven, reaching your own place, marked on the rim. The longer the gap between the P wave and the S wave, the farther away the quake was. That's how a single station measures distance. Your turn: click anywhere on the rim to put a station there, or drag the quake.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Alaska1964
data.value: Alaska, nineteen sixty-four: magnitude nine point two, the second largest ever recorded. The Pacific Plate slipped beneath North America. The ground shook for about four minutes, and parts of the coast rose or sank by several metres.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_ArcVolcano
data.value: A volcanic arc. It stands above the place where the sinking plate is about a hundred kilometres down. So a gently sloping plate puts the volcanoes far from the trench, and a steep one puts them close. Try dragging the slab.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Asia
data.value: The southern edge of Asia. Before the collision it was a coast like the Andes today, with an ocean plate sinking beneath it and volcanoes on top.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Asthenosphere
data.value: The asthenosphere, in the upper mantle, roughly eighty to four hundred kilometres down. It's hot enough to flow very slowly, like extremely thick toffee, and a little of it is molten. The plates glide over it, and it's thought to be where magma comes from.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Axis
data.value: The crest of the ridge. On a slow ridge like the Atlantic's, a rift valley runs along the top. On a fast one like the East Pacific Rise, the crest is a smooth swell. Try both spreading speeds.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Benioff
data.value: The Wadati-Benioff zone: a sloping band of earthquakes inside the sinking plate. It was discovered by tracing quakes deeper and deeper beneath Japan and South America.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Bolivia1994
data.value: Bolivia, nineteen ninety-four: magnitude eight point two, but more than six hundred kilometres down, inside the sinking Nazca Plate. It's one of the biggest deep earthquakes known, and people felt it as far away as Canada.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Chile1960
data.value: Valdivia, Chile, nineteen sixty: magnitude nine point five, the largest earthquake ever recorded. The Nazca Plate lurched beneath South America along a thousand kilometres of fault, and the tsunami crossed the Pacific to strike Hawaii and Japan.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Collision
data.value: A collision zone. When two continents meet, neither is heavy enough to sink, so the crust crumples, thickens and rises into great mountains, like the Himalaya and the Alps.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Crust
data.value: The crust, Earth's thin outer skin. Under the continents it's about thirty-three kilometres thick on average, under the oceans only about six. At this scale, it's thinner than the line that draws it.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Depth
data.value: The colours show how deep each earthquake was. Red ones are shallow, less than seventy kilometres down. Yellow ones are intermediate, and blue ones are deep, down to about seven hundred kilometres. Deep quakes only happen inside sinking plates.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Diffuse
data.value: A diffuse boundary. It isn't one clean line, but a wide zone where the ground is squeezed or stretched, with earthquakes scattered right across it.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Epicentre
data.value: The epicentre, the point on the surface right above where the rupture began. The waves spread out from here: first the faster P wave, then the stronger S wave.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_FarField
data.value: Far from the fault, each side moves smoothly and steadily, a few centimetres a year, just as the plates do. Only near the fault does the movement get stuck and stored up.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Fault
data.value: The fault. Deep down, the rocks creep slowly past each other, but the top fifteen kilometres or so are held by friction, until the stress becomes too great.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Fence
data.value: A fence built straight across the fault. While the fault is stuck, the ground near it is dragged along and the fence bends. In the earthquake it springs back straight, but cut and offset at the fault.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Field
data.value: The compass shows Earth's magnetic field at this moment in the story. When the red end points down, the field is reversed, and a compass would point south.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Focus
data.value: The earthquake's focus, a little way beneath the surface. Drag it round the rim to move the quake, and all the waves will start from there.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Gangdese
data.value: The Gangdese volcanoes, on Asia's edge while the Tethys floor was sinking beneath it. Their granite roots now make up mountains in southern Tibet.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Gutenberg
data.value: The Gutenberg discontinuity, about two thousand nine hundred kilometres down: the boundary between the mantle and the core. Here S waves vanish, and P waves slow down sharply.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Hawaii
data.value: The Hawaiian Islands sit above a hotspot. As the Pacific Plate moves north-west, each volcano is carried away and a new one grows. The chain gets older the farther it is from Hawaii, and its sharp bend shows the plate changed direction about forty-seven million years ago.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Himalaya
data.value: The Himalaya, the highest mountains on Earth, with Everest at about eight thousand eight hundred and forty-nine metres. They're still rising a few millimetres a year, even as erosion wears them down.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_India
data.value: India. After breaking away from the old southern supercontinent, it raced north faster than almost any plate today, and then slowed sharply when it hit Asia.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_InnerCore
data.value: The inner core: a solid ball of iron and nickel, about twelve hundred kilometres in radius. It's as hot as the surface of the Sun, but the enormous pressure keeps it solid.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Lithosphere
data.value: The lithosphere: the crust together with the hard, cold top of the mantle. This is what the plates are made of. Under the ocean it starts thin at the ridge and thickens as it cools, up to about a hundred kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Locked
data.value: The locked zone, the shallow part of the boundary where the plates are stuck. Strain builds up here for centuries, then it's released in the largest earthquakes on Earth, the megathrust quakes.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Magma
data.value: A magma chamber, just a few kilometres beneath the sea floor. Molten rock gathers here and squeezes up into the crack, cooling into the dark rock called basalt.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Mantle
data.value: The mantle, from the Moho down to two thousand nine hundred kilometres. It's hot, solid rock, but it still creeps very slowly, carrying the plates along.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Melt
data.value: This is where the mantle melts. Water driven out of the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the hot rock above, and the melt rises in blobs towards the surface.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Moho
data.value: The Moho, short for the Mohorovicic discontinuity, is the bottom of the crust. Here both P and S waves suddenly speed up, because the mantle rock below is denser and stiffer.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Nepal2015
data.value: Nepal, twenty fifteen: magnitude seven point eight. India slid a few metres further under the Himalaya along the main thrust fault, and Kathmandu shook hard. Nearly nine thousand people died.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_OceanPlate
data.value: The ocean plate: old, cold, dense lithosphere, with a thin basalt crust only about seven kilometres thick. Because it's heavy, it's the one that sinks.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_OldFloor
data.value: Older sea floor. As it moves away from the ridge it cools, shrinks and sinks, so the ocean gets deeper, from about two and a half kilometres at the ridge to more than five kilometres far away.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_OuterCore
data.value: The outer core: liquid iron and nickel. As it churns, it makes Earth's magnetic field. We know it's liquid because S waves can't get through it.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_PCurve
data.value: The P-wave curve shows its speed at each depth. It rises through the crust and the mantle, drops suddenly at the core, and jumps up again at the inner core.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_PShadow
data.value: The P-wave shadow zone, from about a hundred to a hundred and forty-three degrees from the quake. The core bends the P waves away from this ring; only faint waves through the inner core get here.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_PWave
data.value: The P wave, or primary wave, is a push-and-pull wave, like sound. It can travel through solids, liquids and gases, and it's the fastest, so it's the first to arrive.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Place
data.value: This is your place. The card shows which plate you're on, how fast that plate is carrying you, and how far you are from the nearest plate boundary.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Plate
data.value: This is a tectonic plate: a piece of Earth's rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, up to about a hundred kilometres thick. The whole plate moves as one, a few centimetres a year, and most of the action happens at its edges.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Ridge
data.value: A mid-ocean ridge. The plates pull apart here, magma rises into the gap, and new ocean floor is made. Joined up, the ridges are the longest mountain range on Earth, more than sixty thousand kilometres, almost all of it under the sea.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Rift
data.value: A rift valley, where a continent is starting to split apart. East Africa is slowly being torn open. In a few million years the sea may flood in, just as it already has in the Red Sea.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SCurve
data.value: The S-wave curve is always below the P-wave curve. Between two thousand nine hundred and five thousand one hundred and fifty kilometres it drops to zero: that's the liquid outer core.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SShadow
data.value: The S-wave shadow zone: everywhere more than about a hundred degrees from the quake. S waves can't cross the liquid outer core, so none arrive here at all.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SWave
data.value: The S wave, or secondary wave, shakes the rock from side to side. It can only travel through solids, and it's slower than the P wave, but it usually shakes harder.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SanFrancisco1906
data.value: San Francisco, nineteen-oh-six: about magnitude seven point nine, on the San Andreas fault. The ground slipped sideways by up to six metres, and the fires afterwards destroyed much of the city. Studying it, Harry Reid came up with the idea of elastic rebound.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Slab
data.value: The slab, the sinking plate. It's colder and denser than the mantle around it, so it keeps sinking under its own weight. That pull is one of the main forces that drive the plates.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SlabBreak
data.value: The broken-off slab. After the collision, the heavy ocean plate tore away from India's light continent and sank on, deep into the mantle.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Smoker
data.value: A black smoker. Seawater seeps into the hot rock, heats up to around three hundred and fifty degrees, and gushes out full of dissolved minerals. Whole communities of animals live around these vents, without any sunlight at all.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Station
data.value: A seismic station. It records the P wave first, then the S wave, then the slow, strong surface waves. The gap between P and S tells how far away the quake was.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Stress
data.value: This gauge shows how much strain is stored. Every year adds a little more. When it reaches breaking point, the fault slips, and the gauge drops back to empty.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Stripes
data.value: Magnetic stripes. Each band of crust is magnetised the way the field pointed when it cooled. Dark bands formed while the field was as it is today, light bands while it was reversed. The two sides mirror each other.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Sumatra2004
data.value: Sumatra, two thousand and four: magnitude nine point one. The Indian Plate slipped beneath the edge of Asia along about thirteen hundred kilometres. Its tsunami swept across the Indian Ocean and took about two hundred and thirty thousand lives.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_SurfaceWave
data.value: Surface waves run along the outside of the Earth. They're the slowest of all, but the biggest, and they do most of the damage to buildings.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Suture
data.value: The suture, the seam where India and Asia were joined. Along it you can still find scraps of the old ocean floor, squeezed up between the two continents.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Tangshan1976
data.value: Tangshan, nineteen seventy-six: magnitude seven point six, or seven point eight on China's own scale. It was far from any plate boundary, on old faults inside the Eurasian Plate. It struck before dawn and killed about two hundred and forty thousand people.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Tethys
data.value: The Tethys Ocean, between India and Asia. Its floor sank under Asia until it was all gone. Some of its sediments were scraped off and lifted up, and they now sit on top of Mount Everest.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Tibet
data.value: The Tibetan Plateau, on average more than four thousand metres high: the roof of the world. The crust beneath it is about seventy kilometres thick, twice the usual.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Tohoku2011
data.value: Tohoku, Japan, twenty eleven: magnitude nine point one. The Pacific Plate slipped as much as fifty metres beneath Japan. The tsunami was more than ten metres high along much of the coast, and it caused the Fukushima nuclear accident.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Transform
data.value: A transform fault. Here the plates slide past each other sideways, and crust is neither made nor destroyed. They stick and slip, so they shake with shallow and often damaging earthquakes.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Trench
data.value: A deep-sea trench. One plate bends down here and sinks under the other, back into the mantle. Trenches have the biggest earthquakes on Earth, and a line of volcanoes behind them.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Tsunami
data.value: A tsunami. When the sea floor jumps up, it lifts the whole column of water above it. The wave races across the open ocean as fast as a jet plane, and rears up high when it reaches shallow water.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Turkey2023
data.value: Turkey and Syria, twenty twenty-three: magnitude seven point eight on the East Anatolian fault, where the Arabian Plate slides past Anatolia. A second large quake, magnitude seven point five, struck nine hours later. More than fifty thousand people died.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_UpperPlate
data.value: The upper plate. A continent's crust is thick and light, like a raft, so it stays on top. Where two ocean plates meet, the older, heavier one sinks, and the other carries an arc of volcanic islands.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Wedge
data.value: The mantle wedge, squeezed between the sinking plate and the upper plate. The slab drags it downward, and hot mantle flows in from behind to take its place.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Obj_Wenchuan2008
data.value: Wenchuan, Sichuan, two thousand and eight: magnitude seven point nine. Pushed by India, the Tibetan Plateau shoves east against the Sichuan Basin, and the Longmen Shan faults gave way. Nearly seventy thousand people died.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_01
data.value: Here's a map of the world, but look at the dots. Each one is an earthquake of magnitude four and a half or more, about a year's worth. Do they fall just anywhere? No. They crowd into long, narrow belts. The red ones are shallow; the yellow and blue ones are deeper.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_02
data.value: Those belts mark the edges of the plates. Earth's hard outer shell is cracked into about fifteen big pieces, and each one rides slowly on the hotter, softer rock underneath. The biggest of all is the Pacific Plate, almost entirely under the sea.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_03
data.value: Your geography textbook keeps it simple, with six big plates: the Pacific, Eurasian, African, American, Indian Ocean and Antarctic plates. Notice that the Indian Ocean plate takes in India, Australia, and even Arabia. Scientists divide these further, but the big picture is the same.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_04
data.value: The white arrows show which way each plate is moving, and how fast. Just a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. That sounds tiny, but over a million years it adds up to tens of kilometres. The Pacific Plate is one of the fastest.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_05
data.value: Now find the red lines, like the one running right down the middle of the Atlantic. Here two plates are pulling apart. Hot rock rises into the gap and makes brand-new sea floor. This is a mid-ocean ridge, a boundary where plates grow.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_06
data.value: The blue lines with little teeth are trenches. Here plates push together, and one dives under the other, down into the mantle. The teeth point at the plate on top. Trenches ring almost the whole Pacific. That's the famous Ring of Fire, full of earthquakes and volcanoes.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_07
data.value: Here's a question for you. The blue earthquakes happen hundreds of kilometres down. Where on the map do you find them?

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_08
data.value: Where two continents meet, neither one sinks, so the crust crumples up instead. India pushing into Asia raised the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau. That push is felt far inside China. The gold star marks the Wenchuan earthquake of two thousand and eight.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_09
data.value: Plates can also slide past each other sideways, along the green transform faults. The best known is the San Andreas fault in California. In nineteen-oh-six it slipped by several metres in a moment, and the earthquake left San Francisco in ruins.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_10
data.value: Not every volcano sits on a boundary. Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific Plate, above a hotspot: a plume of hot rock rising from deep below. The plate slides over it, so its old volcanoes drift away in a long chain, older and older towards the north-west.

data.name: Narr_Quake_Plates_11
data.value: Your own place is the blue dot, with a dashed line to the nearest plate boundary. Now it's your turn: click a boundary, a plate, or one of the gold stars, and find out what's going on there.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_01
data.value: Now a single raindrop, drawn hugely magnified, with sunlight coming in from the left. A raindrop is a tiny ball of water, and it works a bit like a prism.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_02
data.value: Follow one ray. It bends as it enters the drop, reflects once off the back, and bends again as it comes out, heading back toward the side the sunlight came from.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_03
data.value: This is the ray that turns back the most steeply. Each colour comes out at a slightly different angle from the line back toward the Sun: red at about forty-two degrees, violet a little less. That's how the colours separate.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_04
data.value: Now send rays in across the whole drop. They come out at all sorts of angles, but most of them crowd together near forty-two degrees. That crowding is what makes the rainbow bright.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_05
data.value: So, where in the sky should you look to see a rainbow?

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_06
data.value: With your back to the Sun, because the light comes back out the way it came. And not all of it makes it: some reflects off the outside, some leaks out through the back. Only a small share comes out as rainbow light.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_07
data.value: Some light reflects twice inside before it comes out. It crowds near fifty-one degrees, and makes a fainter second rainbow, with its colours the other way round.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Drop_08
data.value: Your turn. Drag up or down to move where the ray enters the drop, and find where it comes out at the steepest angle.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Antisolar
data.value: The point opposite the Sun, where the shadow of your head falls. Every rainbow is a circle around it, so everyone sees their own rainbow.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_BowAngle
data.value: The rainbow's radius, measured as an angle from the point opposite the Sun: about forty-two degrees for the main bow, and fifty-one for the second.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_BrightInside
data.value: Inside the main bow the sky is brighter: drops at smaller angles still send light back to you, with the colours overlapping into white.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Crests
data.value: The wave crests of the light, drawn more than ten thousand times bigger than real. Where light goes slower, the crests are closer together; the colour doesn't change.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Critical
data.value: The critical angle. Light coming from inside at any steeper slant than this can't get out. The slower the material, the smaller the critical angle, which is why diamonds sparkle so much.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Crowd
data.value: Where the rays crowd together. Rays entering near this point all come out at nearly the same angle, so lots of light goes that way: that's the rainbow angle.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_DarkBand
data.value: Alexander's dark band, between the two bows. No light that has reflected once or twice in a drop comes out at these angles, so the sky there is darker.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Drop
