data.value: A raindrop, one or two millimetres across, drawn hugely magnified. Drag up or down to choose where the followed ray enters it.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Entry
data.value: The angles where the ray enters the drop: outside, measured from the normal, and inside, smaller, because light slows down in water.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_ExitAngle
data.value: The angle between the light coming out and the line back toward the Sun. For the main rainbow it can never be more than about forty-two degrees.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Incidence
data.value: The angle of incidence: how far the incoming beam is tilted from the normal.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Index
data.value: The refractive index, n, says how many times slower light goes in a material than in empty space: about 1.33 in water, 1.5 in glass, and 2.4 in diamond.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Lamp
data.value: The lamp, sending out a narrow beam. Drag anywhere in the picture to aim it: the angle is measured from the normal, the upright dashed line.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Losses
data.value: Light lost on the way: some reflects off the outside of the drop, and at each bounce inside some leaks out through the back.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Normal
data.value: The normal: a line square to the surface where the light meets it. Angles in optics are measured from this line, not from the surface.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Out
data.value: How much of the light that went in comes out along this path, toward someone watching the rainbow.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Primary
data.value: The main rainbow, made by light reflected once inside the drops. Red on the outside, violet on the inside.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Prism
data.value: A triangular prism. Its two faces bend the light the same way, so the colours spread twice as much as at one surface.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Reflected
data.value: The share of light that bounces off the surface. Head-on it's only a few percent; at a grazing angle almost all of it reflects, like the glare off a lake.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Refracted
data.value: The angle of refraction: how far the bent beam is tilted from the normal. Going into a slower material it's smaller than the angle of incidence; coming out, it's bigger.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Secondary
data.value: The secondary rainbow, made by light reflected twice inside the drops. It's fainter, wider, and its colours are reversed.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Spectrum
data.value: The spectrum: white light spread out into its colours, from red, bent the least, to violet, bent the most. Light of a single colour makes just one spot.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Through
data.value: The share of light that goes on through the surface, bent by refraction. Together with the reflected share it adds up to all the light.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Total
data.value: Total internal reflection: the light hits the surface from inside at more than the critical angle, and none of it can get out.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Obj_Turn
data.value: How far the prism turns the beam from its original direction. It's smallest when the light passes through the prism symmetrically.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_01
data.value: A rainbow starts with light changing direction. Here a lamp shines a red beam down onto water. The stripes across the beam are its wave crests, moving along with the light.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_02
data.value: Look at the crests once they're in the water: they bunch up closer together. Light travels about a quarter slower in water, so each wave covers less distance.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_03
data.value: The beam meets the surface at a slant, so one edge of it slows down first, and the whole beam swings closer to the dashed upright line, the normal. That bending is called refraction.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_04
data.value: Not all the light goes in. A little bounces off the surface instead: at this angle, just a few percent. The more slanting the beam, the more is reflected.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_05
data.value: Now think about light going the other way, from inside the water up to the surface, at a very slanting angle. What happens?

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_06
data.value: None of it gets out: it all reflects back inside. Past the critical angle, about forty-nine degrees for water, light can't escape. This total internal reflection is what keeps light trapped inside optical fibres.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_07
data.value: Back to light going into the water, but now it's white light. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount: violet the most, red the least. The difference is drawn five times bigger here so you can see it.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_08
data.value: A glass prism bends the light twice, once going in and once coming out, both times the same way. So the colours fan out even more, into a full spectrum on the screen.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Refraction_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag in the picture to aim the lamp at the prism from a different angle, and watch how the spectrum moves.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_01
data.value: Now the real sky, with rain falling in front of you and the Sun low behind you. The point exactly opposite the Sun is where the shadow of your head falls.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_02
data.value: Every raindrop that sits forty-two degrees away from that point sends its rainbow light straight to your eye. So the rainbow is a circle around the shadow of your head.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_03
data.value: Red is on the outside and violet on the inside. Red light comes out at a slightly bigger angle, so the red you see comes from drops a little higher up.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_04
data.value: Notice that the sky inside the bow is brighter. That's light from drops at smaller angles, all the colours mixed back into white.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_05
data.value: Outside is the fainter second bow, with its colours reversed. And between the two, the sky is darker: a band called Alexander's dark band.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_06
data.value: What do you think happens to the rainbow as the Sun climbs higher in the sky?

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_07
data.value: It sinks. The circle's centre is as far below the horizon as the Sun is above it. Once the Sun is higher than about forty-two degrees, the whole bow is below the horizon. That's why rainbows are usually seen in the morning or late in the afternoon.

data.name: Narr_Rain_Sky_08
data.value: Your turn. Drag the sky up or down to move the Sun, and watch the rainbow rise and sink.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_01
data.value: This is a light clock. A flash of light bounces between two mirrors, and every time it goes up and comes back down, the clock ticks once. The clock on the ground is standing still, so its light just goes straight up and down.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_02
data.value: Up above, an identical clock rides in a ship flying past at six tenths of the speed of light. For the people on board, nothing is odd: their light goes straight up and down too.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_03
data.value: But look at it from the ground. While the light is on its way up, the ship moves on. So the light has to travel along a slanted line, and it draws a zigzag.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_04
data.value: Now here's the key. Light always travels at the same speed, for everyone. And the slanted path is longer. So, seen from the ground, does the ship's clock tick faster, slower, or the same?

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_05
data.value: Slower. Look at the two counters: the ship's clock keeps falling behind. A longer path at the same speed takes more time, so each tick takes longer. This is called time dilation.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_06
data.value: This triangle tells us how much slower. The slanted side is how far the light goes, the bottom is how far the ship moves, and the upright side is the gap between the mirrors. Pythagoras gives us a number called gamma.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_07
data.value: Let's go faster, to nine tenths of the speed of light. The zigzag gets much flatter, and gamma is now more than two: the ship's clock ticks less than half as often as the ground's.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_08
data.value: Now let's ride along with the ship. To us the ship stands still and the ground rushes backwards. Look: now it's the ground's light that zigzags, and the ground's clock that runs slow. Each side sees the other's clock slow, and both are right.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_09
data.value: This isn't just a thought experiment. Tiny particles called muons are made high up in the air, and they last only about two millionths of a second. Most should die long before reaching the ground. Yet we catch lots of them down here, because their clocks run slow.

data.name: Narr_Rel_LightClock_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag sideways across the picture, or use the slider, to change the speed. Notice how little happens at low speeds, and how fast gamma shoots up near the speed of light.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Counter
data.value: These count each clock's ticks, and the dials show each clock's own time. The clock that moves in this picture falls behind.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_EarthLine
data.value: The home twin's line. Earth stays put, so the line goes straight up through time.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_EarthMarks
data.value: Marks on Earth's line, one for each year the home twin lives.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_EarthTwin
data.value: The twin who stays at home, and how many years they've lived since the ship left.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Flash
data.value: The flash of light inside the clock. However fast the clock moves, this light always goes at the same speed, about three hundred thousand kilometres every second.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Frame
data.value: This says whose point of view the picture is drawn from. Click it to switch sides. Both pictures are equally correct; they just disagree about who is moving.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Front
data.value: The light catcher at the front of the train. Seen from the platform, the front runs away from the light, so the light needs longer to catch it.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Gamma
data.value: Gamma is the slow-down factor. It's one divided by the square root of one minus the speed squared. At everyday speeds it's almost exactly one; near light's speed it grows without limit.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Grid
data.value: The spacetime diagram: distance from Earth across, Earth's time up. One light-year is drawn as long as one year.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Ground
data.value: The ground's lane. When you ride with the ship, the ground and everything on it rushes backwards past you.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_GroundClock
data.value: The ground's light clock. For someone standing next to it, its light simply goes up and down between the mirrors, once per tick.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Jump
data.value: The jump. Just before the turn, the traveller's “now” on Earth is early; just after, it's late. Those Earth years are skipped over by the turn.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Lamp
data.value: The lamp in the very middle of the train. It flashes just as it passes the person on the platform. Click it to flash it again.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Light
data.value: The light from the flash, going both ways at the same speed, whoever is watching. That one rule is what makes all the surprises.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_LightLine
data.value: Light's path through spacetime: one light-year per year, so forty-five degrees. Anything with mass must stay steeper than this.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Mirror
data.value: Two mirrors facing each other. Light bounces back and forth between them, and one trip up and back counts as one tick.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Now
data.value: Earth's “now”: a flat line, because for Earth everything on it happens at the same time. Drag up and down to move through the trip.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Observer
data.value: Someone standing on the ground beside the clock. For this person, the ground's clock is the one at rest.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Origin
data.value: This is where the flash happened. Light spreads out from this spot at the same speed both ways, even though the lamp itself moves on.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Platform
data.value: The platform, as long as the train when both stand still. Seen from the moving train, it's the platform that is shorter.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_PlatformClock
data.value: The platform person's clock. It read zero at the flash, just like the train's clock in the middle.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_PlatformLength
data.value: The platform's length here. When the platform is the one moving, it's the one that's shortened.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Rear
data.value: The light catcher at the back of the train. Seen from the platform, the back rushes towards the light, so it's hit early.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Ship
data.value: The ship's lane. The ship carries a light clock just like the one on the ground. Whether it seems to move depends on whose point of view you pick.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_ShipAxes
data.value: The ship's own time and space axes on the way out. They tilt towards the light line from both sides. Everything along the tilted space axis happens at the same time, for the ship.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_ShipClock
data.value: The ship's light clock. It's exactly the same as the one on the ground. On board, its light goes straight up and down, and it keeps perfect time.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_ShipLine
data.value: The traveller's line: out to the star, a sharp turn, and back home. Its clock runs slow by gamma on both legs.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_ShipMarks
data.value: Marks on the traveller's line, one for each year the traveller lives. They're further apart, because the ship's clock runs slow.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_ShipNow
data.value: The traveller's line of “now”: all the events the traveller counts as happening at this moment. It tilts, so it meets Earth's line at a different year.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Signals
data.value: Birthday flashes, sent on every birthday and travelling at forty-five degrees. Green from Earth, pink from the ship. Watch them arrive slowly on the way out, quickly on the way back.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Star
data.value: The star the traveller visits. For Earth it's this far away; for the ship, rushing towards it, the distance is shortened by gamma.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Strip
data.value: Where everyone is right now, on the same distance scale as the diagram above: Earth, the ship and the star.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Time
data.value: The time in the frame you're watching from, in microseconds. In one microsecond, light goes three hundred metres.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Train
data.value: The train. On the train it is six hundred metres long. Seen from the platform while it's moving, it's shorter, and so are its windows and wheels.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_TrainClocks
data.value: Three clocks on the train, set together on the train. Seen from the platform they're out of step: the further forward, the further behind.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_TrainLength
data.value: The train's length here. A moving train is shortened along its motion, by gamma. On the train itself, it's always six hundred metres.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Traveller
data.value: The twin who travels, and how many years they've lived by their own clock. It's always fewer, by the factor gamma.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Triangle
data.value: The light-clock triangle. The slanted side is what light covers, the bottom what the clock covers, and the upright side what the light would cover in the clock's own time. Pythagoras says the slanted trip takes gamma times as long.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Turn
data.value: The turning point, where the traveller reaches the star and heads home. Drag it to change how far the star is and how fast the ship flies.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Watcher
data.value: The person standing on the platform. The lamp flashes right in front of them, and for them the platform is at rest.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Younger
data.value: The age gap between the twins. When they meet again, it's real: the traveller has lived fewer years.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Obj_Zigzag
data.value: The zigzag is the moving clock's light, seen from here. Because the clock moves on while the light bounces, the light runs slanted. The path is longer, so each tick takes longer.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_01
data.value: Here's a train with a lamp in its very middle, and a light catcher at each end. Right now we're riding on the train, so the train stands still and it's the platform that moves.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_02
data.value: The lamp flashes. Light sets off towards the back and the front at the same speed, and both ends are the same distance away.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_03
data.value: So on the train, the light reaches the back and the front at exactly the same moment. Both catchers light up together.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_04
data.value: Now let's watch the very same thing from the platform. The train rushes past to the right, and the lamp will flash just as it passes this person.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_05
data.value: The light still sets off both ways at the same speed, from the spot where the flash happened. But meanwhile, the whole train keeps moving to the right.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_06
data.value: The back of the train is rushing towards the light, and the front is running away from it. So which end does the light reach first?

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_07
data.value: The back. Seen from the platform, the back is hit first and the front only later. Two things that happen at the same time on the train don't happen at the same time on the platform. That's the relativity of simultaneity.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_08
data.value: Look at the lengths too. On the train it's six hundred metres long, but from the platform it's shorter. Moving things are squeezed along their motion, by the same gamma as the clocks.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_09
data.value: These are the train's own clocks, set together on the train. Seen from the platform they don't agree: the one at the front is behind the one at the back. That's how the train and the platform can both be right.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Simultaneity_10
data.value: Your turn. Change the speed, or switch between the train and the platform, and watch the flash again. The faster the train, the bigger the gap between the two hits.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_01
data.value: This is a spacetime diagram. Going across is distance from Earth, in light-years. Going up is time on Earth, in years. Every moment of our story is one point on this picture.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_02
data.value: One twin stays at home. Earth doesn't go anywhere, so the home twin's line goes straight up. Each mark on it is one more birthday.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_03
data.value: Light travels one light-year every year, so on this picture it runs at forty-five degrees. Nothing can go faster, so nothing's line can be flatter than this.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_04
data.value: The other twin flies at eight tenths of the speed of light to a star four light-years away, turns round, and comes straight back. That's this bent line.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_05
data.value: On Earth, the whole trip takes ten years. When the traveller gets home, how many years older will they be?

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_06
data.value: Six. The ship's clock ran slow all the way, so the traveller comes home four years younger than their twin. Count the marks: ten on Earth's line, but only six on the ship's.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_07
data.value: But wait. From the ship, isn't it Earth that's moving? Why isn't it the other way round? Because only the traveller turns round. The traveller switches from one point of view to another; the home twin never does.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_08
data.value: These purple lines show which moment on Earth the traveller calls “now”. On the way out, Earth's clocks seem slow too. But at the turn, the traveller's “now” on Earth jumps forward by years in an instant. That's where the home twin's extra years come from.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_09
data.value: Now suppose both twins send a flash of light on every birthday. On the way out, the traveller receives Earth's flashes slowly; on the way back, quickly. Both twins agree on every flash, and the numbers add up.

data.name: Narr_Rel_Twins_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the turning point to change how far and how fast the traveller goes. The closer the bent line gets to the light lines, the younger the traveller comes home.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_01
data.value: Now let's fly far above the Sun and look down. Here are the orbits of Earth and Mars, drawn to scale. They both go round the same way.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_02
data.value: Earth is on the inside lane. It has a shorter way to go, and it moves faster, about thirty kilometres every second.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_03
data.value: This line is our line of sight: from Earth, through Mars, on towards the distant stars. Its direction is where we see Mars in the sky.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_04
data.value: The numbers mark the line of sight at different moments. In the circle in the corner, they're all drawn from one point, because the stars are so far away that only the direction counts. One, then two: the line turns forward, so Mars drifts east.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_05
data.value: Now Earth catches up with Mars, and overtakes it on the inside. At three, the line stops turning. At four and five, it has swung backwards. That's the retrograde loop.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_06
data.value: So, why does Mars seem to go backwards?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_07
data.value: Once Earth is past, the line swings forward again. Mars never really reverses. It's like overtaking a slower car on the motorway: for a moment, it seems to slide backwards against the hills far away.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_08
data.value: For Mercury and Venus, it's the other way round. They're on the inside lane, so they overtake us, and they go backwards as they pass between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag Earth round its orbit and watch the line of sight, or try another planet.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_01
data.value: For almost two thousand years, people put Earth at the centre of everything. Let's do the same. Hold Earth still, and see where Mars goes.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_02
data.value: Mars draws loop after loop, roughly one every two years. And every loop comes when Mars is closest to us.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_03
data.value: The ancient astronomer Ptolemy explained this with circles. Mars rides on a small circle, the epicycle, and the centre of that circle goes round a big one, the deferent.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_04
data.value: Here's the surprise. The epicycle is just Earth's own orbit, seen from Earth. Its arm always points the same way as the Sun, and it turns once a year.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_05
data.value: What do you think happens if we hold the Sun still instead?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_06
data.value: Copernicus put the Sun in the middle. Watch the loops untangle into a plain, almost circular orbit. The same motion, but a much simpler picture.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_07
data.value: Back to Earth at the centre, this time with Venus. Over eight years, Venus loops five times and draws a five-petalled flower, then starts again almost exactly where it began.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_08
data.value: Your turn. Switch between Earth and the Sun at the centre, or choose another planet and watch its pattern grow.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Conjunction
data.value: Inferior conjunction: the planet passes between Earth and the Sun. It's lost in the Sun's glare, at its closest to us, and going backwards fastest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Deferent
data.value: The deferent: Ptolemy's big circle round Earth. The centre of the epicycle rides round it.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our moving viewpoint. Because we watch from a planet that is itself going round the Sun, the other planets seem to loop.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: Earth's orbit: one lap a year, at about thirty kilometres every second.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_East
data.value: East among the stars. This is the way the planets usually drift, night after night, and the way the Sun and the Moon move against the stars too.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Ecliptic
data.value: The ecliptic: the Sun's path round the sky in a year. The planets' orbits lie almost in the same plane as Earth's, so they always wander close to it.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Epicycle
data.value: The epicycle: the small circle the planet rides on. For Mars, Jupiter and Saturn it is really Earth's own orbit in disguise. For Mercury and Venus it is the planet's own orbit round the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Fan
data.value: The lines of sight, all drawn from one point. The stars are so far away that only a line's direction matters, so here you can see the line turn forward, then back, then forward again.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Frame
data.value: What is held still in the middle. With Earth still, the planets loop. With the Sun still, they go round in plain orbits. Either way, it's the very same motion.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, the giant. It moves so slowly that Earth laps it about every thirteen months, and each time it goes backwards for about four months.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Loop
data.value: A retrograde loop, seen from Earth. Each one comes when Earth and the planet are at their closest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Marks
data.value: The line of sight at seven moments: before the loop, halfway to the first stop, at the first stop, in the middle, at the second stop, halfway on, and after.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, the red planet, one step out from Earth. Earth overtakes it about every twenty-six months, and then it goes backwards for about ten weeks.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the planet nearest the Sun. It goes round in eighty-eight days and overtakes us three or four times a year, so it goes backwards more often than any other planet, for about three weeks each time.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Opposition
data.value: Opposition: the planet is opposite the Sun in our sky, with Earth right between them. It's up all night, near its closest and brightest, and going backwards fastest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_PlanetOrbit
data.value: The planet's orbit, drawn to scale. The farther a planet is from the Sun, the slower it goes, and the longer its year.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Retro
data.value: The retrograde stretch. For these weeks the planet moves west against the stars, the opposite of its usual way.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, the ringed planet. It's so slow that Earth passes it almost every year, and it spends about four and a half months going backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Scale
data.value: A ruler for the sky. Ten degrees is about the width of your fist, held out at arm's length.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_SightLine
data.value: Our line of sight: from Earth, through the planet, on towards the far stars. Its direction is where we see the planet in the sky.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Speed
data.value: How fast each one moves along its orbit. The inner planet is always the faster one, so it's always the one that overtakes.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Stars
data.value: The background stars. Here they're drawn just outside the orbits, but really they're far, far away. Even the nearest one is more than a quarter of a million times farther than the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_StationDirect
data.value: The second station. The backward motion slows to a stop, and then the planet heads east again.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_StationRetro
data.value: The first station. The planet's eastward drift slows down to nothing, and it seems to stand still for a few days before it starts going backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Every planet goes round it the same way. In our sky it moves steadily east along the ecliptic, and it never goes backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the brightest planet. It goes backwards about every nineteen months, for some six weeks, as it passes between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Zodiac
data.value: The zodiac constellations, the star patterns along the ecliptic. The Sun, the Moon and the planets all pass through them.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_01
data.value: This is a strip of the night sky along the zodiac, the band of stars the planets wander through. The bright dot is Mars. Let's watch it for a few months. Night after night, it creeps along among the stars.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_02
data.value: Most of the time, Mars drifts eastward, the way the gold arrow points. All the planets do, because they all go round the Sun in the same direction as Earth.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_03
data.value: But now, look. Mars slows down, and stops. For a few days it hardly moves against the stars at all. This is called a station.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_04
data.value: What do you think Mars does next?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_05
data.value: It turns round and goes backwards, westward, for about ten weeks. Astronomers call this retrograde motion. The orange stretch is the backward part.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_06
data.value: Right in the middle of the backward stretch, Mars is opposite the Sun in our sky. It rises at sunset, shines all night, and is at its closest and brightest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_07
data.value: Then it slows down, stops a second time, and turns east again, as if nothing had happened.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_08
data.value: Here's the whole path. Sometimes it's a loop, sometimes a zigzag, depending on how the planet's orbit is tilted against ours. And it always stays close to the ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_09
data.value: Your turn. Pick another planet and watch its loop, or drag across the sky to move through the days.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_01
data.value: Lots of people think summer is warm because Earth is closer to the Sun. And Earth's path really isn't a perfect circle. It's a very slightly squashed oval.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_02
data.value: So here's one for you to guess. In which month is Earth closest to the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_03
data.value: The answer is early January. That's when Earth is closest to the Sun, at a point called perihelion. Yet January is the coldest time of year in the north!

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_04
data.value: And in early July, Earth is at its farthest, a point called aphelion. But that's the middle of summer in the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_05
data.value: Over the year the distance changes by only about three percent, which hardly affects the temperature. So the seasons aren't really about distance. The real reason is the tilt of Earth's axis.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Aphelion
data.value: This is aphelion. Every year in early July, Earth is farthest from the Sun, about a hundred and fifty-two million kilometres away.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Axis
data.value: This line is Earth's axis, and it always points at the North Star. Because its direction never changes, the north and south take turns leaning towards the Sun as Earth goes around.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_December
data.value: This is the December solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, so the north has its shortest day, and the south its longest.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Earth
data.value: This is Earth. It spins on its axis while it travels around the Sun. One spin is a day, and one trip around is a year. The gold line on it is your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Equinox
data.value: This is an equinox. On this day the axis leans neither towards the Sun nor away from it, so day and night are about the same length all over the world.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_June
data.value: This is the June solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so the north has its longest day, and the south its shortest.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Noon
data.value: This is where the Sun is at noon, its highest point of the day. The number beside it is how high it stands above the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Perihelion
data.value: This is perihelion. Every year in early January, Earth comes closest to the Sun, about a hundred and forty-seven million kilometres away.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Shadow
data.value: This is an upright post and its shadow. In a day, the shadow is shortest at noon. Over a year, noon shadows are shortest in summer and longest in winter.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_SkySun
data.value: This is where the Sun is right now. The higher it is above the horizon, the more directly its light hits the ground, and the more warmth the ground gets.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is the Sun, the source of the energy behind the seasons. The Sun and Earth are drawn far bigger than they really are, or you couldn't see them.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Sunrise
data.value: This is where the Sun rises and sets. Only around the equinoxes does it rise due east and set due west. On other days it rises and sets further north or south.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_01
data.value: This time we're standing on the ground. The little post in the middle marks where you are, and the dome over it is your sky.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_02
data.value: Watch the Sun. It rises in the east, slowly arcs across the sky, and sets in the west. This gold curve is the path it takes today.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_03
data.value: The highest point of the curve is noon. The higher the Sun climbs, the more concentrated its light is, and the more it warms the ground.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_04
data.value: Now look at the post's shadow. When the Sun is high, the shadow is short. When it's low, the shadow is long. Long ago, people tracked the seasons by measuring shadows just like this.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_05
data.value: Now let's run time through a whole year instead. Look at the two dashed curves. In summer the Sun's path is high and long. In winter it's low and short.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_06
data.value: Think about it. Why is summer warmer than winter?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_07
data.value: There are two reasons, working together. The Sun climbs higher, so its light is more concentrated, and the days are longer, so the ground warms for more hours. Drag left and right across the picture to move through the day yourself.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_01
data.value: Have you ever wondered why summer is warm and winter is cold? A lot of people guess it's because Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer. Let's find out together.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_02
data.value: In the middle is the Sun. Earth travels around it along this dashed path, and one trip around takes a whole year.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_03
data.value: Now look at the white line through Earth. It's called the axis, and Earth spins around it. Notice that it isn't upright. It leans over by about twenty-three and a half degrees.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_04
data.value: Here's the clever part. Wherever Earth is on its path, the axis always points the same way, towards the North Star. Keep your eye on it for a moment. It always leans to the upper right.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_05
data.value: Let's stop in June. Right now the northern half of Earth leans towards the Sun. The sunlight comes in more steeply, and the days are longer, so it's summer in the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_06
data.value: Now it's your turn. Drag Earth round to December, or just click on December, and see what happens to the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_07
data.value: In December the axis still points the same way, but now the north leans away from the Sun. The light arrives at a low slant, the days are short, and the north has winter. The south is the other way round. It's having summer.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_08
data.value: Quick question. What would happen if Earth's axis didn't lean at all?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_09
data.value: Let's set the tilt to zero and see. Now every day of the year is much the same. The Sun is always overhead at the equator, day and night are equal, and the seasons disappear.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_10
data.value: So the secret of the seasons isn't distance. It's the tilt of the axis. Try the sliders on the left page with a different tilt or latitude, and watch how the day length and the noon Sun on the card change.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_Air
data.value: The air, drawn many times too thick. Nearly all of it is in the lowest fifty kilometres, a very thin layer compared with Earth.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_BeltOfVenus
data.value: The Belt of Venus, a pink glow just above Earth's shadow. It's air high up, still lit by the reddened light of the setting Sun.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_Box
data.value: The box of air. It stands for all the air the sunlight crosses before it reaches you: a little at noon, and about forty times as much at sunset.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_EarthShadow
data.value: Earth's shadow. After sunset, the air opposite the Sun is no longer lit, and Earth's own shadow shows as a dark blue band rising from the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_EndEye
data.value: This eye looks back along the beam at the Sun. It sees what's left after the scattering: white at noon, orange and red when the Sun is low.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_Overhead
data.value: The air straight overhead. The amount of air the light crosses is counted in units of this.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_Ray
data.value: The path of the sunlight that reaches you, coloured by what's left of the light along the way.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_SideEye
data.value: This eye looks at the side of the beam. It sees only the light bounced out of the beam towards it, and that's mostly blue: the blue sky.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Its light is white, a mix of every colour. It only looks yellow, orange or red when the air has taken some of the blue out of it.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_SunBehind
data.value: The Sun is behind you. Facing away from it after sunset, you can watch Earth's shadow rise.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Obj_You
data.value: You, standing on the ground. Drag around yourself to move the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_01
data.value: Here's a slice through Earth and its air. The air is drawn many times too thick, so you can see it. And this is you, standing on the ground.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_02
data.value: At noon, sunlight comes down to you quite steeply. It crosses only a thin layer of air, so it stays white.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_03
data.value: This dashed line is the air straight overhead. The amount of air that light crosses is measured in units of this.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_04
data.value: Think about it. At sunset, how much air does sunlight cross, compared with the air straight overhead?

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_05
data.value: About forty times as much. The light skims through the thickest, lowest air, and loses its blue along the way. By the time it reaches you, it's orange and red.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_06
data.value: After sunset, the light no longer reaches you. It passes over your head and lights the air high above, while you stand in Earth's shadow.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Path_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag around yourself to move the Sun, and watch how long the light's path becomes.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_01
data.value: Here's a beam of sunlight passing through a box of air. The little coloured streaks are photons, tiny bits of light, in all the colours of sunlight.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_02
data.value: The box stands for all the air the sunlight crosses before it reaches you. At noon, that's not very much.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_03
data.value: Watch the photons. Now and then, one hits a molecule and bounces off to the side. Blue and violet photons bounce far more often than red ones, four or five times as often.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_04
data.value: This eye looks at the side of the beam. It only sees light that was bounced towards it, and that's mostly blue. That's the blue sky.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_05
data.value: This eye looks straight back along the beam, at the Sun. It sees what's left once some of the blue has gone, so the Sun looks a little yellow.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_06
data.value: Think about it. If the Sun were low in the sky, so its light crossed far more air, what colour would the end of the beam turn?

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_07
data.value: Orange, then red. On the long trip, so much blue and green is scattered away that mostly orange and red get through. That's the colour of the setting Sun.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_08
data.value: Now you try. On the left-hand page, change the haze and dust in the air, and watch what happens to the colours.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Scatter_09
data.value: Haze and dust are much bigger than air molecules, and they scatter all colours about the same. So they make the sky paler and more milky white.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_01
data.value: Here's the sky over the sea on a clear afternoon. Sunlight looks white, but it's really a mix of all the colours of the rainbow.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_02
data.value: So why is the sky blue? As sunlight passes through the air, the tiny molecules of air bounce some of it aside, and they bounce blue light far more than red. That scattered blue light reaches us from every part of the sky.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_03
data.value: Think about it. If Earth had no air at all, what colour would the daytime sky be?

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_04
data.value: Black, just like on the Moon. With no air, there's nothing to scatter the light, so you'd see a blazing Sun in a black sky full of stars.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_05
data.value: Now watch the Sun go down. The lower it gets, the more air its light has to cross, and more and more blue is scattered away on the way. What's left turns yellow, then orange, then red.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_06
data.value: After sunset, turn around. Low in the sky opposite the Sun, a dark blue band rises. It's Earth's own shadow, cast on the air. The pink glow above it is called the Belt of Venus.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag up or down in the sky to move the Sun, and watch how the colours change.

data.name: Narr_Sky_Sky_08
data.value: Blue skies and red sunsets have the same cause: air scatters blue light far more than red. The other two views show how.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Ariel
data.value: Ariel, one of the brightest moons of Uranus, crossed by long valleys.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Callisto
data.value: Callisto, one of the most heavily cratered worlds we know. Its surface has hardly changed for billions of years.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Deimos
data.value: Deimos, Mars's smaller moon, only about twelve kilometres across. Both of Mars's moons may be captured asteroids.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Dione
data.value: Dione, an icy moon of Saturn, its surface streaked with bright cliffs of ice.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our home, and the only place we know of with life. Most of its surface is covered by oceans of liquid water.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Enceladus
data.value: Enceladus, a small, bright moon of Saturn. Jets of water shoot out from cracks near its south pole, from an ocean hidden under the ice.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Europa
data.value: Europa, covered in a shell of ice. Underneath there's probably a deep ocean of salty water, one of the best places to look for life.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Ganymede
data.value: Ganymede, the biggest moon in the solar system, even bigger than the planet Mercury.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Iapetus
data.value: Iapetus, a two-faced moon: one side is as dark as coal, and the other as bright as snow.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Io
data.value: Io, the most volcanic place in the solar system. Jupiter's pull squeezes it so hard that hundreds of volcanoes keep erupting.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, the biggest planet, a giant ball of gas. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has been raging for centuries.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, the red planet. Rusty dust gives it its colour, and it has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no air, so its days are hot enough to melt lead, and its nights are freezing.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mimas
data.value: Mimas, a small icy moon of Saturn, with one enormous crater almost a third as wide as the whole moon.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Miranda
data.value: Miranda, a small moon of Uranus with a jumbled-up surface and some of the tallest cliffs in the solar system.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon, Earth's only natural satellite. It always shows us the same face, and it's the only other world where people have walked.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Neptune
data.value: Neptune, the farthest planet, with the fastest winds in the solar system. It was found by mathematics before anyone had seen it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Oberon
data.value: Oberon, the outermost of Uranus's big moons, old and heavily cratered.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Phobos
data.value: Phobos, the bigger of Mars's two little moons. It's slowly spiralling in towards Mars, and one day it will break apart.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Rhea
data.value: Rhea, Saturn's second-biggest moon, a cold, cratered ball of ice and rock.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, famous for its rings, made of countless chunks of ice and rock. It's so light for its size that it would float in water.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun, the star at the centre of our solar system. About a million Earths could fit inside it, and its light takes about eight minutes to reach us.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Tethys
data.value: Tethys, a moon of Saturn made almost entirely of water ice, with a huge canyon stretching most of the way around it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Titan
data.value: Titan, Saturn's biggest moon. It has a thick orange atmosphere, and lakes and seas of liquid methane.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Titania
data.value: Titania, the biggest moon of Uranus, with great canyons cut across its icy surface.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Triton
data.value: Triton, Neptune's big moon. It goes round the wrong way, which suggests Neptune captured it, and it has geysers that shoot out nitrogen.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Umbriel
data.value: Umbriel, the darkest of Uranus's big moons, with a strange bright ring on its surface.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Uranus
data.value: Uranus, an ice giant tipped right over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury. Its thick clouds trap the heat. It also spins backwards, so there the Sun rises in the west.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_01
data.value: This is our solar system, seen from above, with the planets where they really are today. In the middle is the Sun. It holds more than ninety-nine percent of all the mass in the whole solar system.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_02
data.value: The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. Earth is the third one out from the Sun.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_03
data.value: Beyond Mars is the asteroid belt: millions of rocky lumps, left over from when the planets formed.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_04
data.value: Then come the giants. Jupiter is the biggest planet by far. More than a thousand Earths would fit inside it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_05
data.value: Saturn, with its famous rings of ice, is so light for its size that it would float in a big enough bath.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_06
data.value: Far out are the two ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. Neptune takes a hundred and sixty-five years to go once around the Sun.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_07
data.value: In this picture, the planets are spaced out evenly, so they all fit. Think about it: in real life, how far out is Neptune, compared with Earth?

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_08
data.value: About thirty times as far. Now the distances are true to scale. The inner planets huddle close to the Sun, and the outer ones are spread far apart. Even so, the planets themselves are still drawn much too big.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_09
data.value: Let's fly to Earth. Going round it is the Moon, the only other world where people have walked.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_10
data.value: Now you try. Click any planet or moon to fly to it and hear about it.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Antinode
data.value: An antinode: halfway between two nodes, where the string swings the most.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Beat
data.value: Beats: two notes slightly apart in frequency go in and out of step. The loudness swells as many times a second as their frequencies differ.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Body
data.value: The body and sound hole. The guitar's hollow box and the air inside it resonate with the string, making the sound loud enough to fill a room.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Bridge
data.value: The bridge holds the string's far end still, and passes its vibration into the guitar's top, which pushes far more air than the thin string ever could.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_ClosedEnd
data.value: A closed end. The air can't move through the wall, so it stays still here. But this is where its pressure swings the most.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Compression
data.value: A compression: the air here is squeezed slightly, so its pressure is a little above normal. Compressions travel away from the speaker at the speed of sound.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Ear
data.value: The ear. The air's push and pull moves the eardrum; three tiny bones pass the motion on to the cochlea, where hair cells turn it into signals for the brain.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Envelope
data.value: The envelope: how the loudness changes from the start of a note to its end. A sharp start and a slow fade sounds struck or plucked; a slow swell sounds bowed or blown.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Fret
data.value: Frets. Pressing a string behind a fret shortens the part that vibrates. Each fret makes it about six percent shorter, raising the note by one semitone. Click the neck to hold one.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Fundamental
data.value: The fundamental: the lowest frequency in the sound. It usually sets the pitch we hear.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Harmonic
data.value: An overtone: the string splits into equal parts that swing in opposite directions. Its frequency is a whole number times the fundamental. Click the row to hear it alone.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Harmonic1
data.value: The fundamental: the whole string swings as one arch. It's the lowest frequency the string makes, and the pitch you hear. Click the row to hear it alone.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Keyboard
data.value: The keyboard is tuned in equal temperament: every key is the same step up, a frequency ratio of about 1.0595. Twelve steps make exactly a doubling.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Medium
data.value: What the sound travels through. Sound needs a medium, and the harder it is to squeeze for its weight, the faster sound goes: about 343 metres a second in air, 1480 in water, nearly 6000 in steel.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Node
data.value: A node: a point that stays still in this harmonic. The second harmonic has one in the middle, the third has two, and so on.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Octave
data.value: An octave: twelve keys up, twice the frequency. Notes an octave apart sound so alike that they share the same letter name.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_OpenEnd
data.value: An open end. The air here can move in and out freely, so this is where it moves the most, while its pressure stays close to normal.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Overtone
data.value: The overtones: frequencies at two, three, four times the fundamental and up. How strong each one is gives the sound its colour. Drag the bars to change them.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Particle
data.value: One small patch of air. It moves back and forth along the direction the sound travels, but always comes back to the same place. That's why sound is called a longitudinal wave.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Period
data.value: The period: the time for one full repeat of the wave. Frequency is one over the period, so a period of a thousandth of a second means a thousand hertz.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Pipe
data.value: The air column. What vibrates here is the air itself, back and forth along the pipe. Only waves that fit its length can build up: those are the pipe's resonances.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_PipeAntinode
data.value: An antinode: the air here rushes back and forth the most, while its pressure hardly changes.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_PipeMode
data.value: One of the pipe's resonances. An open pipe allows every whole-number multiple of its lowest frequency; a closed pipe, only the odd ones. Click a row to hear it.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_PipeNode
data.value: A node: the air here stays still, but it's squeezed and stretched the most.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Pluck
data.value: Where the string will be plucked. Plucking near an end starts many high harmonics and sounds bright; plucking near the middle sounds soft and round.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Pressure
data.value: The pressure along the way. Up means squeezed, down means stretched. Even loud sounds change the air's pressure by only a tiny fraction.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Rarefaction
data.value: A rarefaction: the air here is spread out slightly, so its pressure dips a little below normal. It follows each compression, half a wavelength behind.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Speaker
data.value: A loudspeaker turns an electrical signal into motion. A coil in a magnet's field pushes the cone back and forth, and the cone pushes the air. Drag the cone to push the air yourself.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_String
data.value: The string. Its note depends on three things: shorter, tighter and lighter strings vibrate faster. Drag it and let go to pluck it.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Timbre
data.value: The instrument and the note. Two instruments playing the same note have the same pitch but a different timbre, because their waves have different shapes.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Waveform
data.value: The waveform: how the air pressure at a microphone rises and falls over a few thousandths of a second. Its shape carries the sound's timbre.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Obj_Wavelength
data.value: The wavelength: the distance from one compression to the next. It equals the speed of sound divided by the frequency, so higher notes have shorter waves.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_01
data.value: A guitar string is held tight at both ends. Pluck it, and the bend you made splits in two and runs back and forth between the ends, again and again.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_02
data.value: That busy motion is really a few simple shapes added together. The simplest is one big arch, swinging up and down. It's called the fundamental, and it sets the note you hear.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_03
data.value: Then come shapes with two, three, four arches. These are the overtones, at exactly two, three and four times the frequency. Together they give the string its bright, rich sound.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_04
data.value: Look at the dots on each row. Those points never move: they're called nodes. Halfway between them, where the string swings the most, are the antinodes.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_05
data.value: Here's a puzzle. If you pluck the string exactly in the middle, which harmonics can't start at all?

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_06
data.value: Plucked in the middle now. The second, fourth and sixth harmonics all have a node right there, and you can't start a wave by pulling a point that has to stay still. So the even ones vanish, and the sound turns round and hollow.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_07
data.value: Now press the twelfth fret. Only half the string can vibrate, and half the length means twice the frequency: the same note, one octave higher.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_08
data.value: Air in a pipe can do the same. At an open end the air moves freely, so there's an antinode there. In this pipe, open at both ends like a flute, the lowest note fits half a wave.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_09
data.value: Now close the far end. The air there can't move, so it becomes a node. Only a quarter of a wave fits, so the note drops about an octave, and only the odd harmonics are allowed.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Strings_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the string and let go to pluck it somewhere new, click the neck to hold a different fret, or click a row to hear just one harmonic.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_01
data.value: Each key on a piano is a pitch: a number of vibrations every second. This A, just above middle C, is 440 hertz. It's the note orchestras tune to.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_02
data.value: Go up twelve keys, one octave, and the frequency doubles. Every step in between is the same small ratio: each key is about six percent higher than the one before.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_03
data.value: This is what a microphone would record from a tuning fork: a smooth, simple wave, repeating over and over, 440 times every second.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_04
data.value: The time for one repeat is the period. Here it's a little over two milliseconds. Higher notes have shorter periods.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_05
data.value: Now the same note on a violin. Same pitch, same period, but look at the shape: jagged, like a saw. That difference in shape is what we call timbre.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_06
data.value: The bars show why. The violin adds lots of overtones, at two, three, four times the frequency and beyond. The tuning fork had almost none.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_07
data.value: Timbre is also about how a note starts and ends. A piano note strikes in an instant and then slowly fades, while a violin can swell and hold its sound.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_08
data.value: Question time. A clarinet and a flute both play this same A. What's different about the two sounds?

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_09
data.value: Now two tuning forks, three hertz apart. They drift in and out of step, so the sound swells and fades three times a second. These are beats. Tuners listen for them to slow down and vanish.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Timbre_10
data.value: Your turn. Pick an instrument and play some keys, or drag the bars to build a sound of your own.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_01
data.value: Every sound starts with something shaking. Here it's a loudspeaker. Watch its cone: it moves forward and back, pushing on the air in front of it, over and over.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_02
data.value: Now follow the red dot. It's a little patch of air. Does it fly off towards the ear? No. It just shuffles back and forth around the same spot.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_03
data.value: Where the dots crowd together, the air is squeezed a little. That's a compression, and its pressure is slightly higher than normal.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_04
data.value: In between, the dots spread apart: a rarefaction, where the pressure dips a little. See how the pattern moves to the right? That moving pattern is the sound.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_05
data.value: So here's a question. When you hear this speaker from across the room, what has actually travelled from the speaker to your ear?

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_06
data.value: The pattern travels; the air stays where it is. From one compression to the next is one wavelength. Now the pitch has doubled. Watch: the new compressions leave the speaker half as far apart.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_07
data.value: This graph shows the pressure along the way: up where the air is squeezed, down where it's stretched. Even this fairly loud sound changes the pressure by less than one part in a million.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_08
data.value: Now let's take the air away. The cone still moves, but there's nothing in front of it to push. In a vacuum, sound can't travel at all.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_09
data.value: And in water? Its molecules are packed close and are very hard to squeeze, so sound races through more than four times faster. The same note now has a much longer wavelength. Check the ruler.

data.name: Narr_Sound_Wave_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the speaker's cone to push the air yourself, or switch on the tone and change its frequency or level. Notice what changes, and what doesn't.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_01
data.value: This is hydrogen, the simplest atom of all: one proton in the middle, and one electron around it.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_02
data.value: The electron can't sit just anywhere. It lives on certain energy levels, like the rungs of a ladder. Right now it's on the lowest rung, the ground level.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_03
data.value: To climb, it has to take in exactly the right amount of energy: a photon that matches the gap between two rungs. Here one arrives and lifts it up to level three.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_04
data.value: It doesn't stay up there. It drops back, and the energy leaves as a new photon. From level three to two, that photon is red.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_05
data.value: Then from two down to one. That gap is much bigger, so the photon carries more energy. It's ultraviolet, invisible to our eyes.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_06
data.value: Each jump always gives the same colour. So hydrogen's light isn't a rainbow, but a few sharp lines, its fingerprint. The visible ones, the Balmer series, all end on level two.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_07
data.value: A question. If we fire red light of six hundred and forty nanometres at the electron on the ground level, what happens?

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_08
data.value: It passes straight through. From the ground, even the smallest step needs ultraviolet. A red photon simply doesn't carry the right amount, and only exact matches are taken in.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_09
data.value: Give it more than thirteen point six electron-volts, though, and the electron escapes altogether. The atom is ionised. Soon it's caught again, and tumbles down, giving out lines on the way.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_10
data.value: In fact the electron isn't a tiny planet on an orbit. Quantum physics says it's a cloud of where it might be found. Each level has clouds of its own shapes, like this dumbbell.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Atom_11
data.value: Your turn. Click a level on the ladder to lift the electron, or choose a colour and fire photons at it.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_01
data.value: Here's a glowing tube of hydrogen. Electricity keeps knocking its electrons up, and as they fall back, the gas glows.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_02
data.value: Its light passes through a narrow slit, then a prism. The prism bends each colour by a different amount and spreads them across the screen.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_03
data.value: Instead of a rainbow, we get a few bright lines: red, blue-green and violet. They're exactly the Balmer lines from the atom view.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_04
data.value: Every gas has its own set of lines. Neon's are crowded in the red and orange, which is why neon signs glow red.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_05
data.value: Sodium shines almost all in one yellow line. But magnify it, and it turns out to be two lines, very close together.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_06
data.value: A hot solid, like a bulb's filament, is different. It gives every colour at once: a continuous rainbow.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_07
data.value: Now suppose we shine the bulb through a cloud of cool sodium vapour. What do you think we'll see in the rainbow?

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_08
data.value: Dark lines, right where sodium shines when it's hot. A cool gas absorbs exactly the colours it would give out.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_09
data.value: Sunlight is crossed by hundreds of these dark lines. By matching them with lamps in the lab, we found out what the Sun is made of, without ever going there.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Lamps_10
data.value: Your turn. Here's a mystery lamp. Compare its lines with the fingerprints in the chart, then make your guess.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_BalmerDark
data.value: The Balmer lines in absorption. They need hydrogen with its electron already on level two, which happens most near ten thousand degrees.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Bulb
data.value: A filament heated white-hot. In a solid the atoms crowd so close that every colour comes out together, a smooth rainbow.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Calcium
data.value: Two strong dark lines of ionised calcium at the violet end, Fraunhofer's H and K. They're the strongest lines in Sun-like and cooler stars.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Cloud
data.value: Where the electron is likely to be found, brighter where more likely. The shapes come from quantum mechanics: s clouds are round, p clouds are dumbbells, d clouds have four lobes.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Compare
data.value: A gas's lines placed under the spectrum. If every line lines up, it's the same gas.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_CoolGas
data.value: A cloud of cool gas between the bulb and the slit. Its atoms absorb exactly the colours they'd give out when hot, so those colours go missing.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_DarkLine
data.value: A colour missing from the rainbow: atoms in a cooler gas in the way absorbed it. It sits exactly where that gas's bright line would be.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Electron
data.value: The electron carries a negative charge. It can only have certain amounts of energy, so it's found only on certain levels, never in between.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Energy
data.value: Each level's energy, in electron-volts. Negative means bound to the atom; zero is just free. The gaps between levels set the colours of the light.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_GasLamp
data.value: A glass tube of thin gas with a high voltage across it. Electrons racing through knock the gas atoms' electrons up, and as they fall back the gas glows in its own colours.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Ground
data.value: The lowest level. An electron here has the least energy, minus thirteen point six electron-volts, and it stays here unless something lifts it.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_HSpectrum
data.value: Every photon given out so far, sorted by wavelength. The lines are always in the same places: hydrogen's fingerprint, from the ultraviolet through the visible into the infrared.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Helium
data.value: Helium holds its electrons tightly, so only very hot stars can lift them enough to absorb visible light. These lines mark blue stars.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Infrared
data.value: Light with longer waves than red, which we feel as warmth rather than see. Small falls between high levels give it.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Ionise
data.value: Above zero the electron is no longer bound: it's free, and the atom has become an ion. From the ground level that takes thirteen point six electron-volts.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Level
data.value: One rung of the ladder. Click it to lift the electron here: a photon of exactly the energy of that jump will be sent in.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Line
data.value: Light of one exact wavelength, given out when the gas's electrons make one particular jump. Its place on the ruler tells you which.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Molecules
data.value: In the coolest stars, atoms join into molecules such as titanium oxide. Molecules absorb in broad bands, not thin lines.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Mystery
data.value: A lamp whose gas is hidden. Its lines are its fingerprint: compare them with the chart and guess.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Nanometre
data.value: The ruler is in nanometres, millionths of a millimetre. Our eyes see from about four hundred, violet, to seven hundred, red.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Nucleus
data.value: Hydrogen's nucleus is a single proton, with a positive charge. It holds the electron by electric attraction, and it's nearly two thousand times heavier.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Orbit
data.value: In Bohr's picture the electron circles on fixed orbits, each a level. The higher the level, the wider the orbit, and the less firmly the electron is held.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Peak
data.value: Where the star shines brightest. Wien's law: the hotter the star, the shorter the wavelength of its peak. Drag it to change the temperature.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_PhotonIn
data.value: A packet of light, its colour set by its energy. It's taken in only if its energy exactly fits a jump the electron can make.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_PhotonLamp
data.value: It fires photons of the wavelength you choose. Try one that matches a jump, and one that doesn't.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_PhotonOut
data.value: When the electron falls, the energy it loses leaves as this photon. A bigger fall gives a bluer photon, with a shorter wave.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Planck
data.value: How much light a hot body gives at each wavelength, from Planck's law. Hotter bodies give more at every wavelength, and most at shorter ones.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Prism
data.value: Glass slows violet light a little more than red, so it bends violet more. The colours fan out in order of wavelength.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Reference
data.value: A hydrogen lamp at rest in the lab, for comparison. Its lines show where the star's lines would be if the star weren't moving.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Shift
data.value: When a source moves away, its waves are stretched and every line moves towards the red; coming closer, towards the blue. The shift gives the speed.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Slit
data.value: A narrow gap lets through a thin line of light. Each colour then lands as a thin line on the screen, so lines close together stay apart.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Star
data.value: A ball of hot gas. Its colour comes from its surface temperature: red for cool stars, white for medium ones, blue for the hottest.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_StarSpectrum
data.value: The star's light spread out, with the dark lines of the gases in its atmosphere. Drag it sideways to make the star move.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_SunLight
data.value: The Sun's surface glows like a hot body at nearly six thousand degrees. The gas above it is cooler and takes out its own colours, leaving dark lines.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Trace
data.value: How bright the light is at each wavelength. Bright lines are peaks, dark lines are dips.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Ultraviolet
data.value: Light with shorter waves than violet, too energetic for our eyes. Falls to the ground level, the Lyman series, all land here.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Visible
data.value: The narrow band our eyes can see. A star's colour depends on how its curve slopes across this band.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Obj_Zoom
data.value: A few nanometres around the picked line, enlarged forty times. Sodium's yellow line turns out to be two lines, six tenths of a nanometre apart.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_01
data.value: Stars are huge balls of hot gas. Their light carries two secrets: how hot they are, and what they're made of.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_02
data.value: Any hot body glows with this curve of colours. The Sun's peak is in the visible, near green, but it gives out all colours together, so it looks white.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_03
data.value: A cooler star peaks in the infrared. Most of its visible light is red and orange, like Betelgeuse in Orion.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_04
data.value: A hot star peaks in the ultraviolet and shines blue-white, like Spica.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_05
data.value: Here's a puzzle. Nearly all stars are mostly hydrogen. Which kind do you think shows the strongest hydrogen lines?

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_06
data.value: A white star of about ten thousand degrees, like Sirius. There, many hydrogen atoms have their electron on level two, ready to absorb Balmer colours. Hotter, the hydrogen is ionised; cooler, it stays on the ground level.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_07
data.value: In the cooler Sun, hydrogen's lines are weaker, and calcium and iron take over.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_08
data.value: In the coolest stars, molecules survive, and carve broad dark bands into the light.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_09
data.value: If a star or galaxy moves away from us, every line slides towards the red: a red shift. Compare it with the lab lamp below. Coming closer gives a blue shift.

data.name: Narr_Spec_Stars_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the curve to change the star's temperature, or drag its spectrum sideways to make it move.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_01
data.value: This is the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, one of the most important maps in astronomy. Across is a star's surface temperature, hottest on the left. Up is how bright it really is.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_02
data.value: Most stars lie along this band, the main sequence. They're all doing the same thing: fusing hydrogen in their cores. The heavier the star, the hotter and brighter it is, so the higher up it sits.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_03
data.value: Here's our Sun, right in the middle of the main sequence.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_04
data.value: Up and to the right are the giants. They're cool, but so big that they shine brightly. Arcturus and Aldebaran are giants.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_05
data.value: Down and to the left are the white dwarfs. They're very hot, but tiny, so they're faint. Sirius B is one.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_06
data.value: Think about it. After the main sequence, where will our Sun go on this diagram?

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_07
data.value: Up and to the right. Watch the path it follows. As it runs out of hydrogen in its core, it climbs up to the giants. At the very end, it drops all the way down to the white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_08
data.value: Now you try. Change the star's mass on the left page, and see how its path changes.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_01
data.value: Every star starts in a cloud of gas. But how it ends depends almost entirely on one thing: how much mass it has when it's born.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_02
data.value: The smallest stars, red dwarfs, burn so slowly that they'll last for trillions of years. Not one has died yet in the whole history of the universe.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_03
data.value: Stars like the Sun become red giants, puff off a planetary nebula, and end as white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_04
data.value: Think about it. What happens to a star more than eight times heavier than the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_05
data.value: It explodes as a supernova. For a few weeks it can shine brighter than a whole galaxy, and the elements made inside it are blown out into space.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_06
data.value: The core left behind is a neutron star: more mass than the Sun, squeezed into a ball the size of a city.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_07
data.value: And the heaviest stars collapse even further, into a black hole, where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_08
data.value: Now you try. Click a row to choose another kind of star, and follow its life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_09
data.value: The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars that died long before the Sun was born. We are made of star stuff.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_01
data.value: Every star begins in a cold, dark cloud of gas and dust. Gravity pulls the cloud together. It spins faster and faster, and the middle gets hotter and hotter.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_02
data.value: When the centre reaches about ten million degrees, hydrogen starts fusing into helium, and a star is born. Our Sun has been shining like this for four and a half billion years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_03
data.value: These dashed circles are the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, drawn on the same scale, so you can see how big the star gets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_04
data.value: Think about it. When the hydrogen in its core runs out, what will happen to the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_05
data.value: It swells into a red giant, more than a hundred times wider than today. It will swallow Mercury and Venus, and perhaps even Earth.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_06
data.value: Later, it gently puffs its outer layers off into space. They glow around the hot core as a planetary nebula, which, despite the name, has nothing to do with planets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_07
data.value: What's left is a white dwarf, about the size of Earth but as heavy as half the Sun. It slowly cools and fades for billions and billions of years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag along the strip of stages at the bottom, and travel through the Sun's whole life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Agb
data.value: A second giant stage, even bigger than the first. Strong winds blow the star's outer layers away into space.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_BlackHole
data.value: A black hole. In the heaviest stars, nothing can stop the core collapsing. Its gravity becomes so strong that not even light can get out.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_BlueDwarf
data.value: A blue dwarf. No star has become one yet: a red dwarf burns so slowly that it won't get here for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassMassive
data.value: Massive stars, about eight to twenty times the Sun's mass. They live for only millions of years, and end in a supernova that leaves a neutron star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassRedDwarf
data.value: Red dwarfs, less than half the Sun's mass. They're the most common stars of all, and they shine for trillions of years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassSunLike
data.value: Sun-like stars, from about half to eight times the Sun's mass. They become red giants and end as white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassVeryMassive
data.value: The most massive stars, more than about twenty times the Sun's mass. After their supernova, the core collapses into a black hole.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Giants
data.value: Giants: stars that have run out of hydrogen in their cores and swelled up. They're cool, but so big that they shine brightly.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_HeliumBurning
data.value: Helium burning. The core has become hot enough, about a hundred million degrees, to fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, and the star settles down for a while.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownAldebaran
data.value: Aldebaran, the red eye of Taurus the Bull. It's an orange giant, about forty-five times wider than the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownArcturus
