data.value: Arcturus, an orange giant. It has used up the hydrogen in its core and swelled to about twenty-five times the Sun's width.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBarnard
data.value: Barnard's Star, another nearby red dwarf, about six light-years away. It moves across our sky faster than any other star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBetelgeuse
data.value: Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder. It's a red supergiant so big that, in the Sun's place, it would reach past the orbit of Mars. One day it will explode as a supernova.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownDeneb
data.value: Deneb, in the constellation of the Swan. It's one of the most luminous stars you can see with the naked eye, about two hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownPolaris
data.value: Polaris, the North Star. It's a yellow supergiant that slowly pulses, growing a little brighter and dimmer about every four days.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProcyonB
data.value: Procyon B, another white dwarf, circling the bright star Procyon. Small and faint, it's the leftover core of a star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProxima
data.value: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, a little over four light-years away. It's a small, cool red dwarf, far too faint to see without a telescope.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownRigel
data.value: Rigel, the bright blue-white foot of Orion. It's a blue supergiant, about a hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusA
data.value: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's a hot, white main-sequence star, about twice the Sun's mass and twenty-five times as bright, less than nine light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusB
data.value: Sirius B, the faint companion of Sirius: a white dwarf about the size of Earth, yet about as heavy as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSpica
data.value: Spica, a very hot blue star. It's really two massive stars, orbiting each other very closely.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSun
data.value: The Sun, a middle-aged star on the main sequence, about four and a half billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownVega
data.value: Vega, a hot, white main-sequence star about forty times as bright as the Sun, one of the brightest stars of summer evenings.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_LateBurning
data.value: The last fuels. Like the layers of an onion, shells of carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn around a growing core of iron. The very last stage lasts only about a day.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequence
data.value: The main sequence, a star's long, steady adult life. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, and the energy this gives out holds the star up against its own gravity.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequenceBand
data.value: The main sequence. Stars spend most of their lives here, fusing hydrogen in their cores. Heavier stars sit higher up: hotter, bigger, and much brighter.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_NeutronStar
data.value: A neutron star: more mass than the Sun, crushed into a ball the size of a city. Many spin several times a second, sweeping beams across space like a lighthouse. Those are pulsars.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Orbits
data.value: The orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, on the same scale. As a red giant, the Sun will reach out to about Earth's orbit.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_PlanetaryNebula
data.value: A planetary nebula: the star's outer layers, thrown off and lit up by the hot core left behind. Through old telescopes they looked a little like planets, which is how they got the name.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Protostar
data.value: A protostar: a ball of gas still pulling itself together inside its cloud. It glows from the heat of falling in, before any fusion has started.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedGiant
data.value: A red giant. The star has swelled to a hundred times its old size or more, and its surface has cooled to orange-red. It's still very bright, because it's so big.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedSupergiant
data.value: A red supergiant, the biggest kind of star. In the Sun's place, it would swallow all the inner planets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Subgiant
data.value: A subgiant. The hydrogen in the core has run out, so hydrogen now burns in a shell around it, and the star starts to swell.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_SunToday
data.value: The dashed circle is the Sun as it is today, drawn on the same scale, so you can compare sizes.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiant
data.value: A supergiant. A massive star burns through its fuel fast and swells hugely, crossing the diagram from blue to red.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiants
data.value: Supergiants, the brightest stars of all: massive stars near the end of their short lives.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supernova
data.value: A supernova. Iron can't be burned to give out energy, so the core suddenly collapses, and the star blows itself apart. For a few weeks it can outshine a whole galaxy.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarf
data.value: A white dwarf: the bare core of a Sun-like star, about as big as Earth. A teaspoon of it would weigh about as much as an elephant. It shines only with its leftover heat.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarfs
data.value: White dwarfs: hot but tiny, so they're faint. They're the leftover cores of stars like the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_01
data.value: Here's Earth seen from above the North Pole, with the Moon going round it. The blue layer is the ocean. Its bulges are hugely exaggerated, so you can see them.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_02
data.value: The Moon pulls on everything on Earth, but not equally. The side facing the Moon is pulled a little harder than Earth's centre, and the far side a little less. These arrows show the difference. It's called the tidal force.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_03
data.value: So the water piles up into a bulge on the side facing the Moon. That's a high tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_04
data.value: And here's the surprise: there's a second bulge on the far side. The water there is pulled less than Earth itself, so it gets left behind.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_05
data.value: Earth turns once a day underneath these two bulges. Think about it: how many high tides does a place by the sea get each day?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_06
data.value: Two. As Earth turns, it carries you through both bulges, so you get two high tides and two low tides a day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_07
data.value: But the Moon moves along its orbit at the same time, so Earth has to turn a little extra to catch up. That's why high tide comes about fifty minutes later each day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag sideways across the picture to turn Earth, and watch the water rise and fall where you are.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_01
data.value: Here's a harbour, seen from the side, with the open sea on the left. Watch the sea come in, and go out again.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_02
data.value: This post on the pier is a tide staff. It measures how high the water is, in metres.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_03
data.value: The arrow shows the height right now, and whether the tide is coming in or going out.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_04
data.value: These lines mark today's high water and low water. The difference between them is called the tidal range.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_05
data.value: Think about it. How long is it from one high tide to the next?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_06
data.value: About twelve and a half hours: half of twenty-four hours and fifty minutes. Boats in the harbour rise and fall with the water. In some harbours, they sit on the mud at low tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag sideways to move through the day, and find high water and low water on the tide staff.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_08
data.value: On real coasts, the shape of the sea floor and the coastline matter a lot. In the Mediterranean, the tide is only a few tens of centimetres. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, it can be more than fifteen metres.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Boat
data.value: A boat at anchor. It rises and falls with the water, and its anchor line goes slack at low tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, turning once a day. The oceans are drawn around it as a blue layer, with the tidal bulges hugely exaggerated.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Force
data.value: The tidal force: the Moon's pull at each place, minus its pull on Earth's centre. It points outwards towards and away from the Moon, and inwards in between.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighFar
data.value: The bulge on the far side. The water here is pulled a little less than Earth's centre, so it's left behind as Earth is pulled towards the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighNear
data.value: The bulge facing the Moon. The Moon pulls the water here a little harder than it pulls Earth's centre, so the water piles up.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighWater
data.value: The highest the water reaches today. The wet sand above the waterline shows where it has been.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Level
data.value: The water level right now, and whether the tide is rising or falling.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Low
data.value: Low tide, halfway between the two bulges. Water has flowed away from here into the bulges.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_LowWater
data.value: The lowest the water falls today. At low water, more of the beach is uncovered.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon. Its pull is a little stronger on the side of Earth facing it, and a little weaker on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Neap
data.value: Neap tide. At first and last quarter, the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles, and the tides are at their smallest.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Range
data.value: The tidal range: how far the water rises from low tide to high tide. It grows towards spring tides and shrinks towards neap tides.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Spin
data.value: Earth turns once a day, from west to east. Seen from above the North Pole, that's anticlockwise.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Spring
data.value: Spring tide. At new moon and full moon, the Sun's bulges add to the Moon's, so high tides are higher and low tides lower.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Staff
data.value: The tide staff. Its marks are in metres above the lowest low water, so sailors can tell how deep the harbour is.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. It raises tides as well, a little under half as big as the Moon's. When the two line up, the tides are biggest.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_You
data.value: You, on the equator. Earth's turning carries you through high and low tide. The label shows your time and what the tide is doing.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_01
data.value: The Sun raises tides too. It's far bigger than the Moon, but also far more distant, so its tides are a little under half as big.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_02
data.value: This gold outline shows the Sun's two bulges, along the line towards the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_03
data.value: And this blue outline shows the Moon's two bulges. The real water is the two added together.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_04
data.value: At new moon, the Sun and the Moon line up, and their bulges add together. The tides are extra big. These are spring tides. They have nothing to do with springtime: the water springs up.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_05
data.value: Now it's first quarter. The Moon is at right angles to the Sun. Think about it: what happens to the tides?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_06
data.value: They get smaller. The Sun's bulges partly fill in the Moon's low tides and take away from its high tides. These weaker tides are neap tides.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_07
data.value: So spring tides and neap tides take turns, twice a month each: spring tides at new and full moon, neap tides at the quarters.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon around its orbit, and watch the tides grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_01
data.value: Point a camera at the night sky, open the shutter, and leave it open for hours. The stars won't stay as little dots. Watch them draw lines across the picture.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_02
data.value: Every trail is part of a circle, and all the circles share one centre: the celestial pole. It's the point the whole sky turns around.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_03
data.value: After four hours, look at the angle each star has swept round the pole: about sixty degrees. The sky turns fifteen degrees every hour. Really, of course, it's Earth turning underneath it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_04
data.value: Here's a question. How long would the shutter have to stay open for the trails to close into full circles?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_05
data.value: A full circle takes a whole day, so the Sun always comes up first. Now look near the horizon. Stars far enough from the pole dip under the ground and come up again, but stars close to the pole stay up all night. They never set.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_06
data.value: Now turn round and face the other way. The trails become wide, gentle arcs: these stars rise in the east, swing across the sky and set in the west.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_07
data.value: Facing east, the stars climb out of the horizon at a slant, all tilted the same way. How steep the slant is depends on how far you are from the equator.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_08
data.value: Let's travel to the equator. The celestial pole now sits right on the horizon, and the horizon cuts every circle in half. Each star spends half its time below the ground: not one stays up all night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_09
data.value: And now to the North Pole. Look straight up: the celestial pole is overhead, and every star circles round parallel to the horizon. Nothing rises, and nothing sets.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the picture to turn the camera, or travel north and south with the latitude slider, and watch how the trails change.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Aquila
data.value: Aquila, the eagle. Altair sits between two fainter stars, like the Cowherd carrying his two children in baskets on a pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_BigDipper
data.value: The Big Dipper: seven bright stars of the Great Bear. Its two end stars point to Polaris, and its handle swings round the pole through the night and through the year.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_CanisMajor
data.value: Canis Major, the great dog, with Sirius on its chest. It follows Orion across the sky.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Cassiopeia
data.value: Cassiopeia, a W of five stars on the other side of the pole from the Big Dipper. It's another way to find Polaris.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Crux
data.value: The Southern Cross, the smallest constellation of all. Its long bar points to the south celestial pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Cygnus
data.value: Cygnus the swan, flying down the Milky Way. It's also called the Northern Cross.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Gemini
data.value: Gemini, the twins, with Castor and Pollux for their heads.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Leo
data.value: Leo the lion: a backward question mark for its head and mane, and a triangle for its tail.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_LittleDipper
data.value: The Little Dipper, in the Little Bear, with Polaris at the end of its handle.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Lyra
data.value: Lyra, the lyre: bright Vega and a small parallelogram of fainter stars.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Orion
data.value: Orion the hunter, with three stars in a row for his belt. He sits on the celestial equator, so he can be seen from everywhere on Earth.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Pegasus
data.value: Pegasus, the winged horse, with its Great Square: a big box of four stars high in autumn evenings.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Sagittarius
data.value: Sagittarius, shaped like a teapot. Look towards it and you're looking towards the centre of our galaxy.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Scorpius
data.value: Scorpius, the scorpion: a long curving hook of stars with red Antares at its heart. In China it's part of the Azure Dragon.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_SummerTriangle
data.value: The Summer Triangle: Vega, Deneb and Altair, three bright stars from three different constellations, with the Milky Way running through it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Taurus
data.value: Taurus the bull: orange Aldebaran for its eye, and the Pleiades star cluster on its shoulder.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Arc
data.value: This angle is how far the sky has turned while the shutter was open: fifteen degrees every hour, a whole circle in a day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Circumpolar
data.value: These stars are close enough to the visible pole that their circles never touch the horizon. They never set: we call them circumpolar.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Compass
data.value: The compass points: north, east, south and west. Drag the picture to turn the camera round.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, taking a year to go round the Sun. Its night side always faces away from the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Equator
data.value: The celestial equator, right above Earth's equator. A star on it rises due east, sets due west, and is up for half of each day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Horizon
data.value: The horizon hides every star below it. Near it, trails dive into the ground and come back up somewhere else.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_NeverRises
data.value: These stars circle the other pole and never come above your horizon. To see them, you'd have to travel towards the other hemisphere.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Night
data.value: At midnight you look straight away from the Sun. As Earth goes round its orbit, this direction sweeps round the sky, bringing new constellations each season.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_NorthPole
data.value: The north celestial pole, straight out from Earth's North Pole. North of the equator it stands above the northern horizon, exactly as high as your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Observer
data.value: This is you, at the centre of the sky. The ground cuts the celestial sphere in half, and you can only see the half above it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Panorama
data.value: This is the sky at nine in the evening on this date. Run the year and watch the constellations slide west, a little earlier every night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Pole
data.value: The celestial pole: the one point of the sky that doesn't move. Every star circles round it, because it lies straight out along Earth's axis.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Risers
data.value: Stars in this band rise and set every day, like the Sun. The nearer they are to the visible pole, the longer they stay up.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Shutter
data.value: The camera's display shows how long the shutter has been open. The longer it's open, the longer every trail.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Sidereal
data.value: One turn of Earth brings the stars back after twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. But Earth has moved along its orbit, so it needs about four more minutes to face the Sun again.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_SouthPole
data.value: The south celestial pole, straight out from Earth's South Pole. South of the equator it stands above the southern horizon, exactly as high as your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Whatever lies behind it is in the daytime sky, and we can't see it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Zenith
data.value: The zenith: the point straight above your head.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_01
data.value: Picture the sky as a giant ball around you, with you at the centre. The ground cuts it in half, so you only ever see the half above the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_02
data.value: The sky seems to turn about an axis through the celestial poles. And here's a neat fact: the pole's height above your horizon is exactly your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_03
data.value: Halfway between the poles runs the celestial equator. A star on it rises due east, sets due west, and is up for exactly half of each turn.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_04
data.value: Stars close enough to the visible pole never touch the horizon. They circle all night, every night. We call them circumpolar.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_05
data.value: Around the other pole there's a matching cap of sky that never rises here at all. Those stars stay hidden below your feet.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_06
data.value: Here's a question. Suppose you walk towards the equator. What happens to the cap of stars that never set?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_07
data.value: At the equator, both poles lie on the horizon. Every star rises and sets, and over a year you can see the whole sky.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_08
data.value: At the North Pole, the celestial pole is straight overhead. Half the sky circles round forever, and the other half you never see at all.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the latitude slider from pole to pole, and watch the two caps grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Achernar
data.value: Achernar spins so fast that it's one of the flattest stars known, much wider across its middle than from pole to pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Acrux
data.value: Acrux is the foot of the Southern Cross. The cross's long bar points towards the south celestial pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Aldebaran
data.value: Aldebaran is the orange eye of Taurus the bull, an aging giant star about sixty-five light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Alkaid
data.value: Alkaid is the tip of the Big Dipper's handle. It's moving through space in a different direction from the middle five stars, so over tens of thousands of years the Dipper's shape slowly changes.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Altair
data.value: Altair is the Cowherd, across the Milky Way from the Weaver Girl. It spins once in about nine hours, so fast that it's flattened like a squashed ball.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Antares
data.value: Antares is the red heart of the Scorpion. Its name means rival of Mars, for its colour.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Arcturus
data.value: Arcturus is the brightest star north of the celestial equator, an orange giant about thirty-seven light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Betelgeuse
data.value: Betelgeuse is Orion's red shoulder, a red supergiant so huge that, put in place of the Sun, it would reach beyond the orbit of Mars. One day it will explode as a supernova.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Canopus
data.value: Canopus is the second-brightest star of the night sky. In old China it was the star of long life, seen low in the south.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Capella
data.value: Capella looks like one star, but it's really two yellow giants circling each other, about forty-three light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Castor
data.value: Castor, the other twin, is really six stars: three pairs, all circling one another.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Deneb
data.value: Deneb is the tail of the Swan. It's probably around two thousand light-years away, which makes it one of the most luminous stars we can see.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Dubhe
data.value: Dubhe is the end star of the Big Dipper's bowl. Draw a line from Merak through Dubhe and carry on about five times as far, and you reach Polaris.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Fomalhaut
data.value: Fomalhaut is a lonely bright star of autumn evenings, circled by a wide ring of dust.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Polaris
data.value: Polaris lies less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so it hardly moves all night. It's about four hundred and thirty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Pollux
data.value: Pollux is the brighter of the Gemini twins, an orange giant with a planet of its own, about thirty-four light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Procyon
data.value: Procyon is a close neighbour, about eleven light-years away. With Sirius and Betelgeuse it makes the Winter Triangle.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Regulus
data.value: Regulus is the heart of Leo. It spins so fast that it bulges at its middle, and it lies almost exactly on the Sun's yearly path.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Rigel
data.value: Rigel is Orion's bright blue-white foot: a supergiant thousands of times brighter than the Sun, about eight hundred and sixty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_RigilKentaurus
data.value: Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to the Sun, just over four light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_SigOct
data.value: Sigma Octantis is the south pole star, about a degree from the south celestial pole, but so faint that you need a dark sky to find it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Sirius
data.value: Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky, only eight and a half light-years away, with a tiny white dwarf companion.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Spica
data.value: Spica is two hot blue stars so close together that they pull each other into egg shapes, about two hundred and fifty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Vega
data.value: Vega is the Weaver Girl, twenty-five light-years away. As Earth's axis slowly wobbles, in about twelve thousand years Vega will become the pole star.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_01
data.value: Why do the evening stars change through the year? Here's Earth going round the Sun. On the night side you look away from the Sun, out to the far-off stars.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_02
data.value: In December, the midnight side of Earth faces Orion. So that's when Orion is up all night, highest around midnight.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_03
data.value: Half a year later, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. Orion is now behind the Sun, lost in the daylight, and Scorpius takes over the night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_04
data.value: Here's a question. The stars rise a little earlier every night. By about how much?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_05
data.value: Here's why. To bring the same star back overhead, Earth needs one full turn: twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. But meanwhile Earth has moved along its orbit, so it has to turn a little more to face the Sun again. That makes our twenty-four-hour day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_06
data.value: Four minutes a night adds up to two hours a month. Watch the evening sky: night after night, the constellations slide west.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_07
data.value: After a whole year, Earth is back where it started, and the evening sky repeats itself.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_08
data.value: Your turn. Drag Earth round its orbit, or pick a date, and see which constellations fill the evening sky.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_01
data.value: Now we slice through the typhoon, from the sea to the top of its clouds, six hundred kilometres wide. The heights are stretched to fit. The sea below is twenty-nine and a half degrees, and that warm water is the storm's fuel.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_02
data.value: Near the sea, warm, moist air spirals in towards the centre, shown in blue. As it skims the warm water, it picks up more and more water vapour.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_03
data.value: At the eyewall the air shoots upward, fifteen kilometres or more. As it rises it cools, and its water vapour condenses into towering clouds and heavy rain. Watch the dots turn from white to orange as they climb.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_04
data.value: Here's a question. Where does a typhoon get the energy for its winds?

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_05
data.value: Right: condensation. Water vapour took heat from the sea when it evaporated, and gives it back as it turns into droplets. That heat warms the core, the pressure falls further, and the wind draws in still more moist air. The storm feeds itself.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_06
data.value: At the top, the air spreads out as a thin sheet of icy cirrus, hundreds of kilometres wide, and far out it slowly sinks back down. In the eye the air sinks too, warming as it's squeezed. That's why the eye is clear.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_07
data.value: Let's cool the sea to twenty-five and a half degrees. Below about twenty-six and a half, the sea can't give enough heat and moisture. Thunderstorms still pop up, but they never organise into a spinning storm.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_08
data.value: Warm sea again, and now the storm comes ashore. I've stopped the clock twelve hours later. Over land the air comes in dry, shown in brown, and the fuel is cut off. The strongest wind has fallen from about seventy-one to about thirty metres a second.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Engine_09
data.value: Your turn. Change the sea's temperature, let the storm come ashore, or drag sideways to turn the hours, and see how strong it can get.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Bands
data.value: Spiral rain bands: long arms of showers and thunderstorms curling in towards the centre. Between them the rain eases for a while, then the next band brings gusts and downpours.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Coast
data.value: The coast, sliding away behind the storm as it moves inland. Over land there's no warm sea to evaporate, and hills and trees slow the wind, so the storm runs down.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Day
data.value: A dot for each day of the storm's life. Click one to jump to that moment.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Edge588
data.value: The 588 line marks the edge of the subtropical high, where the 500 hectopascal surface is 5880 metres high. Forecasters watch how far west it reaches to tell where a typhoon will go.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Eye
data.value: The eye: the calm centre of the storm, usually a few dozen kilometres across. Air sinks here and warms as it's squeezed, so the sky is often clear, even though the fiercest winds are only a few kilometres away.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Eyewall
data.value: The eyewall: a ring of towering storm clouds around the eye. Here the air rises fastest, the rain is heaviest, and the wind is the strongest anywhere in the storm.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_High
data.value: The subtropical high: a vast area of sinking air over the Pacific. The winds around it turn clockwise, and steer typhoons along its edge, like a stream carrying a leaf.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Inflow
data.value: The inflow: warm, moist air spiralling in low over the sea. On the way it picks up water vapour, which carries the heat that will power the storm.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Isobars
data.value: Isobars join places with the same pressure, here one every ten hectopascals. Where they crowd together, the pressure changes quickly over a short distance, and the wind is strong.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Landfall
data.value: Landfall: where the storm's centre crosses the coast. Click it to jump there. The worst wind, rain and storm surge often come in the hours around landfall.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Low
data.value: The centre of the low. Before a proper eye has formed, this is simply where the pressure is lowest, and where the air is drawn towards.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Motion
data.value: The storm is moving north-west at twenty kilometres an hour, carried by the winds around it. Its whole pattern of winds travels along with it.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Outflow
data.value: The outflow: at the top of the storm, often fifteen kilometres up, the risen air spreads out as a shield of icy cirrus. From space, it's the bright white disc of the typhoon.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Pacific
data.value: The north-west Pacific: the busiest typhoon ocean in the world, with about twenty-five named storms a year, most of them in August and September.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Place
data.value: Your place. If the storm comes within reach, a dashed line joins it to the nearest point of the track, with how close the storm came and how strong the wind was there.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Probe
data.value: The probe measures the wind and the pressure at one spot. Drag it anywhere in the storm. The gold arrow is the wind you'd feel there, and the blue arrow is the pressure push towards the centre.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Push
data.value: The pressure push: air is pushed from high pressure towards low, straight at the centre. The Earth's turn bends the moving air aside, so instead of rushing in, it circles round.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Scale
data.value: The scale bar is two hundred kilometres. The whole picture is about twelve hundred kilometres across, wider than many countries.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Sea
data.value: The warm sea is the fuel. A typhoon needs water of at least twenty-six and a half degrees, warm to a depth of about fifty metres. The warmer it is, the stronger the storm can get.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Showers
data.value: Over sea cooler than about twenty-six and a half degrees, thunderstorms come and go, but there isn't enough heat and moisture for them to organise into a typhoon.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_SouthChinaSea
data.value: The South China Sea. Storms can form right here too, close to land, so they can come ashore within a day or two of forming.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Start
data.value: Where the storm formed. Click here to watch it again from the start. You can also click anywhere on the warm sea to start a new storm there.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Steering
data.value: The steering winds. Each arrow shows which way the wind would carry a storm there, and the longer the arrow, the faster. Typhoons follow them, and drift a little north-west on their own.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_StormNow
data.value: The storm right now, its cloud drawn to scale. The label shows its grade, its strongest wind and its central pressure.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_StrongSide
data.value: On this side, the storm's spin and its forward motion point the same way, so the winds add up. In the north it's the right of the track, and sailors call it the dangerous semicircle.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Track
data.value: The storm's track, coloured by its grade: blue for a depression, then green, yellow and orange, up to red and purple for the strongest typhoons. Drag sideways to move along it.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Turn
data.value: Which way the air turns. Deflected by the Earth's turn, it spirals in anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, and clockwise in the southern. Near the equator the deflection is too weak, so typhoons almost never form there.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_WarmCore
data.value: The warm core: the heat given off as water vapour condenses warms the middle of the storm. Warm air is lighter, so the pressure at the surface falls, and the winds blow harder.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_WarmEdge
data.value: The dashed line is where the sea is twenty-six and a half degrees. South of it, storms can grow. By late summer, the warm water reaches further north.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Obj_Wind
data.value: The strongest wind in the storm right now. How warm the sea is sets its limit, and once the storm is ashore, it falls hour by hour.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_01
data.value: This is a typhoon seen from above, about twelve hundred kilometres across. The whole storm turns around one small, calm hole in the middle: the eye. Let's find out why it spins, and where its winds are strongest.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_02
data.value: The dashed circles are isobars, lines of equal pressure, one every ten hectopascals. The pressure falls towards the centre, and near the eye the circles crowd together. The closer they are, the harder the air is pushed inward.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_03
data.value: Look at the probe. The blue arrow is the pressure push, pointing straight at the centre. But the gold arrow, the wind, hardly points inward at all. It blows almost around the storm, angled in only a little.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_04
data.value: So why doesn't the air just rush straight into the low and fill it up? What do you think turns it aside?

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_05
data.value: It's the Earth's turn. I've just switched it off: now the air heads straight for the centre, and the low fills up within a day. On our turning Earth, moving air is deflected to the right in the north, so it circles anticlockwise instead.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_06
data.value: The Earth's turn is back on. I've moved the probe to the eyewall, the ring of cloud just outside the eye. Here the wind is strongest: about forty-eight metres a second, force fifteen. One step inside, in the eye, it is almost calm.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_07
data.value: Now let's deepen the storm to nine hundred and fifteen hectopascals. It becomes a super typhoon. See how the isobars crowd even closer together: a stronger push, and so a stronger wind, about sixty-five metres a second at the eyewall.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_08
data.value: What about south of the equator? There the Earth's turn deflects moving air to the left, so the same storm spins clockwise. That's why these storms turn opposite ways in the two hemispheres.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_09
data.value: Back in the north, let the storm move north-west at twenty kilometres an hour. On the right of its track, the swirling wind and the storm's own motion add together. That's the dangerous side, where the winds are strongest.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Storm_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the pressure slider, switch the Earth's turn or the hemisphere, or move the probe, and watch how the winds change.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_01
data.value: This is a map of the north-west Pacific, where more typhoons form than anywhere else. Our storm is born here, near Guam, in August. Where will it go?

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_02
data.value: This dashed line marks where the sea is twenty-six and a half degrees. All the paler water south of it is warmer than that, and there a storm can grow. North of the line, over cooler water, it starts to weaken.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_03
data.value: This big H is the subtropical high, a huge dome of sinking air. Winds circle it clockwise, shown by the little white arrows. A typhoon hardly moves by itself: these steering winds carry it along.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_04
data.value: Four days later, the storm has been carried west-north-west along the southern edge of the high, growing over the warm sea. The colour of its track shows how strong it was at each point.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_05
data.value: Suppose the high stretches further west, towards the coast of China. What will happen to the storm's track?

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_06
data.value: Right. With the high reaching far west, the steering wind keeps pushing the storm west, and it comes ashore in South China. Over land, cut off from the warm sea, it weakens quickly.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_07
data.value: Now pull the high back east. The storm reaches the high's west end sooner, turns north around it, and heads for Japan instead. Same storm, very different track: it all depends on the high.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_08
data.value: The gold dot is your place. When a storm comes close, a dashed line joins your place to the nearest point of the track, and the label says how close it came and how strong the wind was there.

data.name: Narr_Typhoon_Track_09
data.value: Your turn. Change the month, move the high's west end, or click anywhere on the warm sea to start a new storm, and see where it goes.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_01
data.value: This is a slice through the Earth, from the deep sea, over a coast and mountains, to a volcano. The rocks here are never finished. Over millions of years they're broken, carried, buried, squeezed and melted, and made again. This is the rock cycle.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_02
data.value: Let's start deep down, where it's hot enough to melt rock. This is magma. It's lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_03
data.value: Some magma stops underground and cools very slowly into granite. Some erupts and cools quickly into basalt. Rocks made from cooled magma are called igneous rocks.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_04
data.value: Once rock is at the surface, rain, frost and plant roots slowly break it apart into smaller and smaller pieces. That's weathering.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_05
data.value: Rivers carry the pieces away, sand, mud and even dissolved minerals, all the way down to the sea. That's erosion.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_06
data.value: Where the water slows down, the pieces settle to the bottom in layers: sand near the shore, fine mud farther out, and shells on the reef.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_07
data.value: As more and more layers pile on top, the lower ones are pressed together and glued by minerals into solid rock: sandstone, shale and limestone. These are sedimentary rocks.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_08
data.value: Buried even deeper, rock gets so hot and is squeezed so hard that its minerals change, without melting. Shale turns into slate and then schist, and limestone turns into marble. These are metamorphic rocks.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_09
data.value: Deeper still, rock melts back into magma, and the cycle can start all over again.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_10
data.value: Here's a question: does a rock always have to melt before it can start a new round?

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_11
data.value: No, it doesn't. Follow this grain of sand. It starts in the granite at the top of the mountain. It gets worn off, carried by the river, and laid down on the beach.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_12
data.value: Buried, it became part of a layer of sandstone. Then two plates pushed against each other and lifted the old sea floor up into the mountains. That's why seashells can be found on mountain tops.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Cycle_13
data.value: Now it's being worn away again, and it never melted once. Your turn: choose another grain on the left-hand page and follow it round.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_01
data.value: Here's a volcano cut in half. Far below the mountain is the magma chamber, a pool of molten rock a few kilometres down. Magma is creeping in from deeper still, and the chamber is filling up.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_02
data.value: Look at the pressure gauge. As the chamber fills, the pressure rises, the ground above swells a little, and the rock around it cracks, so small earthquakes crackle. Scientists watch for exactly these signs before an eruption.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_03
data.value: Now the magma forces its way up the conduit. Deep down, its water is dissolved, held in by the weight of the rock above. As it rises, that weight gets less, and the water comes out as bubbles, just like opening a bottle of fizzy drink.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_04
data.value: This dashed line marks where the first bubbles appear. Above it, the higher the magma climbs, the more gas comes out, and the bigger the bubbles grow.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_05
data.value: Stromboli's magma is basalt: hot and runny. Bubbles can rise through it and join into big ones, which burst at the top and fling out glowing lumps of lava. Stromboli has been doing this every few minutes for thousands of years.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_06
data.value: Runny lava also spills out and runs down the slope as a lava flow. It glows while it moves, then cools into a dark crust and becomes a new layer of the volcano.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_07
data.value: Here's a question. What do you think happens if the magma is sticky, like toothpaste, and full of gas?

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_08
data.value: Yes, it explodes! This is Pinatubo in 1991. Its magma is sticky dacite with lots of water. The bubbles can't escape, so the magma is blasted out as a column of ash and gas that shoots more than thirty kilometres into the sky.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_09
data.value: Look at this line in the conduit. Below it, the magma is a froth full of bubbles. Above it, the froth has torn itself apart into ash and gas. The magma is blown to bits before it even reaches the top.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_10
data.value: Later on, the column grows too heavy to hold itself up, and it collapses. A glowing avalanche of hot ash and gas races down the slopes, faster than a car. It's called a pyroclastic flow, and it's the most dangerous thing a volcano does.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_11
data.value: Merapi's magma is sticky too, but it has already lost most of its gas. So instead of exploding, it oozes out slowly and piles up in the crater as a lava dome. When a piece breaks off, it crumbles into a glowing avalanche.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Eruption_12
data.value: Your turn. This is Kīlauea, with runny basalt and very little gas. Move the sliders, or drag the gold dot on the chart, until its magma would erupt explosively.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_01
data.value: Let's watch rock being made, through a magnifier. This is a slice of magma two centimetres wide, deep underground. It's cooling very slowly, about one degree every thousand years.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_02
data.value: Crystals appear, and each mineral starts at its own temperature. White feldspar and dark mica come first, then pink feldspar. Quartz will be last, filling the gaps that are left.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_03
data.value: With so much time, just a few crystals grow big, big enough to see with your own eyes. This is granite.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_04
data.value: What do you think happens if the same magma cools fast instead, in a lava flow?

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_05
data.value: Many more crystals start, but each one has very little time to grow, so they stay tiny, too small to see. This is rhyolite: the same magma and the same minerals, just less time.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_06
data.value: Now cool it in seconds, as when lava pours into the sea. There's no time for crystals at all, and the melt freezes into glass. This is obsidian, sharp enough to make knives.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_07
data.value: And if the lava is full of gas when it freezes, the bubbles are trapped inside. This is pumice. It has so many holes that it floats on water.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_08
data.value: Now for sedimentary rock. A river is pouring muddy water into this tank: gravel, sand, silt and clay all mixed up. Watch which grains reach the bottom first.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_09
data.value: Gravel and sand drop in seconds. Clay is so fine that it takes days to sink just one metre, so here we've sped it up. That's why each layer is coarse at the bottom and fine at the top.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_10
data.value: Over millions of years, more layers bury these ones. The weight squeezes the water out, and minerals glue the grains together. Sand becomes sandstone, and mud becomes shale.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_11
data.value: Now let's bury some shale even deeper. Look closely: it's made of tiny clay flakes, lying every which way.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_12
data.value: Squeezed from above and heated, the flakes turn to lie flat, across the push. This is slate. It splits into thin, flat sheets, perfect for roof tiles.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_13
data.value: Deeper and hotter still, the flakes grow into shiny mica, and red garnet crystals grow among them. This is schist.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_14
data.value: At over six hundred degrees, the light and dark minerals gather into stripes. This is gneiss. It's been changed completely, but it never melted.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Magnifier_15
data.value: Your turn. Here's limestone, full of bits of shell. Push it deeper, with the slider or by dragging the press, until it turns into marble.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_AshFall
data.value: Ash falls out of the cloud like grey snow. But it isn't soft like ash from a fire. It's tiny, sharp bits of rock and glass that can bury fields and stop planes from flying.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Bands
data.value: In gneiss, light quartz and feldspar and dark mica separate into stripes, even though the rock stays solid.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Basalt
data.value: Basalt is lava that cooled quickly at the surface. It's dark, heavy and fine-grained, and most of the ocean floor is made of it.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Biotite
data.value: Biotite is black mica. It grows as thin sheets that peel apart like the pages of a book.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Bombs
data.value: Lumps of lava thrown out when gas bursts. Some are as big as a football or even bigger, and they cool and harden as they fly through the air.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Bubbles
data.value: Water dissolved in the magma comes out as bubbles when the pressure drops, like a fizzy drink when you open it. The higher the magma rises, the bigger the bubbles grow.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Chamber
data.value: The magma chamber is a big pocket of molten rock a few kilometres underground. Magma collects here before an eruption. After an eruption, click it to fill it up again.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Clay
data.value: Clay is the finest of all, just a few thousandths of a millimetre. It takes about three days to sink a metre, so muddy water stays cloudy for a long time.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Column
data.value: A column of hot ash and gas rushing up into the sky. The more magma erupts each second, the higher it goes. Big eruptions reach more than thirty kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Conduit
data.value: The conduit is the pipe the magma pushes up through, from the chamber to the vent. The magma cracks the rock open to make its way.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Cone
data.value: A volcano is built by its own eruptions, layer on layer. Runny lava spreads out into a wide, gentle shield. Sticky lava and ash pile up into a steep cone of layers.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Crystallization
data.value: Magma cools into igneous rock. Underground it cools slowly into coarse granite. At the surface it cools quickly into fine basalt.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Deposition
data.value: When water slows down, it drops what it's carrying, coarse grains first and fine ones last, building up layer after layer.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Dome
data.value: Sticky lava that has lost its gas oozes out like toothpaste and piles up over the vent. When part of a dome collapses, it can turn into a pyroclastic flow.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Erosion
data.value: Rivers, wind, waves and glaciers carry the broken bits away. A river can roll pebbles along, carry sand and mud, and even take away dissolved minerals.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_EruptionStep
data.value: Magma reaches the surface as lava and ash. New rock is made in hours to years, the fastest step in the whole cycle.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Fossil
data.value: These are bits of shell in the limestone. As it turns into marble, the calcite recrystallises and the shells vanish.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Fountain
data.value: Gas rushing out of runny magma throws up a spray of glowing lava, sometimes hundreds of metres high. The drops fall back down and run off as lava flows.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_FragLevel
data.value: When about three quarters of the magma is gas, the sticky froth can't stretch any more. It tears apart into ash and gas, which shoot upwards. This only happens in sticky magma that traps its bubbles.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Garnet
data.value: Red garnet crystals grow in schist at about four hundred and fifty degrees and above. Their size tells geologists how hot and deep the rock once was.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Gauge
data.value: This shows how much the pressure in the chamber is above the pressure of the rock around it. It rises as magma flows in, and drops when the eruption lets the magma out.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Glass
data.value: Volcanic glass is melt that froze before it could crystallise. Its atoms are jumbled up, just like in window glass. Black obsidian is pure volcanic glass.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Grain
data.value: This is the grain you're following. The dotted line shows where it has been, and the label tells you what it is now.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Grains
data.value: In sandstone and limestone, heat and pressure make the grains grow into each other until the gaps between them close. They become quartzite and marble.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Granite
data.value: Granite cooled slowly from magma deep underground, so its crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica are big enough to see. Uplift and erosion have brought it up to the peaks.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Gravel
data.value: Gravel is pebbles a few millimetres across. It sinks fastest, about three and a half seconds for a metre, and lands first, near the river mouth.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_KFeldspar
data.value: Potassium feldspar is the pink feldspar that gives many granites their colour. It crystallises after the white feldspar and the mica.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_LavaFlow
data.value: A river of molten rock. Runny basalt can flow for tens of kilometres, but sticky lava creeps only a few hundred metres. It glows while it's hot, then cools into dark rock.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Layers
data.value: Each pour makes one layer, coarse at the bottom and fine at the top. Geologists call it a graded bed, and they read layers like these like the pages of a history book.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Limestone
data.value: Limestone is made mostly of the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves it and carves out caves.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Lithification
data.value: Buried layers are squeezed by the weight above. The water is pressed out, and minerals crystallise between the grains like glue, turning loose sediment into rock.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Magma
data.value: Magma is molten rock, at about seven hundred to twelve hundred degrees. Where rock melts down here, the cycle begins again.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Marble
data.value: Marble is limestone baked by heat, here right next to the hot granite. Its grains have grown into interlocking crystals, and the fossils have disappeared.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Melt
data.value: This is magma that's still liquid, glowing hot. It gets darker as it cools towards the temperature where everything is solid.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_MeltPocket
data.value: Above about seven hundred degrees, with a little water, the rock starts to melt here and there. Rock that is partly melted is called migmatite.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Melting
data.value: Far below, or where plates sink and water seeps in, rock gets hot enough to melt. The magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it rises.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Metamorphism
data.value: Deep down, heat and pressure change a rock's minerals and texture, while it stays solid. Shale becomes slate, schist and gneiss, and limestone becomes marble.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Mica
data.value: Shale is made of tiny flat flakes of clay. Squeezed and heated, they turn to lie the same way, and grow into shiny mica.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Olivine
data.value: Olivine is a green mineral, the first to crystallise from hot basalt magma. Clear olivine is cut into a gem called peridot.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Overburden
data.value: These are the layers laid down later, pressing down on the ones below. Drag them up or down to bury the layers deeper or shallower.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Plagioclase
data.value: Plagioclase is a white feldspar, often with fine stripes. It's one of the first minerals to crystallise, and the commonest mineral in the Earth's crust.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Press
data.value: The weight of the rock above squeezes the sample: about another thousand atmospheres for every four kilometres down. Drag the press to push it deeper.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_PyroFlow
data.value: A glowing avalanche of hot ash, rock and gas racing down the volcano, faster than a car and hotter than an oven. It's the deadliest danger a volcano has.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Pyroxene
data.value: Pyroxene is a dark green to black mineral, common in basalt and gabbro. It crystallises after olivine.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Quakes
data.value: As magma forces its way in and up, it cracks the rock and sets off swarms of small earthquakes. They're one of the warning signs that an eruption may be coming.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Quartz
data.value: Clear grey quartz is the last to crystallise, so it has to fill whatever gaps are left between the other crystals. It's very hard, and most beach sand is made of it.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_River
data.value: A muddy river flows into the tank. Click it to pour in another load of mud. Each load makes a new layer.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_SandGrain
data.value: Sand grains are about a quarter of a millimetre across. They take about half a minute to sink a metre.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Sandstone
data.value: Sandstone is sand grains cemented together. You can often still see the layers and ripples, and even footprints, made when it was loose sand.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_SatLevel
data.value: Below this depth, the weight of the rock above keeps all the water dissolved. Above it there isn't enough pressure to hold it in, so bubbles form. Wetter magma starts bubbling deeper down.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Schist
data.value: Deep under the mountains, shale has been squeezed and heated into slate, schist and gneiss, with shiny mica flakes and stripes of minerals.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Sediment
data.value: Loose sand, mud and shells, freshly laid down on the sea floor. In time the layers above will bury them and turn them into rock.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Shale
data.value: Shale is mud pressed into rock. It splits easily into thin layers, and it's where many fossils are found.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Silt
data.value: Silt is finer than sand, like flour. It takes about twenty minutes to sink a metre, so it drifts farther out.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Thermometer
data.value: This is the magma's temperature. Below the top mark, the liquidus, crystals start to grow. By the bottom mark, the solidus, everything is solid.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Umbrella
data.value: High up, the column becomes as light as the air around it, so it spreads out sideways into a huge umbrella-shaped cloud, and the wind carries it far away.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Uplift
data.value: When plates collide, rock is folded and pushed up into mountains. Old sea floor and deep rock come up to the surface, where weathering begins again.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Vent
data.value: The vent is the opening where the magma comes out. Click it while the chamber is filling, and the volcano erupts straight away.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Vesicle
data.value: These holes were left by gas bubbles trapped when the lava froze. Pumice is so full of them that it floats.

data.name: Narr_Volc_Obj_Weathering
data.value: Rock at the surface is slowly broken up and rotted by rain, frost, wind, plant roots and the air. Water that freezes in a crack pushes it wider.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_01
data.value: How does a cloud form? Over a sunny field, a bubble of air is warmed by the ground and starts to rise on its own, like a hot-air balloon.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_02
data.value: Follow this parcel of air. As it rises the pressure around it drops, so it expands and cools, by about ten degrees for every kilometre. Its label shows its temperature and its dew point.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_03
data.value: The air cools much faster than its dew point drops, so the two keep getting closer. What happens when they meet?

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_04
data.value: A cloud forms: the air can't hold all its vapour any more, and the rest condenses into droplets. The height where this happens is the cloud base, the flat bottom you often see under summer clouds.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_05
data.value: Now make the air more humid. Its dew point is closer to its temperature from the start, so it reaches it sooner, and the cloud base is much lower. That's why clouds hang low on muggy days.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_06
data.value: Wind can lift air too. Pushed up a mountain, the air cools, builds cloud and drops rain on the windward side. Coming down the far side it warms up again, and arrives warmer and drier than it started.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_07
data.value: Or warm, moist air slides up over a wedge of colder, heavier air. This is a front, and it spreads wide sheets of cloud and long, steady rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_08
data.value: Your turn. Change the ground temperature or the humidity on the left page, and see where the cloud base ends up.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_01
data.value: This is the water cycle, from the sea on the left, over a mountain. The Sun drives all of it: its heat is what lifts water up into the sky.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_02
data.value: Most of it starts at the sea. Sunshine warms the surface, and water evaporates into invisible vapour. The salt stays behind, so the vapour is fresh water.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_03
data.value: Plants add more. They pull water up from the soil through their roots and breathe it out as vapour through tiny holes in their leaves.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_04
data.value: As moist air rises, it cools. Cool air can't hold as much vapour, so some of it condenses into tiny droplets around specks of dust and salt. That's a cloud.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_05
data.value: The wind carries the moist air toward the mountain. What do you think happens when the air is pushed up its slope?

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_06
data.value: It's forced higher, cools even more, and the droplets grow until they're heavy enough to fall: as rain lower down, and as snow above the freezing level.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_07
data.value: Rain on the land runs downhill in streams and rivers, back to the sea. Some soaks into the ground instead, and creeps slowly through the rock as groundwater.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_08
data.value: Behind the mountain, the air has already dropped most of its water, so that side gets very little rain. It's called a rain shadow, and many deserts lie in one.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_09
data.value: Now follow a single drop. It evaporates from the sea, drifts on the wind, falls on the mountain, and rides a river home. The label tells you what it's doing.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_10
data.value: Your turn. Click any label in the picture to light up that part of the cycle and hear what happens there.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Atmosphere
data.value: The atmosphere holds only a little water at any moment, about a thousandth of a percent of the total. It's replaced roughly every nine days.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallAll
data.value: All of Earth's water in one ball, about one thousand four hundred kilometres across. Almost all of it, about ninety-seven percent, is salty sea water.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallFreshLiquid
data.value: All the fresh liquid water, about two hundred and seventy kilometres across. Most of it is groundwater; lakes and rivers are only a small part.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallLakesRivers
data.value: The water in lakes and rivers, a ball only about fifty-six kilometres across. This is the fresh water that's easiest for people to use.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_CloudBase
data.value: The cloud base: the height where rising air has cooled to its dew point. Roughly, it's one hundred and twenty-five metres up for every degree between the air's temperature and its dew point at the ground.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Condensation
data.value: Condensation. Rising air cools to its dew point, and vapour turns into tiny droplets on specks of dust, salt or smoke. That releases the heat the Sun gave it when it evaporated.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Drop
data.value: The drop you're following. It goes from the sea back to the sea by the route chosen on the left page: a river, snow, groundwater, a tree, or straight back into the sea.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, about twelve thousand seven hundred kilometres across. Its water is spread in a thin layer over the surface, which makes it look like a lot more than it is.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Evaporation
data.value: Evaporation. Sunshine gives water molecules at the surface enough energy to escape as invisible vapour. About five sixths of all evaporation is from the oceans.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowLandEvaporation
data.value: Evaporation and transpiration from the land: from soil, lakes and, above all, plants.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowLandPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow onto the land. Part of it comes from the sea, and part from water evaporated and transpired on land itself.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowOceanEvaporation
data.value: Evaporation from the ocean, the biggest flow of all: about four hundred thousand cubic kilometres of water every year.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowOceanPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow onto the ocean. Most of the water that evaporates from the sea falls straight back into it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowRunoff
data.value: Rivers and groundwater flowing back to the sea. Each year it matches the vapour blown over the land, so the cycle stays balanced.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowVapourToLand
data.value: Vapour carried from over the sea to over the land. It's what keeps the land supplied with rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Freezing
data.value: The freezing level: the height where the air is at zero degrees. Above it, cloud water freezes into ice and falls as snow.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Front
data.value: A front, where warm, moist air meets a wedge of colder, heavier air. The warm air slides up over it, cools, and makes wide sheets of cloud.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Groundwater
data.value: Groundwater. Below the water table, water creeps through the rock, often only a few metres a year, toward rivers, lakes and the sea. Wells and springs draw on it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Infiltration
data.value: Infiltration. Rain soaks into the soil. Some stays there for plants to use; the rest seeps on down through cracks in the rock until it reaches the water table.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Land
data.value: The water on land: ice caps and glaciers, groundwater, lakes, soil, rivers and living things. The biggest share is ice, with groundwater close behind.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Leeward
data.value: The leeward side. Air that rained out on the way up comes down warmer and drier than it set off: a foehn wind.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Oceans
data.value: The oceans hold almost all of Earth's water. A water molecule stays in the sea for more than three thousand years, on average, before it evaporates.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Parcel
data.value: The parcel: a lump of air we follow as it rises. The faint dots inside are vapour; once it reaches its dew point they turn into white droplets.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Precipitation
data.value: Precipitation. Cloud droplets merge, or ice crystals grow at their expense, until they're heavy enough to fall: rain below the freezing level, snow above it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_RainShadow
data.value: The rain shadow: the side of the mountain away from the wind. The air arriving here has already rained out on the other side, so it's dry.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Runoff
data.value: Runoff. Water that doesn't soak in or evaporate runs downhill into streams and rivers, and on to the sea. A drop spends only a couple of weeks in a river.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_SnowLine
data.value: The snow line: above it, the snow on the mountain lasts all year. In a warmer world it climbs higher, and there's less snow to feed the rivers.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Snowmelt
data.value: Snowmelt. Snow and glaciers store water through the winter and let it go in spring and summer. Many great rivers get much of their summer water this way.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Sublimation
data.value: Sublimation. In dry, sunny, windy weather, snow and ice can turn straight into vapour without melting first. On high, dry mountains it takes away a good share of the snow.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun, the engine of the water cycle. Its heat evaporates the water and stirs up the winds that carry it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Thermal
data.value: A field warmed by the Sun. It heats the air above it, and a bubble of warm air breaks away and rises, a thermal. Birds and gliders ride them.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Transpiration
data.value: Transpiration. Plants draw water up from the soil and let it out through tiny pores in their leaves. On land, plants send more water into the air than the soil and lakes do.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Transport
data.value: Transport. The wind carries invisible vapour far from where it evaporated, often hundreds or thousands of kilometres, much of it from over the sea to over the land.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Wind
data.value: The wind pushes the air up the windward slope of the mountain. It cools as it climbs, so this side gets the clouds and the rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_01
data.value: Where is all of Earth's water? Here it's gathered into balls, standing on Earth and drawn to the same scale.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_02
data.value: This ball holds all the water on Earth: the oceans, the ice, the groundwater, lakes, rivers and the air. It's only about one thousand four hundred kilometres across.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_03
data.value: This much smaller ball is all the fresh liquid water: groundwater, lakes, swamps and rivers. Almost all of it is groundwater, hidden in the rock.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_04
data.value: And this tiny one is the water in lakes and rivers, the fresh water that's easiest to reach. Look how little of it there is.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_05
data.value: Every year a huge amount of water evaporates. Where do you think most of it comes from?

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_06
data.value: The oceans. This shows the water moving each year, and the widest band is evaporation from the sea. But about nine tenths of it rains straight back onto the sea.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_07
data.value: The rest is blown over the land as vapour. Without this, rain would only fall on the sea, and the land would be desert.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_08
data.value: Every year, just as much water flows back to the sea in rivers and underground. So nothing runs out: the sea, the air and the land stay in balance.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_09
data.value: The air holds only a tiny amount at any moment. A water molecule stays up there for only about nine days, while in the ocean it stays, on average, for more than three thousand years.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_10
data.value: Your turn. Click a ball, a flow or a store in the picture to hear more about it.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_01
data.value: This is a road seen from above. The yellow dot is a source of sound, a horn playing the note A, four hundred and forty hertz. Standing still, its rings spread out evenly in every direction.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_02
data.value: Now it drives at half the speed of sound. Each ring starts from where the source was when it went out. So in front of it the rings are squeezed together, and behind it they're stretched apart.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_03
data.value: Squeezed rings reach your ear more often, and that sounds higher. Stretched rings sound lower. Keep an eye on what the listener hears as the source goes past.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_04
data.value: So, what do you hear as the source goes past you?

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_05
data.value: Yes. High as it comes, low as it goes. That's the familiar 'neee-owww' of a passing car. The horn itself never changed its note. Only the spacing of the rings did.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_06
data.value: Now the source is going at the speed of sound. It keeps up with its own rings, and they all pile up into a wall right in front of it.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_07
data.value: Twice the speed of sound. Now the source outruns its own sound, and the rings pile up into a cone behind it, called the Mach cone. The faster it goes, the narrower the cone.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_08
data.value: The listener hears nothing at all until the edge of the cone sweeps over them. Then comes a sudden bang, a sonic boom. After that they hear two sounds at once: the one it made coming, and the one it made going.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Doppler_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the listener somewhere else, closer to the road or farther away, and listen to the pass from there.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Bunched
data.value: In front of the moving source, the rings are squeezed together. More of them reach you every second, so you hear a higher pitch.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Cone
data.value: The Mach cone. Faster than sound, the rings pile up along its edge. The faster the source, the narrower the cone. When the edge passes over you, you hear a sonic boom.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Difference
data.value: The path difference: how much farther the probe is from one source than the other, counted in wavelengths. A whole number means crest meets crest, and the waves add up. A half means crest meets trough, and they cancel.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_DipperA
data.value: Dipper A: a little ball that dips into the water and lifts out again, over and over. Every dip sends out a ring of ripples. Drag it sideways to move the two dippers closer together or farther apart.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_DipperB
data.value: Dipper B, the twin of A. It dips in the same rhythm, or exactly the opposite way if you choose. Switch it off and there's just one set of plain rings, with no still lines at all.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Heard
data.value: What the listener hears right now: the pitch in hertz, and the nearest musical note. Watch it drop as the source goes past.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Laser
data.value: The laser. Its light is one pure colour, a single wavelength, and it keeps a steady rhythm. That's why it can make clear stripes. Two ordinary lamps can't, because their light keeps changing its rhythm.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Listener
data.value: The listener. They flash each time a ring reaches them, and the label says what pitch they hear right now. Drag them anywhere to hear the pass from somewhere else.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Loud
data.value: A line of the biggest waves. All along it, crest arrives with crest and trough with trough, so the two waves add up and the water heaves about twice as high. Nothing is lost on the still lines; it ends up here.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Order
data.value: The stripe numbers. Stripe one is where one slit is one wavelength farther away than the other; stripe two, two wavelengths; and so on. The middle stripe is zero, because both slits are equally far.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Probe
data.value: The probe. It measures how far it is from each of the two sources, and shows how their waves meet right there. Drag it anywhere to explore.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Quiet
data.value: A still line. All along it, the two waves arrive opposite each other, crest with trough, so they cancel and the water hardly moves. The label says how much farther one dipper is than the other.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Screen
data.value: The screen, where the light lands. It's bright where the two waves arrive in step and dark where they cancel. The chart on the left-hand page shows the real stripes.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Slits
data.value: The slits: narrow cuts in the barrier, only a fraction of a millimetre apart. Each one lets through a little light, which spreads out like the ripples from a dipper.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Source
data.value: The source of sound, playing the note A at four hundred and forty hertz. It always plays the same note; what changes is how its waves reach you. Drag it along the road to step through its pass.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Spacing
data.value: d is the distance between the two slits. Bring the slits closer together and the stripes on the screen spread farther apart.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Stretched
data.value: Behind the moving source, the rings are stretched apart. Fewer of them reach you every second, so you hear a lower pitch.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Tank
data.value: A ripple tank: a shallow tray of water seen from above, ten times slower than real. Bright is a crest, dark a trough. Switch on 'How far it swings' to see how much each spot moves instead.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Obj_Tape
data.value: Tape over the second slit. With just one slit, the light has nothing to overlap with, so the stripes vanish and only a broad glow is left.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_01
data.value: This is a ripple tank, a shallow tray of water seen from above and slowed down ten times. Dipper A bobs up and down, and every dip sends out a ring. The bright rings are crests, the dark ones troughs.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_02
data.value: Now dipper B switches on. It keeps exactly the same rhythm as A. Watch what happens where its rings run into A's.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_03
data.value: It's hard to follow every ripple, so let's look at it another way: how much the water moves at each spot. Bright means it heaves a lot, dark means it hardly moves. Can you see the dark spokes fanning out from between the dippers?

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_04
data.value: Those dark spokes are the still lines, drawn here as dashed lines. The probe sits on one now. It's half a wavelength farther from one dipper than from the other, so a crest from one always arrives with a trough from the other, and they cancel out.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_05
data.value: Now the probe has moved onto a gold line. Here the difference is a whole wavelength, so crest meets crest and trough meets trough. The two waves add up, and the water heaves about twice as high.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_06
data.value: Here's a question. Suppose the dippers moved in opposite ways: A goes down just as B comes up. What happens on the middle line, where the two dippers are equally far away?

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_07
data.value: That's it. With the dippers moving opposite ways, the middle line has gone still, and every still line has swapped places with a gold line. The probe was on a gold line a moment ago. Now it's on a still one.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_08
data.value: Back in step, and now the waves are shorter. See how there are more still lines, packed closer together? Moving the dippers farther apart does the same.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Ripple_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the probe onto a still line, one of the dashed lines, and see the water go quiet there.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Slits_01
data.value: Now the same idea with light. A green laser shines on a barrier with two very narrow slits in it. Light waves are tiny, so here they're drawn thousands of times bigger than real.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Slits_02
data.value: Each slit works just like a dipper in the ripple tank. Light spreads out from it in rings, and the rings from the two slits overlap on their way to the screen.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Slits_03
data.value: Where the light lands on the screen, you get bright and dark stripes. It's the same pattern as the gold lines and still lines in the water.

data.name: Narr_Waves_Slits_04
