Tides are pulling it inward by about 1.8 m per century; in roughly 50 million years it will hit Mars or break up into a ring. Its largest crater, Stickney, is almost 9 km wide.

data.name: SolarSystem_RealScale_Tooltip
data.value: Place the planets at their true distances from the Sun (AU) instead of evenly spaced rings

data.name: SolarSystem_Rhea_Description
data.value: Rhea is Saturn's second-largest moon, a cold, cratered ball of ice and rock. In 2010 Cassini detected a very thin exosphere of oxygen and carbon dioxide around it. In the shade its surface drops to about −220 °C.

data.name: SolarSystem_Saturn_Description
data.value: Saturn, the second-largest planet, is famous for its spectacular rings: countless pieces of ice and rock, from dust grains to house-sized chunks, spread about 280,000 km across yet typically only 10 metres to 1 km thick. Saturn's average density is lower than water's — given a big enough ocean, it would float. It has more known moons than any other planet; Titan has a thick atmosphere, and Enceladus hides a liquid ocean beneath its icy crust.

data.name: SolarSystem_ScaleNote
data.value: Body sizes are not to scale.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Description
data.value: The Sun is a 4.6-billion-year-old yellow dwarf that holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. Its core reaches about 15 million °C and fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. That energy takes tens of thousands of years to work its way to the surface, then about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth as sunlight. The Sun's gravity keeps the planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets on their paths.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Tagline
data.value: The star at the heart of the Solar System

data.name: SolarSystem_Tethys_Description
data.value: Tethys is made almost entirely of water ice, so its density is barely above that of water. It bears a huge crater, Odysseus, about 450 km wide, and a canyon, Ithaca Chasma, that runs some 2,000 km across its surface.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Description
data.value: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen, wrapped in orange haze; the pressure at its surface is about 1.5 times Earth's. It is the only world besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface: lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is due to launch in 2028.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Tagline
data.value: A moon with a thick atmosphere

data.name: SolarSystem_Titania_Description
data.value: Titania is the largest moon of Uranus, discovered by William Herschel in 1787. Fault canyons up to about 1,500 km long scar its surface, signs that its interior once expanded as water froze. A thin layer of liquid water may still lie beneath its crust.

data.name: SolarSystem_Today_Tooltip
data.value: Jump back to today's planet positions

data.name: SolarSystem_Triton_Description
data.value: Triton is Neptune's largest moon and the only large moon that orbits backwards, against its planet's rotation — strong evidence that it is a captured Kuiper Belt object. At about −235 °C it has one of the coldest surfaces known, yet Voyager 2 saw geysers of nitrogen gas rising some 8 km. Tides are slowly drawing it inward, and one day it will be torn apart.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Description
data.value: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's five large moons, with an ancient, heavily cratered surface. A puzzling bright ring about 130 km across, nicknamed the "fluorescent Cheerio", sits on the crater Wunda near its equator.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Tagline
data.value: The darkest of Uranus's large moons

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Description
data.value: Uranus is an ice giant whose methane-rich atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a pale cyan tint. Its axis is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, and each pole gets about 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. It has 13 faint, narrow rings, and its cloud tops can drop to −224 °C, the coldest planetary atmosphere in the Solar System.

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Tagline
data.value: The ice giant that rolls on its side

data.name: SolarSystem_Venus_Description
data.value: Venus is close to Earth in size and mass and is often called Earth's twin. A thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere with clouds of sulfuric acid presses down at about 92 times Earth's surface pressure, and a runaway greenhouse effect heats the surface to around 465 °C — hotter than Mercury. Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, and one rotation takes 243 days, longer than its 225-day year. After the Moon, it is the brightest object in the night sky.

data.name: Sound_Chart_Pipe_Note
data.value: The bars are multiples of the lowest frequency. A pipe closed at one end only allows the odd ones.

data.name: Sound_Chart_Strings_Note
data.value: How strongly each harmonic starts. A cross marks one with a node right where the string was plucked: it cannot start.

data.name: Sound_Chart_Timbre_Note
data.value: Each key is 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.059 times the one before, so every twelve keys the frequency doubles.

data.name: Sound_Chart_Wave_Note
data.value: Below the blue line is too quiet to hear (threshold of hearing, Terhardt 1979). The dot is the speaker's tone: drag it.

data.name: Sound_Hint_Pipe
data.value: Click a row to pick a resonance; change the pipe's length on the left-hand page.

data.name: Sound_Hint_Strings
data.value: Drag the string and let go to pluck it; click the neck to hold a fret; click a row to hear one harmonic.

data.name: Sound_Hint_Timbre
data.value: Click or drag across the keys to play; drag the bars to build your own sound.

data.name: Sound_Hint_Wave
data.value: Drag the speaker's cone to push the air yourself; click a dot to follow it.

data.name: Sound_Label_NoAir
data.value: No air: nothing to carry the sound

data.name: Sound_Lesson_Wave_Choice1
data.value: A pattern of squeezing and stretching

data.name: Sound_Lesson_Wave_Choice2
data.value: The air itself, blown from the speaker

data.name: Sound_Pipe_Closed_Text
data.value: The air cannot move at the closed end (a node) but can at the open one: a quarter wave fits, so the note is about an octave lower and only odd harmonics are allowed.

data.name: Sound_Pipe_Note
data.value: Bore 19 mm across, like a flute's. At an open end the air's swing reaches about 0.6 radius past the tube.

data.name: Sound_Pipe_Open_Text
data.value: The air can move freely at both ends, so both are antinodes: half a wave fits the lowest note, and every harmonic is allowed.

data.name: Sound_PlayNote_Tooltip
data.value: Play the note on the instrument

data.name: Sound_Pluck_Tooltip
data.value: Pluck the string at the pick

data.name: Sound_SoundOn_Tooltip
data.value: The page's own sound on or off (plucks, notes and the tone)

data.name: Sound_State_Heard_Text
data.value: At this pitch it is above the threshold of hearing. Your eardrum follows the air's tiny back-and-forth and passes it on to the inner ear.

data.name: Sound_State_High_Text
data.value: A young ear can hear this, but many adults cannot: the top of our hearing falls with age.

data.name: Sound_State_Infra_Text
data.value: Below about 20 Hz the ear hears no pitch, though very strong infrasound can be felt. Elephants and whales use it.

data.name: Sound_State_Pain_Text
data.value: Near 120–130 dB sound hurts, and even a short time can damage hearing for good.

data.name: Sound_State_Quiet_Text
data.value: At this pitch the ear needs a louder sound. Hearing is most sensitive around 3–4 kHz and much less so for low notes.

data.name: Sound_State_Ultra_Text
data.value: Above 20 kHz is too high for human ears. Bats, dolphins and medical scanners use it.

data.name: Sound_State_Vacuum_Text
data.value: The cone still moves, but there is nothing for it to push. Sound needs a medium: a gas, a liquid or a solid.

data.name: Sound_String_Edge_Text
data.value: Close to an end many high harmonics start strongly: the sound is bright and thin, as guitarists know.

data.name: Sound_String_Middle_Text
data.value: Every even harmonic has a node at the middle, so none of them start: the sound is round and hollow.

data.name: Sound_String_Note
data.value: Guitar scale length 648 mm; tensions typical of light steel strings.

data.name: Sound_String_Plucked_Text
data.value: The string's shape is the sum of its harmonics. The higher ones die away sooner, so the tone mellows as it rings.

data.name: Sound_String_Solo1_Text
data.value: Just the fundamental: one arch, the lowest frequency. On its own it sounds smooth and plain, a little like a flute.

data.name: Sound_String_Solo_Text
data.value: One overtone alone, at a whole multiple of the fundamental. Its nodes split the string into equal parts.

data.name: Sound_String_Tooltip
data.value: The six strings of a guitar in standard tuning, low to high

data.name: Sound_Strings_Fact1
data.value: Each fret raises the note a semitone by making the string 2^(1/12) times shorter, which is why frets crowd together towards the body.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Fact2
data.value: Pitch rises with tension and falls with length and weight: f = √(T/μ) / 2L. Thick, heavy strings play the low notes.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Fact3
data.value: A string alone is quiet: it barely pushes the air. The guitar's top and the air in its body pick up the vibration and pass it on.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Fact4
data.value: Touch a string lightly at its middle and pluck it, and you get a guitar 'harmonic': only the modes with a node there keep ringing.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Fact5
data.value: Flutes are open at both ends; a clarinet behaves as if closed at one end, so it sounds about an octave lower than a flute of the same length.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Note
data.value: Slowed so the lowest harmonic swings about once every two seconds; the string's swing is exaggerated.

data.name: Sound_Strings_Subtitle
data.value: Standing waves on a string and in a pipe

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Clarinet_Text
data.value: Its tube acts as if closed at the reed, so in its low notes the odd harmonics are strong and the even ones weak: a hollow, woody tone.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Custom_Text
data.value: Your own mix of overtones. The pitch stays the same as long as the fundamental is there: only the timbre changes.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fact1
data.value: A4 = 440 Hz is the agreed tuning pitch for most orchestras today (ISO 16); some tune a little higher, to 442 or 443.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fact2
data.value: Your ear splits a sound into its frequencies, much as the bars here do: each place along the cochlea answers to a different pitch.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fact3
data.value: Notes an octave apart share many overtones, one reason they sound like the same note.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fact4
data.value: Equal temperament makes every step the same, so music can move to any key. The price: intervals such as the fifth are very slightly off simple ratios.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fact5
data.value: A telephone cuts off low frequencies, yet a deep voice still sounds deep: the brain fills in the missing fundamental from the overtones.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Flute_Text
data.value: Mostly the fundamental with a few weak overtones: a soft, breathy, simple tone.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Fork_Text
data.value: Almost a pure sine wave: one frequency, so it sounds clean and plain. That is why it is used for tuning.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Note
data.value: The waveform is real and to scale in milliseconds; the instruments' overtone mixes are rounded, for illustration.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Panel_Note
data.value: Click or drag across the keys to play. The overtone mixes are rough averages for a middle note.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Piano_Text
data.value: A hammer strikes the strings and the sound dies away; the high overtones fade first, so the note softens as it rings.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Subtitle
data.value: Why a violin and a flute sound different

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Trumpet_Text
data.value: Its strongest harmonics sit a few steps above the fundamental: a brassy, brilliant tone.

data.name: Sound_Timbre_Violin_Text
data.value: The bow drags the string and lets it slip, over and over: a sawtooth-like wave rich in overtones, bright and full.

data.name: Sound_Tone_Note
data.value: Your speakers set the real loudness, so start with the volume low. Very low notes may be too deep for small speakers.

data.name: Sound_Tone_Tooltip
data.value: Hear the speaker's tone through your computer's speakers

data.name: Sound_Wave_Fact1
data.value: In air at 20 °C sound travels about 343 m/s, roughly 1 km in 3 seconds: count the seconds between lightning and thunder to tell how far the storm is.

data.name: Sound_Wave_Fact2
data.value: The air does not travel with the sound. Each bit only moves back and forth, often by less than the size of a virus.

data.name: Sound_Wave_Fact3
data.value: Decibels count by multiplying: every 10 dB more is ten times the power, and sounds about twice as loud.

data.name: Sound_Wave_Fact4
data.value: Young ears hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The top falls with age, and many adults no longer hear 15 kHz. Dogs hear to about 45 kHz, bats beyond 100 kHz.

data.name: Sound_Wave_Fact5
data.value: In space there is no air to carry sound: explosions in space films should really be silent.

data.name: Sound_Wave_Note
data.value: Lengths to scale (see the ruler); time slowed down hugely and the air's movement exaggerated, or nothing would be visible.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Excited_Text
data.value: Up here the electron soon falls back down, level by level or in one go, and each fall gives out a photon whose energy is the gap it fell.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Fact1
data.value: Niels Bohr explained hydrogen's lines in 1913 with fixed orbits; quantum mechanics later replaced the orbits with clouds but kept his energy levels.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Fact2
data.value: Hα, the red 656 nm line, gives glowing gas clouds in space such as the Orion Nebula their pink-red colour.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Fact3
data.value: It takes 13.6 electron-volts to pull hydrogen's electron off from the ground level.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Fact4
data.value: In Bohr's model the second orbit is four times as wide as the first, the third nine times: radius grows as n².

data.name: Spec_Atom_Fact5
data.value: Johann Balmer found the formula for hydrogen's visible lines in 1885 from just four wavelengths, long before anyone knew why it worked.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Free_Text
data.value: The photon brought more than 13.6 eV, so the electron left the atom altogether. Soon a proton catches an electron again, high up, and it tumbles down giving out lines.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Free_Title
data.value: Set free: the atom is ionised

data.name: Spec_Atom_Ground_Text
data.value: The electron is as low as it can go and stays there. Only a photon with exactly the energy of a jump up (or enough to set it free) can move it.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Note
data.value: Bohr's picture: orbit sizes drawn in proportion to n (really n²), the energy ladder on a square-root scale. The wavelengths are real.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Panel_Note
data.value: The cloud is a slice through the atom: brighter where the electron is more likely to be. Each level has its own shapes (s, p, d …), up to one less than its number.

data.name: Spec_Atom_Subtitle
data.value: Hydrogen's energy levels and its light

data.name: Spec_Chart_Atom_Note
data.value: Each row is the lines that end on one level: Lyman on 1 (ultraviolet), Balmer on 2 (visible), Paschen on 3 and Brackett on 4 (infrared). The shaded band is visible light. Click a line to load it into the lamp.

data.name: Spec_Chart_Lamps_Note
data.value: Each gas's bright lines, 380 to 750 nm. No two are alike. Click a row to compare it with the spectrum.

data.name: Spec_Chart_Stars_Caption
data.value: Which dark lines, at which temperature

data.name: Spec_Chart_Stars_Note
data.value: How strong each family of dark lines is, hottest stars on the left (O B A F G K M). Drag to change the temperature.

data.name: Spec_Class_A_Text
data.value: White stars near 10,000 K, where hydrogen's lines are at their deepest.

data.name: Spec_Class_B_Text
data.value: Blue-white and very hot: neutral helium's lines are strongest, hydrogen's growing.

data.name: Spec_Class_F_Text
data.value: Yellow-white: hydrogen's lines are weakening and calcium's growing.

data.name: Spec_Class_G_Text
data.value: Yellow, like the Sun: calcium's H and K lines are the strongest, with many lines of iron and other metals.

data.name: Spec_Class_K_Text
data.value: Orange and cooler: metal lines everywhere, sodium strong, the first molecules appearing.

data.name: Spec_Class_M_Text
data.value: Red and the coolest: molecules such as titanium oxide survive and cut broad dark bands.

data.name: Spec_Class_O_Text
data.value: The hottest and bluest stars. Their light ionises even helium, so lines of ionised helium show.

data.name: Spec_Event_Pass
data.value: a {0} nm photon passed straight through

data.name: Spec_Fire_Tooltip
data.value: Send one photon of the lamp's colour at the atom

data.name: Spec_Hint_Atom
data.value: Click a level on the ladder to lift the electron there, or fire photons from the lamp.

data.name: Spec_Hint_Lamps
data.value: Click the spectrum to pick a line.

data.name: Spec_Hint_Stars
data.value: Drag the curve to change the temperature, or the star's spectrum to make it move.

data.name: Spec_Label_BlueShift
data.value: blue shift: coming closer at {0} km/s

data.name: Spec_Label_RedShift
data.value: red shift: moving away at {0} km/s

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Bulb_Text
data.value: A hot solid's atoms are packed so close that their levels blur together: it gives every colour, a continuous spectrum, brightest in the red for a bulb.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Fact1
data.value: Helium was found in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before it was found on Earth; its name comes from Helios, the Sun.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Fact2
data.value: Firework colours are spectra: strontium gives red, sodium yellow, barium green and copper blue.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Fact3
data.value: Old low-pressure sodium street lamps shine almost all in sodium's yellow pair, which is why colours look grey under them.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Fact4
data.value: Joseph von Fraunhofer mapped 574 dark lines in sunlight in 1814; we still use his letters for the strongest.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Fact5
data.value: Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed in 1859 that every element has its own lines, and soon discovered caesium and rubidium by theirs.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Lamp_Text
data.value: A hot, thin gas gives out bright lines at the colours of its atoms' jumps, and nothing in between: an emission spectrum.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Mystery_Text
data.value: Which gas glows here? Compare its lines with the fingerprints in the chart below, then make your guess.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Note
data.value: A classroom spectroscope: line wavelengths from the NIST tables, their brightness roughly as the eye sees it.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Panel_Note
data.value: Click a row of the chart below to put that gas under the spectrum and compare.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Subtitle
data.value: Every gas has its own lines

data.name: Spec_Lamps_Sun_Text
data.value: The Sun's hot surface gives a rainbow, and the cooler gases above it take out their own colours: dark lines that show what the Sun is made of.

data.name: Spec_Lamps_ThroughGas_Text
data.value: The cooler gas absorbs the colours it would give out if it were hot, so its strong lines appear dark: an absorption spectrum. A really cold gas takes only the lines that start from its lowest level, such as sodium's yellow pair.

data.name: Spec_Lesson_Lamps_Choice1
data.value: Dark lines where sodium's bright lines were

data.name: Spec_Lesson_Lamps_Choice2
data.value: Sodium's bright yellow lines on top of the rainbow

data.name: Spec_Lesson_Stars_Choice1
data.value: A white star of about 10,000 degrees

data.name: Spec_Mystery_Tooltip
data.value: A lamp of a hidden gas: work out which it is

data.name: Spec_Stars_Fact1
data.value: Cecilia Payne showed in 1925 that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium: their different spectra come from temperature, not from what they are made of.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Fact2
data.value: Spectral types run O B A F G K M from hottest to coolest; the Sun is a G2 star.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Fact3
data.value: Edwin Hubble found in 1929 that the farther a galaxy is, the more its light is red-shifted: the universe is expanding.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Fact4
data.value: The Andromeda galaxy is blue-shifted: it is coming towards us at about 300 km/s.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Fact5
data.value: Planets round other stars were first found by tiny Doppler wobbles in their star's lines, a few metres per second.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Note
data.value: The curve is a black body's; the dark lines' strength by temperature is from Saha–Boltzmann for hydrogen and simplified for the rest.

data.name: Spec_Stars_Panel_Note
data.value: Speeds in km/s, positive moving away. A star's own colour comes from its temperature, not its speed: the shift is tiny for stars and only large for far galaxies.

data.name: Spec_Velocity
data.value: Speed along our line of sight

data.name: Star_Class_Massive_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for only about 10 to 35 million years

data.name: Star_Class_RedDwarf_Ending
data.value: → fades into a helium white dwarf (none has yet)

data.name: Star_Class_RedDwarf_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for hundreds of billions to trillions of years

data.name: Star_Class_SunLike_Ending
data.value: → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf

data.name: Star_Class_SunLike_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for tens of millions to tens of billions of years

data.name: Star_Class_VeryMassive_Lifetime
data.value: Shines for just a few million years

data.name: Star_Core_Agb
data.value: Two burning shells, helium and hydrogen, round a carbon-oxygen core.

data.name: Star_Core_BlackHole
data.value: Nothing inside the event horizon can be seen.

data.name: Star_Core_BlueDwarf
data.value: Hydrogen into helium, nearly all of the star's hydrogen used.

data.name: Star_Core_Caption
data.value: Inside the star (cut open, not to scale)

data.name: Star_Core_HeliumBurning
data.value: Helium into carbon and oxygen in the core, hydrogen in a shell.

data.name: Star_Core_LateBurning
data.value: Each layer burns the ashes of the one outside it, down to an iron core.

data.name: Star_Core_MainSequence
data.value: Hydrogen fuses into helium in the core.

data.name: Star_Core_NeutronStar
data.value: No fusion: neutrons packed as tight as in an atomic nucleus, under a thin iron crust.

data.name: Star_Core_PlanetaryNebula
data.value: The fires are out; the bare carbon-oxygen core lights the gas it has shed.

data.name: Star_Core_Protostar
data.value: No fusion yet: the gas heats up as it falls in.

data.name: Star_Core_RedGiant
data.value: A small, dense helium core, hydrogen burning in a shell, and a huge cool envelope stirred by convection.

data.name: Star_Core_RedSupergiant
data.value: Helium into carbon and oxygen in the core, hydrogen in a shell.

data.name: Star_Core_Subgiant
data.value: The helium core is not burning; hydrogen burns in a shell around it.

data.name: Star_Core_Supergiant
data.value: Hydrogen burning in a shell round a contracting helium core.

data.name: Star_Core_Supernova
data.value: The iron core collapses to neutrons; a shock wave tears the star apart.

data.name: Star_Core_WhiteDwarf
data.value: No fusion: carbon and oxygen (helium, for a red dwarf) pressed so tight that electrons hold it up.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact1
data.value: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell drew the first versions of the diagram independently, around 1910 to 1913.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact2
data.value: About nine in ten stars, the Sun among them, are on the main sequence, because that is where stars spend most of their lives.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact3
data.value: Temperature runs backwards, hot on the left, because the first diagrams were drawn by colour, from blue to red.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact4
data.value: Stars of one size lie along a diagonal: a cool star can only be very bright by being huge, like Betelgeuse.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact5
data.value: Sirius B, the companion of the brightest star in the night sky, is a white dwarf: hotter than Sirius A, but only Earth-sized, so it gives out a twentieth of the Sun's light.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Note
data.value: Temperature across, hot on the left, and brightness up, both on log scales. The dashed line is the star's whole path, the solid one the part it has lived.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Subtitle
data.value: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram: a star's life is a journey across it

data.name: Star_DragHint_Fates
data.value: Click a row to pick a star of that kind

data.name: Star_DragHint_Strip
data.value: Click or drag along the strip of stages at the bottom to move through the star's life

data.name: Star_Duration_Caption
data.value: How long each stage really lasts

data.name: Star_Duration_Note
data.value: On a log scale: each grid line is a thousand times the last. Almost all of a star's life is spent on the main sequence.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact1
data.value: The line between Sun-like and massive stars is about 8 Suns; between neutron stars and black holes perhaps 20 to 25, and it is still debated.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact2
data.value: A white dwarf can weigh at most 1.44 Suns, the Chandrasekhar limit; any heavier and its electrons can no longer hold it up.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact3
data.value: The Crab Nebula is what is left of a supernova Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054; a pulsar spinning 30 times a second sits at its centre.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact4
data.value: Betelgeuse, a red supergiant in Orion, will explode some time in the next 100,000 years and shine about as bright as a half Moon.

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact5
data.value: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.

data.name: Star_Fates_Note
data.value: For single stars like the Sun. The mass limits are approximate, the one between neutron stars and black holes especially.

data.name: Star_Fates_Subtitle
data.value: Four ways to end: a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole

data.name: Star_Hr_AxisT
data.value: Surface temperature (K), hotter to the left

data.name: Star_Hr_NeutronStar
data.value: Neutron star: too small and faint for the chart

data.name: Star_Hr_Supernova
data.value: Supernova: {0} × the Sun, far off the chart

data.name: Star_Lesson_Diagram_Choice1
data.value: Up and to the right, to the giants

data.name: Star_Lesson_Diagram_Choice2
data.value: Straight down to the white dwarfs

data.name: Star_Lesson_Fates_Choice2
data.value: It becomes a white dwarf, like the Sun

data.name: Star_Lesson_Life_Choice1
data.value: It swells into a red giant

data.name: Star_Life_Fact1
data.value: The Sun is 4.6 billion years old, about halfway through its 10 billion years on the main sequence.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact2
data.value: In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant and swallow Mercury and Venus; whether it reaches Earth is still uncertain.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact3
data.value: Heavier stars burn far faster: a star of 10 Suns is thousands of times as bright and lasts only about 20 million years.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact4
data.value: Every atom of carbon, oxygen and iron in your body was made inside stars and spread by them as they died.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact5
data.value: Red dwarfs are the most common stars, about three in four; Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is one.

data.name: Star_Life_Note
data.value: Not to scale: sizes go by the cube root, so a supergiant a thousand times the Sun and an Earth-sized white dwarf both fit. Playback gives each stage its turn; the real lengths are along the bottom.

data.name: Star_Life_Subtitle
data.value: A star's life is decided by its mass: the heavier, the brighter, and the shorter

data.name: Star_Remnant_Note
data.value: Left, a white dwarf beside Earth; right, a thousand times closer in, a neutron star and a black hole. A teaspoon of white dwarf weighs about 5 tonnes, of neutron star about a billion tonnes.

data.name: Star_Stage_Agb_Description
data.value: The core's helium is used up too. Helium and hydrogen burn in two shells round a carbon-oxygen core; the star swells even bigger, pulses, and blows strong winds that carry off its outer layers.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Description
data.value: The core is too heavy even for neutrons to hold it up, and it collapses for ever. Inside the event horizon, a few tens of kilometres across, gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Title
data.value: Black hole: not even light gets out

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Description
data.value: A red dwarf stirs all its hydrogen through the whole star, so it burns nearly all of it. At the very end it grows smaller, hotter and bluer. The universe is too young: no star has got this far yet.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Title
data.value: Blue dwarf: a red dwarf's slow end

data.name: Star_Stage_HeliumBurning_Description
data.value: At 100 million degrees the core ignites helium, fusing it into carbon and oxygen; in a star like the Sun this starts with a flash. The star shrinks back for a while.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Description
data.value: Carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn one after another, each faster than the last: carbon for centuries, silicon for about a day. The core turns to iron, which gives no energy when it fuses: the fire goes out.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Title
data.value: The last fuels, in layers like an onion

data.name: Star_Stage_MainSequence_Description
data.value: In the core, hydrogen fuses into helium at over 10 million degrees. The push of that heat balances gravity, and the star hardly changes for most of its life. The Sun is here now.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Description
data.value: The collapsed core: more mass than the Sun in a ball about 20 km across, made almost entirely of neutrons. It spins many times a second; if its beams sweep over Earth we see a pulsar.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Title
data.value: Neutron star: an atomic nucleus as big as a city

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Description
data.value: The star sheds its outer layers. Its bare core, over 100,000 degrees, lights the spreading gas into a glowing shell for some tens of thousands of years. The name is old: it has nothing to do with planets.

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Title
data.value: Planetary nebula: the outer layers drift away

data.name: Star_Stage_Protostar_Description
data.value: A cold cloud of gas and dust falls in on itself. Shrinking, it heats up and glows red, fed by a spinning disc and blowing jets from its poles. No fusion yet: the heat comes from the fall.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedGiant_Description
data.value: The burning shell pours out energy and the outside balloons to over a hundred times the Sun's size. The surface cools to orange-red, yet the star is thousands of times as bright.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Description
data.value: Helium burns in the core. The star is so big that in place of the Sun it would reach past Mars, some past Jupiter. Betelgeuse in Orion is one.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Title
data.value: Red supergiant: hundreds of times the Sun's size

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Description
data.value: The core is now helium and stops burning. It shrinks and heats up; hydrogen burns in a shell around it, and the star's outer layers begin to swell.

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Title
data.value: Subgiant: the core runs out of hydrogen

data.name: Star_Stage_Supergiant_Description
data.value: The core's hydrogen is gone and it contracts while hydrogen burns around it. In thousands of years the star swells from blue to red, crossing the diagram at nearly the same brightness.

data.name: Star_Stage_Supernova_Description
data.value: The iron core collapses in under a second, from Earth's size to a ball of neutrons 20 km across. The infalling layers rebound in a vast explosion, for weeks as bright as billions of Suns, making heavy elements and scattering them into space.

data.name: Star_Stage_WhiteDwarf_Description
data.value: What is left is the core: about half the Sun's mass squeezed to the size of Earth. Nothing burns any more; it just cools, from white-hot to dim red, over billions of years.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact1
data.value: The tidal force is the difference between the Moon's pull on a piece of ocean and its pull on Earth's centre. It weakens with the cube of the distance, so what matters is how near the Moon is, not how big.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact2
data.value: On the far side the Moon pulls the water less than it pulls Earth itself, so Earth is pulled away from that water: it is left behind as the second bulge.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact3
data.value: The Moon's tidal force is only about one ten-millionth of Earth's gravity. On an ocean covering the whole Earth it would lift the water only about half a metre; coasts and bays turn that into metres.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact4
data.value: While Earth turns once, the Moon moves on about 13° the same way, so Earth needs about 50 more minutes to catch up: the tides come about 50 minutes later each day.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact5
data.value: Tidal friction slows Earth's spin: the day grows about 2 milliseconds longer every century, and the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther away each year.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Note
data.value: Seen from above the North Pole, sunlight from the left; the Moon's tide alone. Not to scale: the bulges are exaggerated millions of times, and the Moon is really 60 Earth radii away.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Subtitle
data.value: Why two high tides a day? The Moon stretches the oceans into two bulges

data.name: Tides_Chart_Caption_Moon
data.value: The water where you are (the Moon's tide alone)

data.name: Tides_Chart_Note
data.value: Metres above chart datum; shaded: night. With the Sun added, the time between high tides varies a little around 12 h 25 min.

data.name: Tides_Chart_Note_Moon
data.value: Shaded: night. Two highs and two lows every 24 h 50 min.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact1
data.value: Tide tables give heights above chart datum, about the lowest the water ever falls, so the depth shown on a chart is the least to expect.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact2
data.value: Rule of twelfths: from low to high water, in each of the six hours the water rises about 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the range, fastest in the middle hours.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact3
data.value: On real coasts high water comes hours after the Moon is highest: the oceans cannot keep up with the bulges and the continents get in the way. The delay is nearly the same each day at a given port, which is how tides are predicted.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact4
data.value: Some coasts have only one high tide a day, such as the Beibu Gulf off Beihai, where the shape of the gulf strengthens the once-a-day tide.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact5
data.value: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tides in the world, up to about 16 m between high and low water; China's largest are in Hangzhou Bay, up to about 9 m.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Note
data.value: A coast at the latitude of {1} ({0}) where the Moon alone would move the water 1 m above and below the mean. Here high water comes when the Moon is highest or lowest; on real coasts it comes hours later.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Subtitle
data.value: At the coast: the sea comes in and goes out twice a day

data.name: Tides_DragHint_Moon
data.value: Drag the Moon along its orbit

data.name: Tides_DragHint_Time
data.value: Drag sideways to move the time: a day across the view

data.name: Tides_Force_Caption
data.value: Why is there a bulge on the far side too?

data.name: Tides_Force_Note
data.value: Exaggerated: the Moon is drawn 3 Earth radii away instead of 60, so the differences show.

data.name: Tides_Force_Pull
data.value: 1. The Moon's pull: strongest on the near side

data.name: Tides_Force_Tidal
data.value: 2. Take away the pull on the centre: the tidal force

data.name: Tides_Kind_Growing_Description
data.value: Heading for new or full moon: the two pairs of bulges come into line and the range grows day by day.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Neap_Description
data.value: Seen from Earth, the Sun and the Moon are at right angles (first or last quarter): the Sun's bulges fill in the Moon's lows, so the range is smallest.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Shrinking_Description
data.value: Heading for a quarter moon: the two pairs of bulges move apart and the range shrinks day by day.

data.name: Tides_Kind_Spring_Description
data.value: The Sun, Earth and the Moon are nearly in line (new or full moon): the Sun's bulges add to the Moon's, so high water is higher and low water lower.

data.name: Tides_Lesson_Coast_Choice1
data.value: About twelve and a half hours

data.name: Tides_Range_Caption
data.value: Range between high and low water through the month

data.name: Tides_Range_Note
data.value: Dashed: the Moon alone. The Sun makes the range swing between 1.1 m and 2.9 m.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact1
data.value: The Sun pulls on Earth about 180 times as hard as the Moon, yet its tidal force is only 46% of the Moon's: it is 389 times as far away, and the tidal force falls with the cube of the distance.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact2
data.value: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season (the name means the water springs up): they come twice a month, around new and full moon, the 1st and the 15th of the Chinese lunar month. Neap tides come around the 8th and the 23rd.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact3
data.value: Real spring tides usually come one to three days after new or full moon, because the oceans take time to respond to the pull. This delay is called the age of the tide.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact4
data.value: When a new or full moon comes with the Moon at its closest to Earth (perigee), its tidal force is nearly 20% stronger than on average and the spring tides are bigger still: perigean spring tides, or king tides.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact5
data.value: The Qiantang River bore near Hangzhou is at its grandest around the 18th of the eighth lunar month: an autumn spring tide pushed into a funnel-shaped estuary rises into a wall of water up to a few metres high.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Note
data.value: Dashed outlines: the Moon's and the Sun's bulges on their own; the blue water is the two added together. Not to scale.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Subtitle
data.value: The Sun joins in: big spring tides and small neap tides

data.name: Tides_Stage_Falling_Description
data.value: Earth's turning carries you away from the bulge, and the water goes out.

data.name: Tides_Stage_High_Description
data.value: High water: this place is under one of the two bulges, the one facing the Moon or the one opposite it.

data.name: Tides_Stage_Low_Description
data.value: Low water: you are halfway between the two bulges.

data.name: Tides_Stage_Rising_Description
data.value: You are turning towards the next bulge, and the water comes in.

data.name: Tides_Today_Text
data.value: Today the Moon is {0:0.0} days old · {1}

data.name: Tides_Upcoming_Note
data.value: From the real dates of the new moon, quarters and full moon in your time zone. The biggest tides usually come one to three days later.

data.name: Trails_Camera_East_Description
data.value: The stars come up out of the horizon in parallel slanting lines. The nearer the equator, the steeper they climb.

data.name: Trails_Camera_East_Title
data.value: Facing east: stars rising at a slant

data.name: Trails_Camera_Equator_Description
data.value: Here the stars rise, arc across the sky and set. Their circles are so big that you only see a gentle curve of each.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Equator_Title
data.value: Away from the pole: wide arcs

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact1
data.value: Star-trail photos are usually hundreds of 20–30 second shots stacked together, so the sky stays dark and every trail stays sharp.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact2
data.value: Polaris is less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so in a northern star-trail photo it draws only a tiny arc near the centre.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact3
data.value: The south celestial pole has no bright star near it; the Southern Cross and the two bright Pointers lead the way to it.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact4
data.value: The sky turns about 15° an hour: a fist held at arm's length covers about 10°.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact5
data.value: Earth's axis slowly wobbles round once in about 26,000 years, so the pole moves among the stars: in about 12,000 years Vega will be close to the north pole.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Note
data.value: A wide-angle camera (120° across) at the latitude chosen on the left page; the shutter opens at 20:00. The bright stars are real, the fainter ones a random fill, and the sky is drawn dark all night.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Pole_Description
data.value: Every trail is an arc round the celestial pole. The longer the exposure, the longer the arcs; stars near the pole draw small circles, stars far from it big ones.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Pole_Title
data.value: Facing the pole: circles round one point

data.name: Trails_Camera_Subtitle
data.value: The sky turns: stars draw circles round the pole

data.name: Trails_Camera_Up_Description
data.value: Overhead the trails are still circles round the pole, which sits as far from the zenith as you are from Earth's pole. Only at a pole are the circles centred right overhead.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Up_Title
data.value: Straight up: circles round the pole, off to one side

data.name: Trails_Camera_West_Description
data.value: The stars go down into the horizon in parallel slanting lines, the mirror image of the east.

data.name: Trails_Camera_West_Title
data.value: Facing west: stars setting at a slant

data.name: Trails_Chart_Hours_Caption
data.value: Hours above the horizon, by declination

data.name: Trails_Chart_Hours_Note
data.value: Declination is a star's latitude on the sky. Gold: never sets; blue: never rises; dots: the stars on the sphere.

data.name: Trails_Chart_Transit_Note
data.value: Each line runs about two hours earlier a month. Shaded: night at this latitude (twilight left out).

data.name: Trails_Hint_Camera
data.value: Drag the picture to turn and tilt the camera.

data.name: Trails_Hint_Sphere
data.value: Drag to turn the sphere; change the latitude on the left page.

data.name: Trails_Hint_Year
data.value: Drag Earth round the Sun, or run the year.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Equator_Description
data.value: Both celestial poles lie on the horizon. Every star is up for half of each day, and over a year you can see the whole sky.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Equator_Title
data.value: At the equator: everything rises and sets

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact1
data.value: The pole's height above the horizon equals your latitude: sailors measured it to find how far north or south they were.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact2
data.value: From the equator you can see every star in the sky over a year; from a pole, only half of them.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact3
data.value: The celestial equator lies straight above Earth's equator, and the celestial poles straight above Earth's poles.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact4
data.value: Near the horizon, stars look about half a degree higher than they really are: the air bends their light.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Fact5
data.value: Canopus, the second-brightest star, never rises north of about 37° N; from southern China it is the famous low 'old man star' of winter evenings.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Middle_Description
data.value: Near the visible pole, stars never set; near the other pole, they never rise; in between, they rise and set, staying up longer the nearer they are to the visible pole.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Middle_Title
data.value: In between: three kinds of stars

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Note
data.value: The celestial sphere seen from outside, with you at its centre on a disc of ground.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Pole_Description
data.value: The celestial pole is overhead and every star circles parallel to the horizon. Half the sky is always up; the other half never is.

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Pole_Title
data.value: At a pole: nothing rises or sets

data.name: Trails_Sphere_Subtitle
data.value: Which stars never set, and which never rise

data.name: Trails_Stat_Earlier_Value
data.value: about 4 min a night, 2 h a month

data.name: Trails_Stat_NeverRise_Value
data.value: stars within {0}° of the other pole

data.name: Trails_Year_Description
data.value: On Earth's night side you look away from the Sun. As Earth goes round, that direction sweeps round the sky: each season brings different constellations, and the stars rise about four minutes earlier every night.

data.name: Trails_Year_Exaggerated
data.value: Earth's step along its orbit drawn 15 times too big

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact1
data.value: A sidereal day is 23 h 56 min 4 s, a solar day 24 h. In a year Earth turns once more against the stars than against the Sun: about 366¼ times.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact2
data.value: Stars rise about 4 minutes earlier each night, so about 2 hours earlier each month.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact3
data.value: Orion fills the evening sky from about December to March; Scorpius from about June to August.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact4
data.value: Chinese astronomy divides the sky along the Moon's path into 28 lunar mansions; Antares, 心宿二, is the heart of the Azure Dragon of the east.

data.name: Trails_Year_Fact5
data.value: The zodiac constellations are the ones the Sun passes in front of during the year, Ophiuchus included, though most horoscopes leave it out.

data.name: Trails_Year_Note
data.value: Earth's orbit seen from above the north pole; the constellations really lie far, far beyond it. The evening sky is shown at 21:00 local sun time.

data.name: Trails_Year_StarBack
data.value: 23 h 56 min: the star is back

data.name: Trails_Year_Subtitle
data.value: Why the evening sky changes with the seasons

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Decay_Note
data.value: As measured (Kaplan and DeMaria 1995): it loses a tenth at the coast, then about 9.5% of what is left above 13.7 m/s each hour.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Intensity_Note
data.value: The strongest wind day by day; the red lines are landfalls. It grows over warm sea, weakens over cooler water and dies over land.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Potential_Caption
data.value: How strong the sea lets it get

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Potential_Note
data.value: The strongest wind a storm can reach over sea of this temperature (an empirical fit, DeMaria and Kaplan 1994). Most storms stay below it.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Profile_Caption
data.value: Wind and pressure from the centre out

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Profile_Note
data.value: Gold: the wind, calm in the eye, strongest at the eyewall, slowly falling off outward. Blue: the pressure. The dashed line is the probe.

data.name: Typhoon_Chart_Season_Note
data.value: Named storms a month over the north-west Pacific, averages for 1991–2020 (Japan Meteorological Agency, rounded): about 25 a year.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact1
data.value: A typhoon needs sea of at least 26.5 °C down to about 50 m, moist air, and winds that change little with height, so the storm is not torn apart.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact2
data.value: The heat given off by the rain of a typical hurricane is about 6 × 10¹⁴ W, some 200 times the average power of all the world's electricity; only about a four-hundredth of it goes into the wind.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact3
data.value: The air shoots up the eyewall to 15 km or more, then spreads out at the top as a sheet of cirrus hundreds of kilometres wide: the white disc seen from satellites.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact4
data.value: In the eye the air sinks and warms as it is squeezed, which is why the eye is clear and the storm's core is warmer than its surroundings.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Fact5
data.value: A typhoon cools the sea behind it by stirring up colder water from below, sometimes by several degrees; a slow storm can weaken itself this way.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Landfall_Description
data.value: Over land there is no warm sea to evaporate: the air coming in is dry, hills and trees slow it down, and the storm runs down within a day or two. It can still pour down huge amounts of rain.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Note
data.value: A slice 600 km wide and 18 km high, heights stretched about 15 times. The storm is 90% as strong as the sea allows (DeMaria and Kaplan 1994); after landfall it fades as measured (Kaplan and DeMaria 1995).

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Running_Description
data.value: Warm, moist air spirals in over the sea, rises in the eyewall and its water vapour condenses. The heat given off warms the core, the pressure falls further and the wind draws in still more moist air. The warmer the sea, the stronger it can get.

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Running_Title
data.value: A heat engine on warm sea

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_Subtitle
data.value: A heat engine running on warm sea

data.name: Typhoon_Engine_TooCool_Description
data.value: Below about 26.5 °C the sea cannot give enough heat and moisture: thunderstorms come and go but never organise into a spinning storm.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_Depression_Description
data.value: 10.8–17.1 m/s, force 6–7: a low whose thunderstorms are starting to circle.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_None_Description
data.value: Below 10.8 m/s: just a low, not yet a tropical cyclone.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SevereTropicalStorm_Description
data.value: 24.5–32.6 m/s, force 10–11: trees are uprooted and the sea runs high.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SevereTyphoon_Description
data.value: 41.5–50.9 m/s, force 14–15: a clear eye ringed by violent winds; damage is widespread.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_SuperTyphoon_Description
data.value: 51 m/s or more, force 16 and above: the most destructive storms, with a sharp, round eye.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_TropicalStorm_Description
data.value: 17.2–24.4 m/s, force 8–9: the storm gets its name. Showers circle a centre that has no eye yet.

data.name: Typhoon_Grade_Typhoon_Description
data.value: 32.7–41.4 m/s, force 12–13: an eye has usually formed; roofs and signs are torn off.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Engine
data.value: Change the sea's temperature, or let the storm come ashore and watch it run down; drag sideways to turn the hours.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Storm
data.value: Click or drag the probe anywhere in the storm; switch off the Earth's turn, or go south of the equator, to see why it spins.

data.name: Typhoon_Hint_Track
data.value: Move the subtropical high's west end and change the month; click on the sea to start a storm there; drag sideways to turn the days.

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice1
data.value: The heat given off when water vapour condenses

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice2
data.value: The spin of the wind itself

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Engine_Choice3
data.value: Sunlight warming the tops of the clouds

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice1
data.value: The Earth's turn deflects the moving air

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice2
data.value: The waves push the air sideways

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Storm_Choice3
data.value: The eye blows the air back out

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Track_Choice1
data.value: It keeps heading west, into South China

data.name: Typhoon_Lesson_Track_Choice3
data.value: It stops and stays where it is

data.name: Typhoon_Pressure_Note
data.value: The lower the pressure, the stronger the wind (further right is deeper).

data.name: Typhoon_Ridge
data.value: West end of the subtropical high

data.name: Typhoon_Ridge_Note
data.value: Reaching far west, it steers storms into South China; pulled back east, it lets them turn north towards Taiwan, Zhejiang, Japan or out to sea.

data.name: Typhoon_Start_Caption
data.value: Where it forms (or click on the sea)

data.name: Typhoon_Stat_Pass_Far
data.value: {0}: too far away to feel it

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Anticlockwise
data.value: Northern hemisphere: the air spirals in anticlockwise

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Clockwise
data.value: Southern hemisphere: the air spirals in clockwise

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact1
data.value: Typhoon, hurricane and cyclone are the same kind of storm: a typhoon in the north-west Pacific, a hurricane in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact2
data.value: The eye is calm and often clear, most of them 30–60 km across. The strongest winds and heaviest rain are in the eyewall right around it.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact3
data.value: Air rushing towards the low is turned aside by the Earth's turn (to the right in the north), so it circles anticlockwise instead of filling the low. Within about 5° of the equator the effect is too weak, and typhoons almost never form there.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact4
data.value: In the north the right side of the track is the dangerous one: there the storm's forward motion adds to its swirl.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Fact5
data.value: The lowest sea-level pressure ever measured was 870 hPa, in Typhoon Tip over the north-west Pacific in October 1979.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_NoSpin
data.value: Without the Earth's turn the air rushes straight in and fills the low

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_NoSpin_Description
data.value: The air heads straight for the low and fills it within a day. It is the Earth's turn (the Coriolis effect) that bends the air aside, so that it circles round instead of in and the low can deepen.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Note
data.value: Seen from above, 1200 km across. Winds from the Holland (1980) profile and the north-west Pacific wind–pressure relation; the cloud is illustrative; time runs about 900 times faster.

data.name: Typhoon_Storm_Subtitle
data.value: A typhoon from above: eye, eyewall and rain bands

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact1
data.value: About 25 named storms form over the north-west Pacific each year, more than over any other ocean, most of them in August and September.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact2
data.value: A typhoon hardly moves by itself: it is carried by the winds around it, above all those round the subtropical high. Chinese forecasters watch its edge as the 588 line, where the 500 hPa surface is 5880 m high.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact3
data.value: When the high reaches far west, storms head straight into South China, Hainan or Vietnam; when it pulls back east, they turn north towards Taiwan, Zhejiang, Shanghai, Korea or Japan, or curve away over the sea.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact4
data.value: On average about seven tropical storms or stronger come ashore in China each year, most in Guangdong, Hainan, Taiwan, Fujian and Zhejiang.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Fact5
data.value: Far inland a weakened typhoon can still bring days of heavy rain, to Hunan, Jiangxi or Guangxi; floods are often the biggest danger there.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Growing_Description
data.value: Over sea warmer than 26.5 °C the storm draws in more heat and strengthens, carried along by the winds round the subtropical high.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Land_Description
data.value: Cut off from the warm sea, the storm weakens quickly, but its rain spreads far inland.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Note
data.value: A simplified steering model: the subtropical high as a ridge, the westerlies north of it and the storm's own drift north-west, with growth over warm sea and decay over land. Real tracks also depend on troughs, other storms and the monsoon.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Over_Description
data.value: It has died out over land, left the map, or gone north into cold air and become an ordinary low. Click on the sea to start another one.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Sea_Description
data.value: It goes where the steering winds take it. Over cooler water further north it can no longer grow.

data.name: Typhoon_Track_Subtitle
data.value: Where typhoons go, and where they come ashore
