data.name: Volc_Chart_Bowen
data.value: Hot at the top; all solid at the dashed line

data.name: Volc_Chart_Cooling_Caption
data.value: Bowen's order: which mineral crystallises first

data.name: Volc_Chart_Cooling_Note
data.value: Each bar starts at the temperature its mineral begins to crystallise; the white line is the temperature now.

data.name: Volc_Chart_Cycle_Note
data.value: The arrows are the steps; the dashed one is a shortcut: rock pushed up and worn down again without melting. The step the followed grain is on lights up.

data.name: Volc_Chart_Eruption_Caption
data.value: Sticky and gassy: how it erupts

data.name: Volc_Chart_Eruption_Note
data.value: Drag the gold dot: stickier to the right, more water upwards. The white dots are real volcanoes.

data.name: Volc_Chart_Settling_Caption
data.value: Time to sink one metre in still water

data.name: Volc_Chart_Settling_Note
data.value: Real times, on a scale of powers of ten: clay sinks nearly 100,000 times more slowly than gravel.

data.name: Volc_Chart_Squeezing_Note
data.value: Dashed line: the usual 25 °C more for every kilometre down. Drag the gold dot to change the depth.

data.name: Volc_Cooling_Note
data.value: A slice 20 mm wide, as under a microscope; the cooling is sped up to seconds.

data.name: Volc_Cooling_Panel_Note
data.value: Slow cooling deep down gives big crystals; fast cooling at the surface gives small ones, or glass. 'Slow, then fast' gives big crystals in a fine background: porphyry.

data.name: Volc_CycleStat_Metamorphic
data.value: changed by heat and pressure: marble, schist

data.name: Volc_CycleStat_Sedimentary
data.value: from layers of bits: sandstone, shale, limestone

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Fact1
data.value: The top of Mount Everest is limestone that formed on a sea floor about 450 million years ago.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Fact2
data.value: The oldest known pieces of the Earth are tiny zircon crystals from Australia, about 4.4 billion years old.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Fact3
data.value: The world's rivers carry about 20 billion tonnes of sediment to the sea every year.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Fact4
data.value: A full trip round the rock cycle can take hundreds of millions of years, and many rocks never finish one.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Fact5
data.value: Michelangelo's David is carved from Carrara marble: limestone from an ancient sea, baked when the Alps' mountains were pushed up.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Note
data.value: A sketch, not to scale: one round of the cycle takes tens to hundreds of millions of years.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Panel_Note
data.value: Click a step or a rock in the picture to hear about it.

data.name: Volc_Cycle_Text
data.value: Igneous rock is worn into sediment, sediment hardens into sedimentary rock, heat and pressure turn it into metamorphic rock, and that melts into magma, which cools into igneous rock again. Rocks can also skip steps.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Fact1
data.value: About 1,350 volcanoes on land could erupt again; in a typical year 50 to 70 of them erupt.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Fact2
data.value: Most of the gas in magma is water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Fact3
data.value: Pinatubo's 1991 eruption put so much sulfur gas high into the sky that the whole world cooled by about half a degree for two years.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Fact4
data.value: Changbaishan's eruption in the year 946 was one of the biggest of the last 2,000 years; its ash fell as far away as Japan. Its caldera now holds Heaven Lake.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Fact5
data.value: Wudalianchi in Heilongjiang erupted from 1719 to 1721; its lava dammed a river into the five linked lakes that give it its name.

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Note
data.value: Depths below the ground and heights above it are drawn to different scales (see the ruler on the right).

data.name: Volc_Eruption_Panel_Note
data.value: More silica makes magma stickier (and cooler); more water means more gas. Runny magma lets its gas out gently; sticky magma traps it, and with enough gas it explodes.

data.name: Volc_Hint_Cooling
data.value: Click a crystal to name its mineral; drag sideways to run the cooling back and forth.

data.name: Volc_Hint_Cycle
data.value: Pick a grain to follow on the left-hand page; drag sideways to move it along.

data.name: Volc_Hint_Eruption
data.value: Drag sideways to run the eruption back and forth; click the vent to erupt now.

data.name: Volc_Hint_Settling
data.value: Click the river to pour in mud; drag the rock on top to bury the layers deeper.

data.name: Volc_Hint_Squeezing
data.value: Drag the sample or the press up and down to bury it deeper or shallower.

data.name: Volc_Magnifier_Fact1
data.value: The crystals in granite took tens to hundreds of thousands of years to grow.

data.name: Volc_Magnifier_Fact2
data.value: A freshly broken edge of obsidian is only a few nanometres thick, sharper than a steel scalpel.

data.name: Volc_Magnifier_Fact3
data.value: Rafts of floating pumice from undersea eruptions can drift across the ocean for months.

data.name: Volc_Magnifier_Fact4
data.value: Slate splits into thin sheets because all its tiny flakes lie the same way; it has been used for roofs and blackboards.

data.name: Volc_Magnifier_Fact5
data.value: Clay sinks so slowly that a muddy pond can stay cloudy for days after a storm.

data.name: Volc_Phase_Calm_Text
data.value: The chamber has let out its pressure. Steam still rises, the new lava cools into a layer, and the chamber slowly fills again.

data.name: Volc_Phase_Recharge_Text
data.value: Magma flows in from below. The pressure builds, the ground swells a little and small earthquakes crack the rock.

data.name: Volc_Phase_Rising_Text
data.value: Magma forces its way up the conduit. As the pressure on it falls, its water comes out as bubbles, which grow as it rises.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Basalt
data.value: Lava cooled in hours to days: tiny crystals, dark and heavy. It is the commonest rock at the Earth's surface.

data.name: Volc_RockText_BasaltGlass
data.value: Basalt lava quenched in water: black glass with only a few tiny crystals.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Dolerite
data.value: Basalt magma cooled in a thin sheet underground: medium-sized crystals, between gabbro and basalt.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Gabbro
data.value: The slowly cooled, coarse-grained twin of basalt: dark pyroxene, white feldspar and green olivine.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Gneiss
data.value: Above about 600 °C the minerals separate into light and dark bands, and the rock is still solid.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Granite
data.value: Cooled over hundreds of thousands of years deep underground: few crystals, but with time to grow big enough to see.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Limestone
data.value: Made of the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, glued together by calcite.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Marble
data.value: Limestone recrystallised by heat: interlocking calcite crystals, and the fossils are gone.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Microgranite
data.value: Cooled in a thin sheet of magma underground, in years to centuries: its crystals are smaller than granite's.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Migmatite
data.value: So hot that it has begun to melt: pockets of melt sit among the bands. Any hotter and it becomes magma.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Obsidian
data.value: Lava frozen in seconds to minutes: no time for crystals, just glass, black and sharp-edged.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Phyllite
data.value: A little hotter: the flakes have grown into fine mica that gives it a silky shine.

data.name: Volc_RockText_PorphyriticBasalt
data.value: Basalt with big olivine or feldspar crystals that grew before it erupted.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Porphyry
data.value: Big crystals grew slowly deep down, then the magma rose and the rest froze into a fine-grained background around them.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Pumice
data.value: Frothy lava frozen with its gas bubbles inside: so full of holes that it floats.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Quartzite
data.value: Sandstone heated until its quartz grains grow into each other and the gaps close: one of the hardest rocks.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Rhyolite
data.value: Granite magma cooled quickly at the surface: the same minerals, but in crystals too small to see.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Sandstone
data.value: Sand grains cemented together, with tiny gaps between them that can hold water or oil.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Schist
data.value: Hot enough for mica to grow big and shiny, and for garnets to grow among it.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Scoria
data.value: Basalt lava frozen around its gas bubbles: dark, rough and full of holes, but heavier than pumice.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Shale
data.value: Mud pressed into rock: flakes of clay too small to see, lying every which way.

data.name: Volc_RockText_Slate
data.value: Squeezed at about 200 to 330 °C: the flakes all lie one way, so it splits into thin, flat sheets.

data.name: Volc_Settling_Note
data.value: Sinking is sped up (clay takes days to sink a metre); burial squeezes the layers to scale.

data.name: Volc_Settling_Panel_Note
data.value: Pour a few times to build up layers, then bury them: from about 1.5 km down the grains are cemented into rock.

data.name: Volc_Squeezing_Note
data.value: A sample about a centimetre across, deep inside a continent, 25 °C warmer for every kilometre down.

data.name: Volc_Squeezing_Panel_Note
data.value: Shale becomes slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss in turn; sandstone becomes quartzite; limestone becomes marble.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_0
data.value: This piece of rock is gneiss, deep under the mountains and close to melting.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_1
data.value: It melts. The magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it starts to rise.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_2
data.value: It collects in the magma chamber under the volcano.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_3
data.value: The volcano erupts, and the magma pours out as lava.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_4
data.value: In the open air the lava cools within days into basalt, with tiny crystals.

data.name: Volc_Step_Magma_5
data.value: Rain starts to rot the new basalt into clay, and the next round begins.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_0
data.value: This speck starts in a basalt lava flow on the side of the volcano.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_1
data.value: Rain slowly rots the basalt, and its minerals turn into soft clay.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_2
data.value: The river carries the clay away as mud, making the water cloudy.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_3
data.value: Far out in the deep sea, where the water is still, the fine mud slowly settles.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_4
data.value: Buried under more layers, the mud is squeezed into shale.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_5
data.value: Buried deeper still, heated and squeezed, the shale becomes schist, full of shiny mica.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_6
data.value: Deep enough and hot enough, the rock melts into magma.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_7
data.value: The magma rises but stops underground, cooling slowly over a million years into granite.

data.name: Volc_Step_Mud_8
data.value: Over tens of millions of years the mountains rise and the rock above wears away, until the granite is at the top.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_0
data.value: This grain of quartz is part of the granite at the top of the mountain, pushed up from deep underground.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_1
data.value: Frost and rain loosen the granite. The feldspar rots to clay, but the hard quartz breaks free as a grain of sand.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_2
data.value: A stream picks it up and the river rolls it down towards the sea, rounding its corners on the way.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_3
data.value: At the coast the river slows, and the grain settles on the beach with millions of others.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_4
data.value: More sand and mud bury it. Squeezed, and glued by minerals, the sand becomes sandstone.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_5
data.value: Plates collide and fold the old sea floor up into the mountains. The sandstone is lifted into the open air again.

data.name: Volc_Step_Sand_6
data.value: Weathering frees the grain again: back to sand, ready for another round, without ever having melted.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_0
data.value: This shell belongs to a sea creature on the reef. It built it from calcium dissolved in the seawater.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_1
data.value: When the creature dies, its shell breaks up into shell sand on the sea floor.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_2
data.value: Buried and glued together, the shell sand becomes limestone.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_3
data.value: Hot magma rises beside it and bakes the limestone into marble.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_4
data.value: The mountains rise, and the marble ends up in a cliff, out in the rain.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_5
data.value: Rainwater is slightly acidic, so it slowly dissolves the marble, and the river carries the calcium back to the sea.

data.name: Volc_Step_Shell_6
data.value: In the sea, a new creature uses that calcium to build a new shell.

data.name: Volc_StyleText_Dome
data.value: Sticky magma that has lost its gas squeezes out slowly and piles up over the vent. Pieces break off as glowing avalanches.

data.name: Volc_StyleText_Hawaiian
data.value: Runny basalt with little gas: the bubbles slip out easily, throwing up lava fountains, and the lava runs far down the slopes.

data.name: Volc_StyleText_Plinian
data.value: Sticky magma full of gas: the froth tears apart into ash and gas, which roar up as a column tens of kilometres high.

data.name: Volc_StyleText_Strombolian
data.value: Runny magma with more gas: bubbles gather into big ones that burst at the top every few seconds, throwing out lava bombs.

data.name: Volc_StyleText_Vulcanian
data.value: Sticky magma with some gas plugs the vent until the pressure blasts it open: short explosions of ash and lava bombs.

data.name: Volc_Tank_Empty_Text
data.value: Click the river, or 'Pour in mud', to let a muddy river flow in.

data.name: Volc_Tank_Rock_Text
data.value: Minerals have filled the gaps and glued the grains: gravel is now conglomerate, sand sandstone, silt siltstone and clay shale.

data.name: Volc_Tank_Settled_Text
data.value: Each pour leaves a layer, coarse at the bottom and fine at the top. Pour again, or bury the layers.

data.name: Volc_Tank_Sinking_Text
data.value: Gravel and sand sink fast and land near the river mouth; silt and clay drift farther and take much longer.

data.name: Volc_Tank_Squeezed_Text
data.value: The weight of the rock above squeezes the water out of the gaps, and the layers get thinner.

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Caption
data.value: If all the water were one litre

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Note
data.value: The scale goes up ten times at each line. A drop from a dropper is about 0.05 mL: of the litre, all the world's rivers would be about a thirtieth of a drop.

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Caption
data.value: The parcel's temperature and dew point

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Note
data.value: Below the cloud the two lines close in; they meet at the cloud base and go up together. Dashed: the way down the far side of the mountain.

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Caption
data.value: How much vapour air can hold

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Note
data.value: The curve doubles about every 10 °C. The white dot is the landscape's sea-level air today; the slider warms or cools its world.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Back_Description
data.value: Without rain on the way up, the air arrives as warm and as humid as it set off. Only air that has rained out its water arrives warmer: that is the foehn.

data.name: Water_Cloud_DescendingBack_Description
data.value: No rain fell, so any cloud droplets evaporate again as the air sinks and warms: it comes down just as it went up.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Descending_Description
data.value: Having rained out its water, the air sinks down the far side and warms by about 10 °C per kilometre all the way.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact1
data.value: Rising air cools by about 10 °C per kilometre until it reaches its dew point; inside the cloud it cools more slowly, about 4 to 7 °C per km, because condensing vapour gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact2
data.value: You can estimate the cloud base: about 125 m for every degree between the air's temperature and its dew point. On humid days the clouds are low.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact3
data.value: Cloud droplets are tiny, about 0.02 mm across; one raindrop holds about a million of them.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact4
data.value: Outside the tropics most rain starts as snow high in the cloud and melts on the way down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact5
data.value: Air that rains out on one side of a mountain comes down the other side warmer and drier: the foehn in the Alps, the chinook in the Rockies. Deserts lie behind many mountain ranges.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Foehn_Description
data.value: The air arrives warmer and drier than it set off: it kept the heat its condensing vapour gave back, but lost the water as rain. This is a foehn wind, and the land here lies in a rain shadow.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Freezing_Description
data.value: Above the 0 °C line the droplets stay liquid at first (supercooled), but ice crystals start to form and grow at their expense.

data.name: Water_Cloud_InCloud_Description
data.value: The air has cooled to its dew point and cannot hold all its vapour: it condenses into droplets. From here it cools more slowly, as the condensing water gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_NoCloud_Description
data.value: The air never cooled to its dew point: it was too dry for the height it was lifted to. Raise the humidity to bring the cloud base down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Note
data.value: Heights are to scale; the land is squeezed sideways. The parcel is one lump of air followed as it rises, not mixing with the air around it.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Raining_Description
data.value: The cloud is deep enough for droplets to grow into raindrops, or into snowflakes that melt on the way down. Water that evaporated far away falls back.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Rising_Description
data.value: The air rises into lower pressure, expands and cools by about 10 °C every kilometre. Its dew point falls only about 2 °C per km, so the two close in.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Snowing_Description
data.value: The air near the ground is cold enough that the snowflakes do not melt before they land.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Subtitle
data.value: Air that rises cools, until its vapour condenses into a cloud

data.name: Water_Cloud_ThinCloud_Description
data.value: The cloud is too thin for its droplets to grow big enough to fall. Lift the air higher, or make it more humid.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact1
data.value: Every year about 500,000 km³ of water evaporates, as much as a metre of water over the whole Earth, and the same amount falls back as rain and snow.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact2
data.value: About 90 % of the water that evaporates from the sea falls straight back onto the sea; the rest is blown over land and comes back by rivers and groundwater.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact3
data.value: A water molecule stays in the air for about 9 days on average, in a river a couple of weeks, in the ocean about 3,000 years, and in deep groundwater or Antarctic ice for up to hundreds of thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact4
data.value: Plants move a great deal of water: a big tree can give off over a hundred litres on a summer day, and transpiration is more than half of all the water rising from land.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact5
data.value: Warmer air holds about 7 % more water vapour for every degree, so a warmer world has heavier downpours, more of its snow falls as rain, and the snow line moves up the mountains.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Note
data.value: Heights are real but the land is squeezed sideways: the picture is a few hundred kilometres across. Trees and the river are drawn much bigger than real.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Subtitle
data.value: Water goes round: from the sea into the air, onto the land, and back

data.name: Water_Flow_OceanPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow on the sea

data.name: Water_Hint_Cloud
data.value: Change the air's temperature and humidity on the left page and watch the cloud base move.

data.name: Water_Hint_Cycle
data.value: Click a label to light up that part of the cycle, or follow one drop all the way round.

data.name: Water_Hint_Stores_Flows
data.value: The dots run along each flow; the wider the band, the more water each year.

data.name: Water_Hint_Stores_Spheres
data.value: Switch the picture to the yearly flows to see how water moves between sea, air and land.

data.name: Water_Leg_Condensation_Description
data.value: The air carrying it rises and cools to its dew point; the drop condenses onto a speck of dust and becomes a cloud droplet.

data.name: Water_Leg_Evaporation_Description
data.value: Warmed by the Sun at the surface, the drop escapes into the air as vapour: invisible, and leaving its salt behind.

data.name: Water_Leg_Groundwater_Description
data.value: Now groundwater, the drop creeps through the rock toward the sea, perhaps only metres a year. Shallow groundwater takes years to centuries; deep groundwater thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Leg_Infiltration_Description
data.value: The drop soaks into the soil and trickles down through cracks and gaps until it reaches the water table.

data.name: Water_Leg_Ocean_Description
data.value: The drop is one of some 1.3 billion km³ of sea water. On average water stays in the ocean for over 3,000 years before it evaporates.

data.name: Water_Leg_Rain_Description
data.value: About a million cloud droplets have merged into one raindrop, heavy enough to fall. From a cloud a couple of kilometres up it lands in a few minutes.

data.name: Water_Leg_River_Description
data.value: Streams join into a river that carries the drop back to the sea. A river holds its water only a couple of weeks on average.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowfall_Description
data.value: Above the 0 °C line the water freezes onto an ice crystal and falls slowly as a snowflake onto the mountain.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowmelt_Description
data.value: In spring the Sun melts the snow, and the drop trickles down the slope toward a stream.

data.name: Water_Leg_Snowpack_Description
data.value: The drop waits in the snow through the winter. In a glacier it could wait for centuries; deep in Antarctic ice, for hundreds of thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Leg_Transpiration_Description
data.value: Through a tiny pore in the leaf the drop escapes as vapour. Over land, plants send more water into the air than the soil and lakes do.

data.name: Water_Leg_Transport_Description
data.value: As vapour, the drop travels with the wind, often hundreds or thousands of kilometres. Water stays in the air about 9 days on average.

data.name: Water_Leg_Uptake_Description
data.value: Roots take the drop up from the soil; it rises through the trunk to a leaf within days.

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cloud_Choice1
data.value: The vapour condenses into a cloud

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cycle_Choice1
data.value: It cools, and rain or snow falls

data.name: Water_Lesson_Cycle_Choice2
data.value: It warms up, and the clouds vanish

data.name: Water_Process_Condensation_Description
data.value: Rising air expands and cools. Once it cools to its dew point, vapour condenses onto tiny specks of dust, salt or smoke as cloud droplets about 0.02 mm across, giving back the heat the Sun put in when the water evaporated.

data.name: Water_Process_Evaporation_Amount
data.value: about 413,000 km³ from the sea, 73,000 km³ from land and plants

data.name: Water_Process_Evaporation_Description
data.value: Sunlight gives water molecules at the surface enough energy to escape into the air as invisible vapour. The salt stays behind, so rain is fresh water. Most evaporation, about 85 %, is from the oceans.

data.name: Water_Process_Groundwater_Amount
data.value: most of it feeds rivers and lakes; a few percent seeps straight into the sea

data.name: Water_Process_Groundwater_Description
data.value: Below the water table, water creeps through the rock, often only metres a year, toward rivers, lakes and the sea. Wells and springs tap it. It is the largest store of liquid fresh water by far.

data.name: Water_Process_Infiltration_Amount
data.value: about 13,000 km³ refills groundwater, a tenth of the rain on land

data.name: Water_Process_Infiltration_Description
data.value: Rain soaks into the soil. Some stays there for plants; some trickles on down through gaps in the soil and rock to the water table, below which every gap is full of water.

data.name: Water_Process_Overview_Description
data.value: The Sun warms the sea and water evaporates as invisible vapour. The wind carries it; rising air cools and the vapour condenses into clouds; rain and snow fall; water runs back to the sea in rivers or slowly through the ground. Nothing is lost: the same water has gone round for billions of years.

data.name: Water_Process_Precipitation_Amount
data.value: about 373,000 km³ on the sea, 113,000 km³ on land

data.name: Water_Process_Precipitation_Description
data.value: Cloud droplets merge, or ice crystals grow at their expense, until they are heavy enough to fall. Below the 0 °C line it reaches the ground as rain, above it as snow. Air pushed up a mountain rains on the near side and leaves the far side dry.

data.name: Water_Process_Runoff_Amount
data.value: about 40,000 km³ back to the sea, with groundwater

data.name: Water_Process_Runoff_Description
data.value: Water that does not soak in or evaporate runs downhill in streams that join into rivers and flow to the sea. A drop spends on average only a couple of weeks in a river.

data.name: Water_Process_Snowmelt_Amount
data.value: the main water supply of about a sixth of the world's people

data.name: Water_Process_Snowmelt_Description
data.value: Snow and glaciers store water through the winter and let it go in spring and summer. Rivers such as the Yangtze, the Ganges and the Indus get much of their summer water from snow and ice far upstream.

data.name: Water_Process_Sublimation_Amount
data.value: a small share worldwide; on dry high mountains a fifth of the snow or more

data.name: Water_Process_Sublimation_Description
data.value: In dry, sunny, windy air, snow and ice can turn straight into vapour without melting first. It takes much more energy than melting, but high on dry mountains it removes a good part of the snow.

data.name: Water_Process_Transpiration_Amount
data.value: about 45,000 km³, some 60 % of what evaporates from land

data.name: Water_Process_Transpiration_Description
data.value: Plants draw water up from the soil through their roots and stems and give it off as vapour through tiny pores in their leaves. It cools them, like sweating, and pulls more water up behind it.

data.name: Water_Process_Transport_Amount
data.value: about 40,000 km³ from over the sea to over land

data.name: Water_Process_Transport_Description
data.value: Water vapour is invisible. Winds carry it far from where it evaporated, much of it inland from the sea. Without this, rain would fall only over the sea and the land would be desert.

data.name: Water_Stat_RainDepth_Value
data.value: about a metre of rain and snow a year

data.name: Water_Store_Land
data.value: Land: ice, groundwater, lakes, soil, rivers

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Description
data.value: The bands show how much water moves each year. The air gains as much as it loses, and so do the sea and the land: the vapour carried over land each year comes back by rivers and groundwater.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact1
data.value: Each year about 413,000 km³ evaporates from the sea and 73,000 km³ from land and plants; 373,000 km³ falls back on the sea and 113,000 km³ on land.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact2
data.value: The 40,000 km³ of vapour blown from sea to land each year comes back down rivers and through the ground; the Amazon alone carries about a sixth of it.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact3
data.value: On land almost two thirds of the rain and snow goes back into the air from soil, lakes and plants; only about a third runs off to the sea.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact4
data.value: The air's water is replaced about every 9 days: 12,900 km³ in the air, against about 500,000 km³ falling out of it each year.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Fact5
data.value: The Sun drives it all: evaporating water uses about half the sunlight the ground and sea absorb, and the heat comes back out where the vapour condenses into clouds.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Note
data.value: Band widths are to scale with the yearly amounts (Trenberth and others, 2007); the stores are from the USGS.

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Subtitle
data.value: Each year about a metre of water rises from the whole Earth, and falls again

data.name: Water_Stores_Flows_Title
data.value: Where the water goes each year

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Description
data.value: The big ball is all of Earth's water: oceans, ice, groundwater, lakes, air, everything. The middle one is the liquid fresh water: groundwater, lakes, swamps and rivers. The tiny one is the fresh water in lakes and rivers, the water we can use most easily.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact1
data.value: Gathered into one ball, all of Earth's water would be only about 1,380 km across, about a ninth of Earth's diameter.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact2
data.value: Over 96 % of it is salty sea water. Of the 2.5 % that is fresh, about 69 % is frozen in ice caps and glaciers and about 30 % is underground.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact3
data.value: All the fresh water in the world's lakes and rivers would fit in a ball 56 km across. Lake Baikal alone holds about a fifth of the unfrozen fresh water on the surface.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact4
data.value: The air holds only about 13,000 km³ of water: if it all fell at once, it would cover Earth about 2.5 cm deep.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Fact5
data.value: The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 90 % of the world's ice; if it all melted the sea would rise by about 58 m.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Note
data.value: Earth and the balls on it are to the same scale; on the right the same balls are enlarged.

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Subtitle
data.value: All of Earth's water would make a surprisingly small ball

data.name: Water_Stores_Spheres_Title
data.value: All the water in three balls

data.name: Waves_Diagram_HearsTwo
data.value: Hears {0} Hz and {1} Hz at once

data.name: Waves_Diagram_TankSwing
data.value: How far the water rises and falls: bright a lot, dark not at all

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Approaching_Description
data.value: The source chases the waves it sent ahead and bunches them up, so more of them reach you each second: you hear {0} Hz, higher than its own 440 Hz.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Boom_Description
data.value: The cone sweeps over you: waves sent out over a long stretch of the way pile up on its edge and arrive all at once, as one loud bang.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Fact1
data.value: Christian Doppler predicted it in 1842. In 1845 Buys Ballot tested it with trumpeters on a moving train and musicians on the platform naming the notes.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Fact2
data.value: A car passing at about 120 km/h drops by about three and a half semitones, from about 489 Hz to 400 Hz for a 440 Hz horn: the familiar 'neee-owww'.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Fact3
data.value: Police radar, weather radar and ultrasound scans of blood flow all measure speed from the Doppler shift of the waves bounced back.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Fact4
data.value: Light does it too: the light of distant galaxies is shifted to red because they are moving away from us. This is how we know the universe is expanding.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Fact5
data.value: A supersonic plane drags its boom along the whole way, not just once: everyone it flies over hears the bang. A whip's crack is a tiny sonic boom from its tip.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Note
data.value: A road seen from above, 5× slower than real. Each ring stands for every 22nd wave the source sends out, one each 1/20 s.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Passing_Description
data.value: What reaches you now was sent out as the source went past you, neither coming nor going: you hear {0} Hz, near its own pitch, and falling fast.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Receding_Description
data.value: The source runs away from the waves it sends back and stretches them out, so fewer reach you each second: you hear {0} Hz, lower than 440 Hz.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Silent_Description
data.value: The source outruns its own sound. It may already be close, but you hear nothing until the cone behind it sweeps over you.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Still_Description
data.value: The rings are circles round it, as close together on every side: everyone hears its own 440 Hz.

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Subtitle
data.value: Coming closer it sounds higher, going away lower

data.name: Waves_Doppler_Two_Description
data.value: After the bang you hear both the sound it made going away and the sound it made coming, and that one arrives backwards: its last part first.

data.name: Waves_DragHint_Doppler
data.value: Drag the listener to hear the pass from somewhere else.

data.name: Waves_DragHint_Ripple
data.value: Drag the probe across the water to see how the two waves meet there.

data.name: Waves_DragHint_Slits
data.value: Drag the probe (right of the slits) to see how much farther it is from one slit than the other.

data.name: Waves_Lesson_Doppler_Choice3
data.value: The same note all the way

data.name: Waves_Lesson_Slits_Choice3
data.value: Half of the stripes are left

data.name: Waves_MachChart_Caption
data.value: Pitch straight ahead and straight behind

data.name: Waves_MachChart_Note
data.value: Ahead the pitch climbs without limit as the source nears the speed of sound; behind it only falls to a third even at twice the speed of sound.

data.name: Waves_PitchChart_Caption
data.value: What the listener hears through the pass

data.name: Waves_PitchChart_Note
data.value: The pitch falls as the source goes past, fastest when it is closest. Faster than sound there is silence, then the bang, then two sounds at once.

data.name: Waves_ProbeChart_Note
data.value: Blue is how high A's wave lifts the water, pink B's, gold the two together, which is what the water really does. In step they add up; opposite they cancel.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Between_Description
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther, neither a whole number nor a half: the waves partly add up, and the water rises and falls, but not the most.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Between_DescriptionOpposite
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther, neither a whole number nor a half: the waves partly add up, and the water rises and falls, but not the most.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Fact1
data.value: Noise-cancelling headphones listen to the noise and play the same sound turned upside down: crest meets trough and the noise mostly cancels.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Fact2
data.value: Two loudspeakers playing the same tone do this with sound: walk across the room and the tone grows loud and quiet again and again.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Fact3
data.value: No energy is lost on the still lines: what is missing there goes into the lines of big waves on either side.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Fact4
data.value: Move the dippers apart or make the waves shorter and there are more still lines, closer together: about 2d/λ of them.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Fact5
data.value: The colours of soap bubbles and oil on a wet road are interference too: light reflected from the top and bottom of a very thin film.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_InStep_Description
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther than the other, close to a whole number: the waves arrive in step, crest on crest and trough on trough, and the water heaves the most.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_InStep_DescriptionOpposite
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther, close to a whole number and a half. The dippers move opposite ways, and that half wavelength puts them back in step: the water heaves the most.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Note
data.value: A ripple tank seen from above, 10× slower than real. Bright is a crest, dark a trough.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_OutOfStep_Description
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther, close to a whole number and a half: one wave's crest arrives with the other's trough, they cancel, and the water hardly moves.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_OutOfStep_DescriptionOpposite
data.value: Here one dipper is {0} wavelengths farther, close to a whole number. But the dippers move opposite ways, so crest still meets trough: they cancel and the water hardly moves.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Single_Description
data.value: Only A is moving: its rings spread out evenly and weaken as they go, and nowhere is the water still. Switch B on and watch the two waves meet.

data.name: Waves_Ripple_Subtitle
data.value: Crest on crest adds up, crest on trough cancels out

data.name: Waves_ScreenChart_Note
data.value: The stripes are λL/d apart: longer light, a farther screen or closer slits spread them out. Each slit on its own makes the broad glow they sit under.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Between_Description
data.value: This point is {0} wavelengths farther from one slit than the other: the beams partly add up, neither bright nor dark.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Bright_Description
data.value: This point is {0} wavelengths farther from one slit than the other, close to a whole number: the two beams arrive in step and add up to a bright stripe.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Dark_Description
data.value: This point is {0} wavelengths farther from one slit than the other, close to a whole number and a half: crest meets trough, the beams cancel, and light added to light gives darkness.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Fact1
data.value: Thomas Young first showed it in the early 1800s. Stripes of light and dark could only come from waves, against Newton's view that light was made of particles.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Fact2
data.value: Green light's wavelength is about half a thousandth of a millimetre, around a hundredth of the width of a hair. That is why the slits must be so close and the screen far.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Fact3
data.value: Sent through one at a time, single photons or electrons still build up the same stripes dot by dot: each one goes through both slits as a wave.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Fact4
data.value: The rainbow on a CD comes from the same effect: its tracks, 1.6 thousandths of a millimetre apart, act like thousands of slits.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Fact5
data.value: Two ordinary lamps never make stripes together: their light keeps changing its rhythm at random, far faster than the eye can follow, so any stripes jump about and blur. A laser keeps its rhythm.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Note
data.value: Not to scale: the light's waves are drawn about ten thousand times bigger, so the stripes fan out far wider. The chart on the left-hand page shows the real stripes on the screen.

data.name: Waves_Slits_One_Description
data.value: With one slit covered, the screen shows only a glow, brightest in the middle. The stripes came from the two slits' light adding up and cancelling, which only waves do.

data.name: Waves_Slits_Subtitle
data.value: Light is a wave too: two slits make bright and dark stripes

data.name: Waves_Slits_White_Description
data.value: Each colour makes its own stripes, violet closest together and red farthest apart. In the middle every colour is bright, so it is white; farther out they slip apart into coloured stripes that soon blur together.

data.name: Waves_Slits_White_Title
data.value: White light: a white middle, rainbow edges

data.name: Waves_Stat_Ahead_None
data.value: nothing: the sound can't get ahead

data.name: Waves_Stat_InGlow
data.value: Bright stripes in the middle glow
